item.title: Christmas Greetings and Christian Hostility
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
An atheist accepts a Christmas greeting. A Christian announces that goodwill can go up your ass. Our pal the Godless Gardener has found the season’s most revealing Christmas message.

December is upon us, and the seasonal grievance department is already open for business.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

In a clip featured in the Godless Gardener’s “Happy Holidays Crashout,” a woman makes an announcement: she will be saying “Merry Christmas.” Nobody in the exchange presented has forbidden this. Nobody has confiscated her decorations or demanded that she renounce Jesus at the checkout. Nevertheless, she has prepared a public statement.

People offering “Happy holidays,” she explains, can “shove it up your ass.” Her explanation follows: “this is a Christ-filled home.”

The juxtaposition requires very little editorial assistance. She provides the religious credential and the contempt in the same breath.

Peace on Earth. Read the exclusions.

Her declaration becomes even more revealing when she explains that she will answer a Hanukkah greeting with thanks and “Merry Christmas,” adding that this is about as diverse as she intends to get.

Reciprocal greetings can be perfectly warm. A Jewish person wishing a Christian a happy Hanukkah and receiving a merry Christmas in return need not be a diplomatic incident. People can share the celebrations that mean something to them. But this woman frames the exchange as the outer boundary of her willingness to acknowledge difference. She wants credit for approaching that boundary without crossing it.

She has turned an opportunity for kindness into a demonstration of how little accommodation she owes anyone else.

The Gardener’s sharpest response is also his simplest: “Happy holidays includes Christmas.”

It does. The greeting leaves room for her celebration and for somebody else’s. Her Christmas has not disappeared. It has acquired neighbors.

That is what makes this particular performance so useful. The inclusive greeting already accommodates her. She responds with hostility anyway. The apparent requirement is that the greeting single out her holiday before she will accept the goodwill behind it.

Christmas must be named. Other people can take a number.

A seasonal greeting becomes a small test of hierarchy: whose celebration receives explicit recognition, whose language sets the terms, and who must absorb the insult when those expectations go unmet. The woman announces her preferred answer before anyone has even addressed her.

There is agency here. She chooses the insult. She chooses to connect it to her Christianity. She chooses to make that connection public.

Treating that performance as an innocent misunderstanding would erase the most obvious fact about it: she understands that people are offering a greeting and has prepared a hostile response. The contempt is deliberate enough to warrant its own announcement.

This is the vitriolic Christianity worth exposing: the version in which declaring your devotion gives you permission to treat other people badly, and their objection becomes further evidence that your faith is under attack. Once that arrangement is accepted, accountability becomes almost impossible. The believer supplies the aggression and claims the wounded status.

The Gardener offers a much more ordinary account of living alongside other people. He is an atheist. When someone wishes him a merry Christmas, he thanks them. He can receive greetings associated with other religions without worrying that courtesy will alter his convictions.

His atheism survives the encounter. Presumably, a Christian faith capable of surviving centuries could endure a cashier using a plural noun.

The difference in the clip is practical. One person can recognize goodwill across a religious boundary. The other announces that goodwill arriving in the wrong words deserves abuse. We can judge those choices without pretending the entire religious identity of either speaker explains everything about them.

Nor do we need to establish who counts as a “real Christian” before holding a Christian accountable. That theological escape hatch is remarkably convenient: the religion receives credit for every act of generosity while its public aggressors are written out of the membership register.

She invokes Christ to explain herself. That makes the use she is making of Christianity a legitimate subject of criticism. Anyone who considers her conduct a betrayal of their faith can say so. Their disagreement does not undo her attempt to recruit that faith as an alibi.

One clip cannot count how many Christians behave this way. It can show the behavior clearly, and it gives us a precise question of responsibility: what happens when religious belonging is offered as an excuse for hostility?

The answer cannot be that everyone else must become more accommodating of the hostility.

Mutual tolerance depends on people accepting one another’s equal right to exist, celebrate, speak, and decline participation. It asks no one to profess a creed they reject. A Christian can say “Merry Christmas.” A Jewish person can say “Happy Hanukkah.” An atheist can enjoy the lights, exchange presents, or ignore the whole production.

Nobody acquires the right to make strangers affirm their religious precedence. And nobody owes an indulgent smile to someone who responds to a friendly greeting with an insult.

This matters because the demand so often travels in one direction. The person issuing the insult expects deference to her convictions; the person receiving it is expected to respect those convictions by swallowing the abuse. The greeting becomes an examination, and only the religious aggressor gets to grade it.

We should refuse that arrangement. Religious freedom protects her ability to practice her faith. Her attempt to dress contempt in sacred language remains open to criticism, ridicule, and rejection.

There is no obligation to romanticize the cruelty because it has a Christmas soundtrack.

The Gardener’s clip also exposes how unnecessary the performance is. She could celebrate Christmas. She could enjoy her home, her faith, and the people she loves. A stranger wishing her happiness need take up no more than a pleasant second of her day.

Instead, she has made room in the celebration for a preemptive insult and invited an audience to admire her resolve.

That is an impoverished way to approach a season supposedly devoted to generosity. Every unfamiliar greeting becomes another chance to demonstrate refusal. Every acknowledgment of someone else becomes a concession to be resisted.

Let her say “Merry Christmas.” Let her decorate every available surface and celebrate with complete religious conviction. The rest of us retain the same freedom to speak, celebrate, and belong.

And when someone tells you to shove your goodwill up your ass, take the statement seriously. She has explained how she intends to treat you. The reference to Christ does not soften it.

Happy holidays.

Christmas is included. Her permission is unnecessary

Sources

  • Godless Gardener — Happy Holidays Crashout: the woman’s opening declaration, approximately 0:00–0:26; the Gardener’s response, approximately 0:27–2:15. Quotations and discussion are based on the supplied transcript.

item.title: The GOP’s War on Reading
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
America has a literacy problem. Republican leaders are restricting books, dismantling federal education capacity, and treating independent expertise as an enemy.

A teacher describes seventh- and eighth-graders struggling with basic spelling, punctuation, and writing. She wants them to read. Her principal, she says, has banned her entire classroom library.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

She offers to document the books’ suitability. She spends an unpaid day doing it. Then, according to her account, the restrictions shift again: even middle-school books are unacceptable. Students face seventh- and eighth-grade assessments while being permitted books pitched at third- and fourth-grade levels.

Her anger is entirely intelligible. She is being held responsible for an outcome while someone above her obstructs the work required to achieve it.

Republican officials have passed laws restricting school books. The Trump administration dismissed federal complaints about book removals and branded the issue a hoax. It ordered steps toward closing the Department of Education and began cutting its workforce. Across other agencies, it has displaced scientific advisers and dismantled environmental protections.

The accusation is straightforward: confronted with a population that needs more support to read, evaluate evidence, and exercise independent judgment, Republican leaders have repeatedly chosen policies that restrict access to knowledge and weaken the institutions responsible for providing it.

They did not invent every cause of America’s literacy crisis. They are responsible for what they choose to do about it.

First, read the evidence

Sabrina Cruz’s Answer in Progress video makes a distinction that political commentary too often bulldozes: difficulty reading and hostility to intellectual life are different problems.

A person struggling to understand a document needs support. A politician who understands the evidence and chooses to suppress it deserves scrutiny. Confusing them turns an institutional indictment into another opportunity to humiliate people whom institutions have already failed.

The measurements also matter.

The 2024 National Assessment of Educational Progress found that approximately 40 percent of fourth-graders and a third of eighth-graders scored below its Basic reading benchmark. Average reading scores fell in both grades compared with 2022. The National Assessment Governing Board explicitly describes a decline that began before the pandemic.

Those findings establish serious educational failure. They do not establish that every student below NAEP Proficient cannot read. The assessment’s categories describe different levels of performance; collapsing them into a binary produces a more sensational headline and a less accurate account.

Adult results are troubling, too. The National Center for Education Statistics reports that the proportion of American adults ages 16–65 performing at Level 1 or below in literacy rose from 19 percent in 2017 to 28 percent in 2023. That is a specific finding from a specific assessment, rather than a license to declare half the country incapable of thought.

The chronology rules out an easy partisan fairy tale. Trump’s second administration cannot have caused test results collected before it took office. Poverty, instructional failures, disrupted schooling, absenteeism, and changes in how people encounter information all belong in the investigation.

The political charge concerns the response: officials inherited a serious problem and chose to remove books, diminish oversight, and attack expertise.

The books really are being removed

PEN America recorded 6,870 instances of school book bans during the 2024–2025 school year. Florida accounted for 2,304, Texas for 1,781, and Tennessee for 1,622.

Together, those three Republican-led states accounted for roughly 83 percent of the recorded instances.

PEN’s subsequent reporting puts the 2025–2026 total at nearly 12,000 instances, its highest annual tally since tracking began in 2021.

These figures need their definitions attached. An instance is not a unique title: the same book can be restricted in multiple places. PEN’s tracking also includes temporary removals and restrictions, rather than counting only permanent prohibitions.

That distinction does not make an inaccessible book available to a child who wants to read it.

Florida’s legislative record shows how restriction becomes routine. The state Senate’s summary of the 2023 HB 1069 explains that materials alleged to contain specified sexual content must be suspended while an objection is resolved.

An allegation can therefore interrupt access before the review is complete.

Selecting books for a school library requires professional judgment. A system that makes an accusation sufficient to suspend access creates a different incentive: removal becomes the immediate administrative response, while defending access requires additional work.

The teacher’s account cannot prove that this particular law governed her classroom. It illustrates the burden such systems can impose: an educator spending time justifying books while students wait.

And “parental rights” offers no adequate defense for giving one family’s objection authority over everybody else’s reading.

A parent choosing a book for their own child exercises a family decision. A government restricting that book for other families exercises state power. The children whose parents want access have parents, too.

Washington’s answer: call it a hoax

On January 24, 2025, the Department of Education announced that it had dismissed 11 complaints related to school book removals, was dismissing six additional pending allegations, and would eliminate the book-ban coordinator’s role.

Its announcement was titled “U.S. Department of Education Ends Biden’s Book Ban Hoax.”

The administration described the removals as legitimate decisions about inappropriate material and rejected the civil-rights rationale for federal intervention.

That position deserves to be stated accurately. Dismissing a complaint does not establish that every challenged removal violated federal law. Neither does calling the controversy a hoax establish that students retained access to the books.

The administration’s political choice was unmistakable: withdraw this avenue of federal scrutiny and publicly vindicate the officials making the removals.

A government concerned about literacy could investigate how restrictions affect access, instructional time, and students’ opportunities to read. This government announced that the controversy itself was fraudulent.

The shelves do not refill because a press office changes the vocabulary.

Dismantling the department while invoking failure

On March 20, 2025, Trump signed an executive order directing the education secretary to take steps, within the law, to facilitate the Department of Education’s closure.

The order invoked poor reading and mathematics results as evidence against the federal education bureaucracy.

There is an extraordinary sleight of hand here. Education is already primarily a state and local responsibility. The department’s own explanation says so. Its authority does not amount to running every classroom or prescribing a national curriculum.

Federal responsibilities include administering assistance, enforcing civil-rights protections, and supporting education research and statistics. Those functions matter precisely because local resources and local treatment are unequal.

The department had already announced a workforce reduction on March 11, 2025. A June 2026 inspector general review reported staffing changes across 16 of its 17 offices and an overall workforce reduction of at least 40 percent.

The distinction between dismantling and completed abolition matters. The department continued to exist, and in October 2026 it reported that interagency agreements had routed more than $3.4 billion in grants through partner agencies. Transferring administration does not, by itself, establish that those grants disappeared.

But the administration’s own record establishes an ongoing effort to break up the institution. Its consequences deserve scrutiny beyond the slogans.

The Government Accountability Office found that about half the Office for Civil Rights staff had been placed on paid administrative leave in March 2025, and seven of its twelve regional offices closed. Those personnel actions were later reversed: affected staff were recalled, and the office’s reduction-in-force actions were rescinded in early January 2026.

That reversal belongs in the account. So does GAO’s finding that the department had failed to document a comprehensive assessment of costs and savings. Paying affected staff while they were not working may have cost up to $38 million.

This is a remarkable performance from officials advertising efficiency: sideline workers, incur substantial costs, reverse the personnel action, and fail to demonstrate the promised savings.

Children struggling to read require sustained institutional competence. They received a demolition campaign.

The people struggling to read are not the villains

In his 2016 Nevada victory speech, Trump declared: “I love the poorly educated.”

The context matters. He was celebrating support across demographic groups, including both highly and poorly educated voters. He did not say “I love illiteracy.” Education credentials and reading ability are not interchangeable.

The quotation alone cannot establish an intention to keep people uneducated.

The policy record carries the accusation.

It is perfectly possible to respect people denied educational opportunities while condemning politicians who exploit resentment toward educators and experts. Indeed, respect requires refusing to treat educational deprivation as a natural condition that people should simply endure.

A struggling reader deserves resources, time, and dignity. An official restricting those resources deserves accountability.

Sneering at the reader lets the official escape.

The assault on expertise extends beyond schools

Scientific literacy involves learning how claims are tested, how uncertainty is handled, and why evidence can outweigh personal conviction.

That makes the treatment of scientific institutions relevant to the same political argument.

On June 9, 2025, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. removed all 17 sitting members of the federal Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. The administration presented the wholesale replacement as restoring trust.

Its announcement also complained that existing appointments would otherwise have prevented the administration from selecting a committee majority until 2028.

That is a revealing explanation for an action advertised as scientific renewal: the existing membership obstructed the incoming administration’s control.

Climate policy supplies another example. In February 2026, the Environmental Protection Agency finalized the rescission of the greenhouse-gas endangerment finding and repealed the associated motor-vehicle greenhouse-gas standards. The agency framed its action around statutory authority and deregulation.

An administration can change a legal interpretation. It cannot legislate greenhouse gases out of atmospheric physics. The IPCC’s scientific assessment attributes observed global warming unequivocally to human activities, principally greenhouse-gas emissions.

Across these examples, the recurring political demand is that independent institutions yield to executive preference. Libraries must accommodate ideological objections. Education oversight must retreat. Scientific bodies must be reconstituted. Regulatory protections must give way.

Each action has its own legal and factual questions. Together, they reveal a governing movement repeatedly hostile to institutions capable of challenging its claims.

We already have evidence that investment matters

Any honest indictment must include Mississippi.

Its Republican-led government pursued literacy reforms involving teacher training, reading coaches, assessment, and intervention. State education records describe deploying specialist coaches and providing intensive training in the science of reading. Its fourth-grade reading performance improved substantially over the following decade.

That does not make every component of its policy beyond criticism, nor does a rising ranking prove which intervention produced which gain.

It demonstrates that Republican officials can choose sustained educational investment.

That makes censorship and institutional demolition harder to excuse. There is a practical alternative, including one implemented under Republican leadership: support teachers, identify difficulties, provide instruction, and maintain the effort.

Teaching children to decode words and ensuring they have books worth reading are complementary obligations.

A phonics initiative does not excuse censorship. A library cannot substitute for effective instruction. Children need both.

Hold the people making these choices responsible

We do not need to invent a secret memorandum ordering Americans to become less literate.

The public record is sufficient: laws restricting access to books; federal officials dismissing scrutiny of removals; an executive order pursuing the education department’s closure; large workforce cuts; scientific institutions subjected to political control.

The evidence does not assign every lost reading point to the Republican Party. It assigns responsibility for specific decisions made in the face of a known educational emergency.

The democratic danger follows from those choices. People need access to information and the skills to interrogate it—to read the legislation, examine the evidence, recognize the contradiction, and challenge the official demanding obedience.

Republican leaders are making that work harder while presenting themselves as children’s protectors.

The teacher in that video understands the immediate obscenity: students are being judged for outcomes adults are obstructing.

Put the responsibility where it belongs. Fund effective instruction. Protect libraries. Defend independent research and enforce students’ rights. Make the officials restricting knowledge answer for the opportunities they take away.

A party that removes books while lamenting reading failure deserves an accusation, not another opportunity to blame the children.

Sources

Videos and the teacher’s account

  • Answer in Progress — Sabrina Cruz’s literacy investigation. Discussed using the supplied transcript.

  • Teacher’s account as circulated in the reaction upload. The supplied transcript supports attribution of her statements, rather than independent verification of school policy.

  • Reporting identifying @wickedwomenauthor as the teacher’s original account.

Literacy measurements

  • National Assessment Governing Board — 2024 reading results and the decline predating the pandemic.

  • NCES — 2023 adult literacy results and comparisons with 2017.

Book restrictions

  • PEN America — 2024–2025 totals and state breakdown.

  • PEN America — book-ban indexes, including nearly 12,000 instances in 2025–2026.

  • PEN America — analysis of the normalization of school book censorship.

  • Florida Senate — HB 1069 summary, including suspension of challenged materials.

  • Department of Education — January 2025 dismissal of book-removal complaints.

Dismantling federal education capacity

  • White House — March 20, 2025, executive order directing steps toward closure.

  • Department of Education — federal, state, and local responsibilities.

  • Department of Education — March 2025 workforce-reduction announcement.

  • Education inspector general — June 2026 review of staffing and operational changes.

  • GAO — civil-rights staffing disruption, subsequent reversals, and undocumented costs and savings.

  • Department of Education — October 2026 account of interagency grant administration.

Political rhetoric and scientific institutions

  • AP Archive — Trump’s Nevada remarks, including “I love the poorly educated”.

  • HHS — June 2025 removal of all 17 sitting vaccine advisory committee members.

  • EPA — February 2026 rescission of the greenhouse-gas endangerment finding and vehicle standards.

  • IPCC — scientific assessment of human-caused warming.

Evidence of an alternative

  • Mississippi Department of Education — initial literacy-coach deployment and teacher training.

  • Mississippi Department of Education — 2024–2025 annual report and long-term fourth-grade gains.

item.content:encoded:
From coffee pods to printer ink, companies keep discovering ways to charge customers for the freedom to use what they already bought.

A coffee maker has a straightforward assignment: put hot water through coffee.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

In 2014, Keurig added another requirement. Before its new Keurig 2.0 would brew, it checked whether the pod belonged to the approved commercial ecosystem. Insert an unlicensed pod, and the machine could refuse.

The coffee was there. The water was there. The machinery worked.

The supplier hadn’t passed the revenue test.

Keurig had brought the printer-cartridge business model to breakfast: sell someone a machine, then use the machine to control their future purchases. Other coffee brands could participate through licensing, but customers couldn’t simply assume that a physically compatible pod would work in their own appliance.

There is a particular kind of corporate arrogance in engineering a product to become less useful when its owner shops elsewhere. It treats the sale as the beginning of a claim on the customer’s wallet, with no obvious point at which that claim should end.

Making money from a useful product becomes insufficient. The next objective is to prevent anyone else from making money around it.

Printer owners had already spent years finding ways around that arrangement.

In Brazil in the early 2000s, I remember cartridge-refilling kiosks appearing everywhere. Then came the external tanks: cartridges connected by little hoses to bottles of ink sitting beside the printer. Some setups used two-liter soda bottles. Color printers could have a small procession of bottles feeding them.

On one side stood a business model built around selling tiny quantities of ink in proprietary containers. On the other stood someone with tubing and an empty soft-drink bottle.

The bottle made a compelling argument.

That memory doesn’t establish that Brazil invented the system. External reservoirs feeding disposable cartridges through tubing appear in a U.S. patent filed in 1993. The homemade soda-bottle version belongs to a less neatly documented history of people adapting technology to their needs.

What is clear is that external ink systems existed long before manufacturers turned refillable tanks into a mainstream selling point.

Epson’s own corporate history acknowledges that users were modifying printers with external tanks to run cheaper third-party ink. It introduced its L100 and L200 tank printers in Indonesia in 2010. Within a year, tank models accounted for nearly half its printer sales in that country.

Customers had demonstrated demand by physically rebuilding the product’s ink supply.

Eventually, the manufacturer sold them a version of what they had been trying to achieve.

A factory-built tank printer can offer real improvements over a homemade conversion: better integration, easier filling, fewer improvised connections. Those improvements deserve credit. The revealing question is why customers had been willing to accept the inconvenience and risk of modifying their printers in the first place.

The answer was sitting in the price of the cartridges.

There is nothing mysterious about a company charging enough to cover development, manufacturing, support, and profit. Nor is every proprietary component evidence of abuse. Components can differ for legitimate engineering reasons.

But restrictions deserve scrutiny when the manufacturer deliberately makes the product reject a competing supply.

HP provides a particularly explicit example. Its documentation warns that, on printers with Dynamic Security, cartridges using non-HP chips or modified circuitry may work initially and later stop working following changes to the authentication system, including firmware updates. The restriction concerns the cartridge’s electronics; it does not mean every refilled cartridge is blocked.

Consider that relationship from the customer’s side. You purchase a printer. You purchase a cartridge that works. Later, the printer’s software changes, and your working supply becomes unacceptable.

The manufacturer has retained the technical power to narrow your purchasing choices after taking your money for the machine.

That is an extraordinary privilege to normalize.

Keurig’s experiment exposed the same impulse in a setting where its absurdity was easier to see. People understand coffee. A machine declining to brew because it disapproves of the lid invites a fairly immediate judgment.

The Rogers Family Company helped make that judgment tangible. It distributed a free plastic attachment called the Freedom Clip that bypassed the Keurig 2.0 restriction. Other workarounds existed too, but the clip gave the dispute a wonderfully concrete form: a company had built a commercial barrier into a kitchen appliance, and a competitor was mailing out the means to defeat it.

The restriction also alienated customers who wanted to use their own ground coffee. The new system had excluded the previous My K-Cup reusable accessory. In May 2015, Keurig’s CEO acknowledged the mistake and announced its return.

Keurig reported a 23 percent decline in brewer and accessory sales revenue for its second fiscal quarter of 2015, alongside a slower-than-expected transition to Keurig 2.0. The lockout cannot be blamed for every dollar of that decline. But the attempt to tighten control accompanied commercial disappointment, customer backlash, and a retreat over the reusable filter.

This is where the pursuit of extraction can become self-defeating.

A company can make its supplies attractive through price, quality, convenience, and reliability. Or it can spend resources making alternatives unusable. The second approach creates an additional cost: customers learn that the manufacturer may use its technical control against them.

A blocked purchase can produce an approved sale today and a lost customer tomorrow. It can also create demand for precisely the competing products, modifications, and workarounds the restriction was supposed to suppress.

The soda bottle and the Freedom Clip belong to that history. Both demonstrate customers taking action to recover a choice that the product’s commercial design had denied them.

There are limits to what consumer ingenuity can accomplish. People shouldn’t need technical skills, spare time, or the willingness to risk a messy repair simply to obtain reasonable running costs. A functional market cannot depend on every household maintaining its own small engineering resistance movement.

Manufacturers should have to earn repeat purchases. A customer who buys the official refill because it works well is evidence of a successful product. A customer who buys it because the machine refuses everything else is evidence of a successful restriction.

Corporate greed becomes especially visible when a company is willing to damage usefulness, trust, and even its own sales in pursuit of tighter control over the next transaction.

At that point, the customer’s satisfaction has become negotiable. The company’s claim on their spending has become sacred.

The printer needed ink. The coffee maker needed coffee.

The demand for permission came from the company.

Sources

  • TIME — Keurig’s pod restrictions and licensing model

  • U.S. patent US5369429A — External reservoirs feeding disposable cartridges, filed in 1993

  • Epson — Modified printers, its 2010 tank-printer launch, and adoption in Indonesia

  • HP — Dynamic Security and cartridges that may stop working after authentication changes

  • WIRED — The Freedom Clip and resistance to Keurig’s restrictions

  • Ars Technica — Keurig’s acknowledgment and the return of My K-Cup

  • Keurig — Fiscal second-quarter 2015 results, filed with the SEC

item.title: Vaccines Worked Then We Forgot
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Vaccination made deadly diseases disappear from everyday life. Kennedy turned that success against the protection that produced it. Accountability must extend beyond resignation. The empty polio ward should have settled the argument. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself: ☕ Buy us a coffee Children who never needed an iron lung. Parents who never buried a child killed by measles. Adults who lived without smallpox scars. Vaccination helped make those ordinary lives possible
item.content:encoded:
Vaccination made deadly diseases disappear from everyday life. Kennedy turned that success against the protection that produced it. Accountability must extend beyond resignation.

The empty polio ward should have settled the argument.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Children who never needed an iron lung. Parents who never buried a child killed by measles. Adults who lived without smallpox scars. Vaccination helped make those ordinary lives possible. Its success also created a political vulnerability: the people it protected often cannot see what they escaped.

Nobody interviews the parents outside the hospital their child never entered. There is no photograph of the funeral that never happened.

The injection remains visible. The catastrophe it prevented disappears.

Vaccine opponents exploit that imbalance. They point to a world made safer by vaccination and insist that vaccination was unnecessary. They inherit protection built through generations of scientific work, then undermine the institutions and habits that sustain it.

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. brought that agenda into the federal government.

His departure from office would stop him exercising its powers. It would not answer what responsibility he bears for how he used them.

Before the American measles vaccination program began in 1963, an estimated three million to four million people contracted the disease annually. Among reported cases, approximately 400 to 500 people died each year, 48,000 were hospitalized, and 1,000 developed encephalitis.

That was the ordinary burden of a disease now dismissed as an ordinary childhood illness. The word “ordinary” concealed the hospitalizations, brain injuries, and funerals.

Polio’s retreat was equally concrete. The United States reported more than 21,000 paralytic cases in 1952. After vaccination began, the number fell to 2,525 in 1960 and 61 in 1965.

Those figures represent people spared paralysis. The classmates who could keep walking. The children who could breathe without mechanical assistance. The families who did not spend their lives organizing care around a preventable injury.

A WHO-led modeling study estimated that immunization against 14 diseases saved 154 million lives between 1974 and 2024, including 101 million infants. Measles vaccination accounted for approximately 94 million lives saved.

These are scientific estimates of deaths prevented, rather than individually counted people whose alternate lives can be observed. The scale is nevertheless extraordinary: vaccination changed who survived childhood.

Precision matters. Smallpox is the only human disease eradicated worldwide. Polio has been pushed toward eradication. Measles, mumps, and whooping cough have not been globally eradicated, nor are all three on the verge of it.

Their diminished presence in many people’s lives reflects protection that must be maintained. A disease suppressed by vaccination does not become harmless when people forget why they vaccinate.

The empty ward is evidence that prevention worked. It cannot justify dismantling prevention.

Kennedy’s public conduct supplies ample grounds for scrutiny without jokes about his reported parasite infection or attacks on his history of addiction. Neither establishes culpability. His statements and decisions are the relevant evidence.

On March 11, 2025, during an active measles outbreak, Kennedy told Sean Hannity that the measles vaccine “does cause deaths every year.” FactCheck.org found no evidence supporting that annual-death claim and documented other misleading assertions in the interview.

Vaccines can have adverse effects. Serious complications must be investigated, disclosed, and placed in their proper statistical context. Inflating those risks while minimizing the disease corrupts the informed consent Kennedy claims to defend.

The protective alternative was already established. Two doses of MMR are approximately 97% effective against measles. Some people cannot safely receive this live vaccine; others are too young for routine vaccination. Their vulnerability makes protection in the surrounding community especially important.

Kennedy has also endorsed MMR. That belongs in the record.

In April 2025, he publicly identified vaccination as the most effective means of preventing measles transmission. Later that same day, however, he promoted claims that doctors had healed hundreds of children using treatments lacking evidence for treating measles. FactCheck.org’s subsequent timeline documented supportive statements appearing alongside misleading claims that could discourage vaccination.

A health secretary cannot expect one accurate sentence to erase the consequences of the next misleading one.

Then came the exercise of institutional power.

On June 9, 2025, HHS announced that Kennedy had removed all 17 sitting members of the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, the panel advising CDC on vaccine use. The department described the purge as a way to restore public trust. Its announcement also complained that existing appointments would have prevented the administration from choosing a majority until 2028.

HHS itself made political control part of the explanation for removing the experts.

On August 5, 2025, HHS announced a wind-down of BARDA’s mRNA vaccine development investments, affecting 22 projects worth nearly $500 million through cancellations and reductions.

Those projects involved a different vaccine technology from MMR. Their cancellation is not evidence that Kennedy caused measles deaths. It demonstrates the wider reach of his agenda: vaccine skepticism was being translated into decisions about public research and preparedness.

The consequences of inadequate measles protection were already visible. In April 2025, Texas announced a second death in its outbreak: an unvaccinated child with no reported underlying conditions.

By November 24, 2026, CDC had recorded 6,039 confirmed U.S. measles cases that year, compared with 2,289 in 2025 and 285 in 2024. Those surveillance figures remain preliminary.

On November 17, federal health authorities acknowledged that the United States had lost its measles elimination status. The country had first achieved that status in 2000. Losing it marked the return of sustained domestic transmission, rather than the appearance of an occasional imported infection.

Kennedy did not create every condition behind the resurgence. Vaccination coverage was falling before he took office. CDC reports kindergarten MMR coverage declining from 95.2% in 2019–2020 to 92.4% in 2025–2026. National averages also conceal communities with much larger gaps.

That history prevents an honest account from assigning the entire outbreak to him. It also establishes the vulnerability he inherited. His responsibility was to strengthen protection against a known threat. His record includes misleading statements about that protection and the wholesale removal of the experts guiding it.

There was ample warning of what collapsing vaccination coverage could produce.

Samoa’s 2019 measles epidemic involved 5,707 cases and 83 deaths. Coverage had fallen sharply before the outbreak. WHO and UNICEF documented the catastrophe and the emergency response.

Kennedy visited Samoa before the epidemic. Associated Press later reported that newly obtained emails undermined his account of the trip; Samoan officials said the visit strengthened anti-vaccine activists’ credibility. Those findings do not establish that he personally caused Samoa’s deaths. They place his activity within a documented history of vaccine distrust and lethal consequences.

The accusation against Kennedy concerns foreseeable harm. A public official need not desire deaths for his conduct to warrant investigation into responsibility for them. The relevant questions include what he knew, which warnings he received, what he chose to do, and what harm those choices caused.

Declaring a homicide offense proved would run ahead of the evidence. Treating resignation as sufficient would abandon the effort to establish it.

Congressional oversight and independent investigation should preserve and examine the records: scientific briefings, internal warnings, communications about public guidance, decisions affecting vaccination programs, and any interference with disease surveillance or reporting.

Investigators must distinguish existing failures from damage Kennedy added. Prosecutors must assess applicable law, jurisdiction, causation, and the evidence of his knowledge and conduct. Where that evidence supports criminal charges, they should pursue them.

Prison must remain a possible consequence if a prosecutable crime is established. Resignation must not become an escape hatch.

Responsibility also extends to the people who entrusted him with power. Trump appointed him. The senators who confirmed him authorized his leadership of the nation’s health department. Their decisions deserve scrutiny alongside his.

Vaccination gave millions of people the privilege of growing up without firsthand knowledge of these diseases. Anti-vaccine politics exploits that privilege while endangering the next generation.

Children should not have to acquire their grandparents’ diseases to teach adults their grandparents’ lessons.

The empty polio ward was an achievement. Officials who undermine the protection that emptied it owe the public far more than a resignation letter.

Sources

  1. CDC — History of Measles. Annual disease burden before vaccination and the introduction of the vaccine in 1963.

  2. CDC — Pink Book, Poliomyelitis. Historical paralytic polio figures.

  3. WHO — Global immunization efforts have saved at least 154 million lives over the past 50 years. April 24, 2024; summary of the WHO-led modeling study, including infant survival and measles vaccination.

  4. CDC — Vaccine-Preventable Diseases. Distinction between control, elimination, and eradication; smallpox remains the only eradicated human disease.

  5. WHO — Poliomyelitis. Global progress toward polio eradication.

  6. FactCheck.org — RFK Jr. Misleads About Measles Vaccine in Hannity Interview. March 21, 2025; review of Kennedy’s March 11 statements.

  7. CDC — Measles Vaccination. MMR effectiveness, eligibility, and precautions.

  8. FactCheck.org — A Timeline of RFK Jr.’s Mixed Messaging on the Measles Vaccine. May 28, 2026; documented endorsements, misleading statements, and promotion of unsupported treatments.

  9. HHS — Reconstituting ACIP. June 9, 2025; the department’s announcement removing all 17 members and its stated reasons.

  10. HHS — Winds Down mRNA Vaccine Development Under BARDA. August 5, 2025; 22 projects worth nearly $500 million affected.

  11. American Academy of Pediatrics — Second school-age child dies from measles amid Texas outbreak. April 7, 2025; reporting of the state’s findings on the second child’s death.

  12. CDC — Measles Cases and Outbreaks. Figures through November 24, 2026; preliminary national case counts.

  13. CDC — Joint Statement on Loss of U.S. Measles Elimination Status. November 17, 2026.

  14. CDC — Vaccination Coverage and Exemptions among Kindergartners. Coverage and exemption data, including the 2025–2026 school year.

  15. WHO and UNICEF — Pacific measles situation report. January 22, 2020; Samoa’s 5,707 cases and 83 deaths.

  16. WHO — Measles in Pacific Island Countries and Areas. December 2019; low vaccination coverage preceding Samoa’s epidemic.

  17. Associated Press — Newly obtained emails undermine RFK Jr.’s testimony about 2019 Samoa trip. Reporting on the trip’s purpose and Samoan officials’ assessment of its effects.

item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s headline promises an astronomer’s rebuttal to Elon Musk and an explanation of how someone could “own” the public’s view of the sky. The supplied material establishes none of it. It contains only a string of names and political search terms, with no astronomer, no Musk proposal, no quotation, no event and no reported outcome.

The promised dispute is absent

There is no factual account from which to identify the astronomer, describe Musk’s alleged “sci-fi silliness,” or explain what control over the sky supposedly means. The material does not establish whether the dispute concerns satellites, spaceflight, astronomy, advertising or something else entirely.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Nor does it provide evidence about who possesses institutional authority, what decision was made, or who would bear its consequences. Any attempt to supply those details would be invention, not reporting.

A headline cannot substitute for evidence

The unexplained list—George Conway, Noam Chomsky, Kayleigh McEnany, Melania Trump, Paul Krugman, Lindsey Graham and others—does not substantiate the headline’s claim or form a coherent account of political power. Treating it as one would merely convert search-engine debris into a fabricated story.

The only defensible conclusion is therefore narrow: the provided text does not answer the headline’s question or support a standalone article about Musk, astronomy or control of the night sky.

item.title: Jared Kushner reveals 'idiocy' driving Trump admin’s 'strategic witchcraft'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Jared Kushner’s rare interview laid bare the governing logic behind the Trump administration’s approach to Russia: praise Vladimir Putin, fault Ukraine and Europe, and offer Kyiv a security guarantee designed never to be used. Writing in The Atlantic , conservative security strategist Eliot Cohen called that formula “magic diplomacy”—an attempt to substitute flattery and wishful thinking for enforceable commitments in a war begun by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Kushner, President Donald Trump’s
item.content:encoded:
Jared Kushner’s rare interview laid bare the governing logic behind the Trump administration’s approach to Russia: praise Vladimir Putin, fault Ukraine and Europe, and offer Kyiv a security guarantee designed never to be used. Writing in The Atlantic, conservative security strategist Eliot Cohen called that formula “magic diplomacy”—an attempt to substitute flattery and wishful thinking for enforceable commitments in a war begun by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kushner, President Donald Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy, described Putin as a “grand master of politics” and “a historic figure” who “wants peace.” He called Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev “an incredible friend” and Russian National Security Adviser Yuri Ushakov “fantastic.” These were not stray pleasantries. They accompanied an account of the war that repeatedly adopted Moscow’s preferred framing while directing suspicion toward the governments Russia has attacked or threatened.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Russia’s war becomes everyone’s miscalculation

Kushner attributed the conflict to “bad decisions and miscalculations by many leaders over the years,” obscuring the decisive act identified in the reporting: Russia invaded Ukraine. Responsibility dissolves into a fog of collective error, allowing the state that launched the war to appear as merely one participant trapped by unfortunate circumstances.

He also credited Russia with doing the West a major favor by agreeing “not to use nuclear weapons.” That formulation turns nuclear restraint—the minimum expected of a nuclear-armed government—into a concession for which Moscow should apparently receive diplomatic gratitude.

Cohen, who served on the Defense Policy Advisory Board Committee during George W. Bush’s administration, contrasted Kushner’s admiration for Putin with the consequences of Russian rule and war. He pointed to 700,000 Russian dead, larger numbers permanently injured, domestic shortages, and roughly a million people who left the country. In Cohen’s assessment, Kushner’s remarks revealed “moral blindness” as well as “political idiocy.”

Whatever Putin’s tactical skill, calling him a grand master is political image management masquerading as strategic analysis. It treats accumulated devastation as evidence of greatness and shifts attention from what Russian power has done to how impressive its ruler appears to an American presidential relative.

Allies are scolded; Putin gets a veto

Kushner’s indulgence stopped at NATO’s border. He dismissed allegations that the Trump administration had withheld intelligence and resources from Ukraine as “misinformation,” criticized Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, and said European fears were “unfounded.” Cohen noted that this posture disregarded assassinations, attempted assassinations, and Russian “grey zone” operations against NATO countries.

Kushner also explained Europe’s exclusion from peace talks in Abu Dhabi through Putin’s objections. According to Kushner, the Russian president regarded European statements and actions as provocative and therefore did not consider European governments “ready for peace.” Kushner’s rhetorical response—who could blame Putin?—is revealing because it grants the invading power authority to determine which of Ukraine’s allies may participate in negotiations over European security.

That is not neutral mediation. It privileges Moscow’s grievances while treating allied resistance as the obstacle to peace. Russia receives understanding for excluding Europeans; Europeans receive a lecture for responding to Russian conduct.

The power imbalance matters. Putin does not need Kushner’s sympathy to command the Russian state or prosecute the war. Ukraine needs weapons, intelligence, and credible security commitments from the United States. When a White House envoy disparages the dependent ally and flatters the aggressor, the consequences do not fall evenly. Washington’s chosen language can weaken Ukraine’s bargaining position before any agreement is signed.

A guarantee engineered not to guarantee anything

The sharpest evidence of Cohen’s “strategic witchcraft” is Kushner’s proposal for Ukraine to receive “a credible Article 5–like guarantee, backed by deterrence and deconfliction arrangements.” Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty treats an attack on one NATO member as an attack on all, making collective response the foundation of deterrence.

But Kushner said Trump would accept such an arrangement only if it were “highly unlikely that the guarantee would ever be invoked.” That qualification exposes the contradiction. A security guarantee deters attack because an adversary expects it to be honored when tested. Designing one around Washington’s desire not to fulfill it produces a pledge whose credibility depends on everyone pretending not to notice its escape hatch.

The problem is more serious than diplomatic naivety. A hollow assurance could pressure Ukraine to accept risk now while leaving the United States room to retreat later. Moscow would have every incentive to test the difference between “Article 5–like” language and an actual defense obligation.

Cohen concluded that the interview displayed “amoral, vapid, and self-serving geopolitical delusion.” The reported remarks support a narrower but equally damning judgment: Kushner’s diplomacy asks the vulnerable party to trust an intentionally conditional promise while extending deference to the government that made such protection necessary. Calling that peace does not change who receives the guarantee and who receives the benefit of the doubt.

item.title: Trump's 'verbal vomit' to deployed troops leaves veterans disgusted
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump turned a Thanksgiving call with deployed U.S. service members into a celebration of stock prices, a warning that a Marine could be readily replaced, and a claim that war would end whenever he chose. The remarks drew disgust from veterans who heard the president treating troops as an audience for his branding rather than people spending the holiday away from home. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump turned a Thanksgiving call with deployed U.S. service members into a celebration of stock prices, a warning that a Marine could be readily replaced, and a claim that war would end whenever he chose. The remarks drew disgust from veterans who heard the president treating troops as an audience for his branding rather than people spending the holiday away from home.

Calling Thursday night from Mar-a-Lago with first lady Melania Trump beside him, Trump was asked what made him most thankful. According to The Independent’s reporting, he began with his campaign slogan and then pointed to the market.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“As of the election, we have created a value in terms of stock markets — we have the highest stock markets in history,” Trump said.

The answer established the call’s priorities. Deployed personnel and their families were present, but Trump’s gratitude centered on a financial benchmark he could claim as a political achievement.

A holiday message about replaceability

Coast Guard veteran Evaristus Odinikaeze identified the omission: “Not the troops on the call. Not their families keeping an empty seat at the table. Not the wife sitting right next to him.”

Odinikaeze, who said he had spent holidays on duty, described what deployed personnel needed to hear instead: “that someone back home sees you.”

Trump offered Marine Lt. Col. Matthew S. Andrews a different message. After boasting about military recruitment while Andrews was deployed at Al Dhafra Air Base in the United Arab Emirates, the president converted those numbers into a joke about the officer’s disposability.

“In other words, what I’m saying to you, Matthew, is that if you ever leave, we’re going to replace you very easily, so don’t leave, Matthew, OK? Don’t leave,” Trump said.

“Thank you, Mr. President,” Andrews replied. “I appreciate it.”

That exchange was structurally unequal: a commander in chief speaking publicly to a deployed officer, who answered with the deference his position demanded. Treating Andrews’ response as evidence that the remark landed harmlessly would ignore who possessed institutional power in the conversation.

Army veteran Chad Scott was less constrained. He called Trump’s performance “an endless stream of verbal vomit,” adding that the president had been given the elementary task of saying something kind about troops on Thanksgiving and failed to do it.

War reduced to presidential whim

Trump’s most consequential remark concerned the Iran war. After asking a fighter pilot whether he would trade lives with him, Trump said the deployment would continue because “we have victory at hand.”

“It’s going to be — whenever sort of — whenever I want it to be, to be honest,” he added.

The phrasing presented the duration of war as an extension of presidential preference. Whatever authority a president exercises as commander in chief, troops absorb the consequences through deployments, separation and physical danger. Trump’s formulation erased every constraint and every person between his will and their exposure.

Even a service member’s question about Thanksgiving dessert became an opportunity to attack Joe Biden. Trump dismissed it as “a Joe Biden question,” complained that Biden had supposedly received easy questions about ice cream, and only then answered: pumpkin pie with vanilla ice cream.

The reflex was revealing. A ceremonial call designed to recognize military service repeatedly became a vehicle for campaign slogans, market claims, personnel boasts and complaints about a political rival.

The market as applause meter

Trump’s invocation of record stock prices also followed a sharply different market message the previous day. He had complained on social media that stocks were “down sharply because of the November Third Election results,” arguing that markets and retirement accounts would have been “BOOMING” had he been on the ballot.

Taken together, the statements show Trump using the market as a personal political scoreboard: credit belongs to him when prices rise, while voters and election results take the blame when they fall. On Thanksgiving, deployed troops became the captive audience for that self-assessment.

Democratic influencer Harry Sisson accused Trump of spending the holiday “rambling on social media” at Mar-a-Lago before telling service members that the stock market was what made him most thankful. But the veterans’ criticism carried a more specific indictment. They were not objecting merely to an awkward joke or poor holiday manners. They were responding to a commander in chief who spoke to deployed personnel about their replaceability, described war’s timetable as his personal choice, and reserved his clearest gratitude for an asset market.

item.title: Judges give permission to 'fight back' against Trump extortion: legal expert
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to drag several ABC affiliates into an early license-renewal process, finding that the Federal Communications Commission singled them out for retaliation. The Nov. 25 restraining order does not grant corporations some new permission to resist presidential pressure. It demonstrates something more basic: capitulation was never their only option. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan called the dispute “not a close case.” According to Alter
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has blocked the Trump administration’s attempt to drag several ABC affiliates into an early license-renewal process, finding that the Federal Communications Commission singled them out for retaliation. The Nov. 25 restraining order does not grant corporations some new permission to resist presidential pressure. It demonstrates something more basic: capitulation was never their only option.

U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan called the dispute “not a close case.” According to AlterNet, she found that FCC Chair Brendan Carr imposed standards on the ABC affiliates that the commission did not apply equally to others—and that Carr “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The regulator followed the president’s grievance

The affiliates’ licenses were not due for renewal until October 2028 at the earliest. Carr nevertheless ordered them to file early on April 28, one day after Trump demanded Jimmy Kimmel’s firing over a joke about Melania Trump.

That sequence was reinforced by the president’s own public campaign. AliKhan identified at least 11 instances in which Trump urged the FCC to revoke ABC licenses. This was not an ordinary regulatory review that happened to inconvenience a company the president disliked. As former federal prosecutor Barbara McQuade put it, the government was “singling out ABC for mistreatment and retaliation.”

The administration’s pressure followed backlash against Kimmel and Trump’s long-running feud with ABC’s daytime program The View. The relevant power relationship is straightforward: Trump supplied the grievance, while Carr controlled an agency capable of imposing expensive and potentially consequential regulatory proceedings. Whatever the eventual legal outcome, the FCC’s authority gave presidential hostility an institutional vehicle.

Retaliation works before punishment arrives

AliKhan also found that the threats had already influenced ABC’s editorial judgments, including decisions about carrying Trump’s speeches and booking political guests on The View. That is the central consequence. Government coercion does not need to end in a revoked license to shape coverage. A regulator can alter newsroom behavior merely by making clear that unfavorable speech may bring exceptional scrutiny.

Trump’s public attacks supplied the message; Carr’s order supplied the enforcement mechanism. The resulting pressure reached decisions about what viewers would see and whom they would hear. Calling that a fight over “bias” or programming preferences would obscure the institutional act at issue: a federal official used regulatory power in a way the court found discriminatory and retaliatory.

McQuade described the campaign as an effort to “extort” ABC. Her characterization is analysis, not the court’s formal legal conclusion. But the reported conduct fits the political structure she identified: presidential demands backed by the prospect of government-inflicted harm.

Corporate surrender was a choice

McQuade contrasted ABC’s challenge with the conduct of organizations that abandoned diversity, equity and inclusion programs after Trump targeted law firms, universities and corporations with social-media attacks and boycott calls. She said organizations across the country had voluntarily dismantled such programs because they feared becoming the next target.

That pattern matters because it is often described as if institutions were simply caught in a confusing political environment. McQuade instead invoked historian Timothy Snyder’s warning about “obeying in advance”: powerful organizations surrendering before the state has compelled them to do so.

Corporations and elite institutions are not powerless dissidents. They have lawyers, money, public platforms and access to courts. When they preemptively erase policies to avoid presidential displeasure, they are making an institutional calculation. Their compliance lowers the cost of the next threat and shifts the consequences onto employees, students, clients and audiences with far less leverage.

ABC’s lawsuit exposed the alternative. The company sought judicial relief, and a judge stopped the FCC’s accelerated process. That does not make ABC heroic, nor does it erase any earlier accommodation. It establishes that resistance could produce a concrete result while obedience merely taught the administration that intimidation worked.

The injunction interrupts, but does not end, the pressure

McQuade expects the administration to appeal and believes the case could reach the Supreme Court. The restraining order therefore settles neither the larger constitutional dispute nor ABC’s long-term exposure.

For now, however, the ruling places responsibility where the record described by AliKhan puts it: not on television hosts for offending the president, and not on affiliates for attracting controversy, but on an FCC chair who converted Trump’s public demands into selective regulatory action.

The administration’s campaign depended on institutions assuming that surrender was safer than litigation. AliKhan’s order disrupted that calculation. The licenses were years away from renewal, the president repeatedly demanded retaliation, and Carr moved the process forward anyway. Once ABC challenged him, the court found the arrangement unmistakable.

item.title: WH insider: Trump’s $4B windfall is making everything you buy more expensive
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump and his family have reportedly gained roughly $4 billion since his return to the White House, while his administration has pursued policies that reward access, weaken competition and expand federal deficits. The connection to higher prices is not that every checkout receipt contains a measurable Trump-family surcharge. It is structural: University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers told AlterNet that when companies can prosper by courting the president instead of offering better,
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump and his family have reportedly gained roughly $4 billion since his return to the White House, while his administration has pursued policies that reward access, weaken competition and expand federal deficits. The connection to higher prices is not that every checkout receipt contains a measurable Trump-family surcharge. It is structural: University of Michigan economist Justin Wolfers told AlterNet that when companies can prosper by courting the president instead of offering better, cheaper goods, “expensive products will win.”

That is the central economic cost of corruption. It does not stop at the money collected by an officeholder or his relatives. It changes what businesses compete for—and forces consumers to pay for the resulting market.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

When access becomes the product

Wolfers, also a nonresident senior fellow at Brookings and the Peterson Institute, described a market economy as competition over price and quality. Political favoritism replaces that discipline with a different contest: who can bring gifts to the White House, secure a favorable rule or get a rival excluded.

“If the best way for me to get ahead is to go to the White House bearing gifts,” he told AlterNet in September, corporate resources move away from improving products and toward winning presidential favor. Executives spend less effort lowering prices or developing better goods and more effort cultivating Trump at Mar-a-Lago.

Wolfers carefully distinguished between conduct satisfying a legal definition of corruption and conduct fitting the word’s ordinary meaning. But the economic mechanism does not depend on a criminal conviction. If official decisions confer advantages according to proximity, patronage or gifts, competition deteriorates regardless of whether prosecutors can prove a charge.

The reported $4 billion gained by Trump and his family is therefore not merely a story about personal greed. AlterNet also cited allegations placing as much as $377 billion in administration-related corruption and abuses of power, a broader figure that should be treated as an allegation rather than an adjudicated total. The political issue is the concentration of public power in an administration whose leader and relatives reportedly profit on an unprecedented scale while that administration controls regulations, contracts and enforcement.

The White House answers a different accusation

When AlterNet asked the White House about criticism from Brookings senior fellow Bill Galston, spokesperson Lauren Bis did not address the specific allegations against Trump. Instead, she said the president had launched “an all-out war on fraud across the entire federal government,” accused congressional Democrats of refusing to stop waste and claimed they unanimously opposed the Stop Insider Trading Act.

The last claim was false on the facts AlterNet supplied: 13 Democrats voted for the measure.

More importantly, the response substituted government waste and congressional trading for the conduct of the president. Fraud elsewhere does not answer whether Trump has used presidential power to enrich himself or his family. Nor does an accusation against Democrats rebut allegations against the person who controls the executive branch.

Bis’s evasion is especially revealing because, as Lauren Bowman, she once demanded far more exacting scrutiny of government public-relations spending. Writing with Romina Boccia for The Daily Signal in 2016, she questioned whether federal advertising had become an unaccountable “black box.” She cited a Government Accountability Office estimate of about $1 billion in annual advertising and public-relations spending from 2006 through 2015 and warned that the figure might be incomplete.

A decade later, confronted with allegations involving presidential self-enrichment on a vastly larger scale, Bis redirected the question toward Democrats. AlterNet reported that she did not answer its follow-ups. The standard did not become more sophisticated when she entered the White House. It became more convenient.

Fiscal restraint ends where Republican priorities begin

The same selective accounting governs Trump’s budget record. Bis previously argued that the United States needed a “saner fiscal path.” Yet AlterNet reports that federal debt has reached $40 trillion after Trump backed costly tax reductions and a major expansion of military spending.

Robert Shapiro, an economic adviser in the Clinton administration, told AlterNet in August that policies inherited from Joe Biden would have produced a gradually declining deficit over the following decade as the economy grew. Trump instead chose tax changes with large budgetary costs and substantially higher defense spending, he said, putting deficits on course to equal 6 or 7 percent of gross domestic product.

Shapiro attributed a majority—but not all—of the current fiscal problem to Trump. That qualification matters. So does the allocation of responsibility: the administration did not stumble into its budget choices. It enacted priorities that reduced revenue and increased military expenditures.

Galston likewise resisted treating Trump as the lone author of the Republican program. The legislation branded the “One Big Beautiful Bill,” he noted, combined longstanding party commitments, including tax cuts and reductions to programs such as Medicaid. Trump supplied the leadership and signature, but congressional Republicans supplied the votes and the ideological machinery.

That distinction exposes another useful misdirection. Trump’s dominance of the party does not absolve the lawmakers who enacted its agenda. Republicans who object to his personal enrichment while supporting policies that shift resources upward are disputing the management of the spoils, not rejecting the governing arrangement.

Accountability narrowed by the Supreme Court

Galston described the scale and openness of enrichment during Trump’s second term as its defining departure from his first. “There is really no effort to hide what he and the family are doing,” he told AlterNet. He said the conduct was larger, more blatant and less apologetic than anything the country had previously seen, while stopping short of declaring it criminal.

That restraint is necessary. AlterNet’s reporting presents accusations of corruption and evidence of extraordinary self-enrichment; it does not establish that the reported gains were all illegally obtained. Galston said it remains unclear whether the conduct reaches outright criminality.

The absence of a settled criminal finding, however, is not exoneration—particularly when the institutions responsible for presidential accountability have weakened the available remedies. Galston said legal efforts to hold Trump responsible have fared poorly and that the Supreme Court has made accountability more difficult.

He distinguished that failure from political accountability. According to Galston, voters connected presidential corruption with their own financial losses, and Democrats successfully campaigned on that relationship. He cited a recent midterm result in which Democrats won the national popular vote by 14 percentage points, calling it an “earthquake” and arguing that public revulsion over self-enrichment helped produce the Republican defeat.

That result does not recover money, unwind favoritism or repair a market distorted by political access. It shows only that impunity has acquired an electoral price. The harder question AlterNet put to Galston—whether Democrats can stop the enrichment and claw back any illicit gains—remains unanswered. His response was blunt: “I don’t know.”

That uncertainty is the consequence of an accountability system narrowed by judicial protection, partisan obedience and executive control. The White House can announce a war on fraud while refusing to answer allegations against the president. Businesses can calculate that access is more valuable than innovation. Consumers then encounter the result not as an ethics seminar but as fewer choices, worse products and higher prices.

item.title: Senate floor curse-out reveals one GOP lawmaker is done playing nice
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: John Cornyn is the Republican senator who is done playing nice—at least now that his own political career has reportedly been cut short. On an otherwise quiet Senate floor earlier in November, the Texas senator berated Ted Cruz over a federal judicial nominee, declared that he no longer found his colleague credible and accused an unidentified person of “ending my career.” The Washington Sun’s Igor Bobic witnessed the confrontation, which exposed more than a personality clash: it showed what happ
item.content:encoded:
John Cornyn is the Republican senator who is done playing nice—at least now that his own political career has reportedly been cut short. On an otherwise quiet Senate floor earlier in November, the Texas senator berated Ted Cruz over a federal judicial nominee, declared that he no longer found his colleague credible and accused an unidentified person of “ending my career.” The Washington Sun’s Igor Bobic witnessed the confrontation, which exposed more than a personality clash: it showed what happens when a party’s radicalization finally consumes one of the officials who spent years accommodating it.

A nomination fight turns personal

The immediate dispute concerned an effort by Cruz and other conservatives to install an out-of-state nominee on the federal bench in Dallas. Cornyn objected on institutional grounds, arguing that allowing presidents to appoint judges from outside a state would erode home-state senators’ influence over nominations.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The disagreement escalated well beyond Senate procedure. According to Bobic, Cornyn shouted at Cruz: “I don’t find you credible. I’m mad at you.” He then said he was angry at someone “for ending my career!” Bobic could not determine whether Cornyn meant Cruz or President Donald Trump, whose endorsement of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton in the Republican primary reportedly proved decisive against Cornyn.

When Cruz answered him on the nomination, Cornyn erupted again: “Oh, that’s bulls——!”

Cruz later confirmed to Fox News that Cornyn had been “yelling loud enough” for others to hear. That volume matters. This was not merely private resentment accidentally overheard; Cornyn was no longer making much effort to contain it.

The rightward ratchet catches Cornyn

The conflict had been developing since Cruz entered the Senate on the Tea Party wave. Cornyn represented an older Reagan-Bush Republican establishment, while Cruz built his career through the insurgent politics that treated establishment Republicans as nearly as suspect as Democrats.

Their alliance was consequently transactional and brittle. Cornyn declined to participate in Cruz’s 2016 presidential campaign. Cruz remained silent when Cornyn sought the Republican leadership post in 2024, even as Cornyn’s supporters suspected he preferred John Thune, who won. Cruz also kept quiet when his political operatives joined Paxton’s campaign against Cornyn.

That history clarifies the power structure. Cornyn once aspired to lead Senate Republicans, but seniority and institutional loyalty could not protect him from a primary electorate pulled steadily rightward. Cruz did not need to attack Cornyn openly. Silence was enough while Trump and Paxton supplied the force.

The episode is therefore not best understood as an ideological moderate confronting extremism. Cornyn remained inside the Republican coalition as its incentives shifted and its internal purges intensified. His anger became public only after those incentives turned against him personally.

Independence after defeat

The Sun described Cornyn as entering “YOLO mode” after losing to Paxton, becoming more outspoken in his criticism of the Trump administration. That newfound freedom may produce genuine resistance to presidential overreach. It also arrives when the political cost has sharply diminished.

Cornyn framed the judicial dispute as a defense of the Senate’s constitutional authority. In a post following the confrontation, he wrote that if a president could appoint someone from another state, senators would lose meaningful influence over appointments in their own states. He invoked the Constitution’s “advise and consent” clause.

That is a substantive institutional argument, even if Cornyn wrapped it in a taunt. “Everyone knows that I am a notorious cusser and screamer and that Ted is a fragile thing,” he wrote before redirecting attention to the nomination dispute.

The remark also served a useful purpose for Cornyn: it turned a visible loss of control into a performance of defiance. Yet the central fact remains that a senator reportedly became willing to challenge his party’s dominant faction only after Trump’s endorsement helped end his career. The independence is real enough to inconvenience Cruz. Its timing shows how thoroughly Republican discipline depends on the threat of political retaliation.

Cornyn may now insist on having the last word, but Trump, Paxton and the primary electorate had the consequential one. His Senate-floor fury did not reverse that outcome. It merely made audible the resentment of an establishment Republican discovering that the machine he tolerated has no obligation to spare him.
