item.title: Ex-Trump official freaks over Dems killing GOP's electoral advantage forever
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The former Trump official in question is Hogan Gidley, a onetime Trump campaign press secretary. Appearing Thursday on Newsmax’s “Finnerty,” Gidley said the prospect of Democrats using anticipated congressional and state-level power to weaken Republican electoral advantages made him “sick to the stomach.” His complaint was revealing: Democrats might admit Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., as states, change the Supreme Court and prevent the Electoral College from awarding the presidency to a cand
item.content:encoded:
The former Trump official in question is Hogan Gidley, a onetime Trump campaign press secretary. Appearing Thursday on Newsmax’s “Finnerty,” Gidley said the prospect of Democrats using anticipated congressional and state-level power to weaken Republican electoral advantages made him “sick to the stomach.” His complaint was revealing: Democrats might admit Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C., as states, change the Supreme Court and prevent the Electoral College from awarding the presidency to a candidate who loses the national popular vote.

AlterNet reports that Democrats were poised to enter January with substantial House and Senate majorities. Gidley’s response was not an argument that the existing system fairly represents voters. It was alarm that Democrats might alter institutions from which Republicans benefit.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A panic built around losing structural advantage

“This is what they wanted to do,” Gidley said, accusing Democrats of preparing to drive the country “right into the ditch” after obtaining “the keys to the car.”

He then listed several Democratic proposals: statehood for Puerto Rico and Washington, D.C.; expanding the Supreme Court; and ending the Electoral College. These are separate measures involving different institutions and legal processes, but Gidley bundled them into a single image of unchecked Democratic rule.

“Elections have consequences,” he said, before expressing dismay at the consequences he expected Democrats to pursue. That contradiction is the substance of the segment. Gidley accepted electoral power as legitimate only up to the point where voters might empower a governing majority to change arrangements favorable to his party.

He later warned that Democrats would “wield power like we’ve never seen before” through a “top-down methodology on people who thought they were just electing somebody.” But electing officials to enact publicly discussed policies is not a bait-and-switch. By Gidley’s own account, Democrats had campaigned around these ideas. His objection was not that voters had been deceived; it was that the winners might govern.

Newsmax turns majority rule into a Democratic plot

The segment’s framing shifted attention away from the people whose representation is constrained and toward Republican anxiety about losing institutional leverage.

Statehood for Washington, D.C., and Puerto Rico would concern political representation for populations currently denied the same federal status as residents of states. Gidley presented that possibility principally as a threat to Republicans. The people affected disappeared behind the partisan arithmetic.

The same inversion shaped the discussion of presidential elections. States elect governors and senators through direct statewide voting, but the presidency is awarded through the Electoral College. AlterNet notes that the system originally enhanced the influence of less populous slave states and now advantages Republicans by giving disproportionate weight to smaller, rural states.

That advantage has produced concrete results. George W. Bush and Donald Trump each reached the White House without winning the national popular vote. Gidley’s panic makes sense only if that mismatch is treated as a Republican entitlement rather than a democratic defect.

Maddow’s claim was broader than the mechanism described

Rachel Maddow, identified by AlterNet as an MS NOW host, argued that Democrats could act within six months if enough states with Democratic governors and legislatures joined an arrangement carrying more than 270 electoral votes.

“You could have enough Democratic state legislatures say, ‘yeah, we’re part of this thing,’” she said, adding that changing the effective operation of the Electoral College “kind of seems doable.” She also suggested that age limits for Supreme Court justices might be within reach if Democrats decided to “swing for the fences.”

The report describes that state-based route as “getting rid of the Electoral College,” but the distinction matters: the mechanism Maddow outlined would change how participating states allocate their electoral votes once the necessary threshold was reached. The supplied reporting does not describe a constitutional amendment formally abolishing the institution. Nor does it establish that every Democratic trifecta would join such an effort.

That uncertainty did not moderate the Newsmax reaction. The panelists reportedly shuddered, and Gidley treated the possibility of reform as an impending abuse of power.

His fear ultimately resolves the headline’s teaser. Gidley was not panicking because Democrats had concealed an authoritarian program. He was panicking because they might use electoral victories to reduce a system that allows Republican presidential candidates to win while receiving fewer votes. The “ditch” in his metaphor is a country where the candidate supported by the most voters has a better chance of taking office.

item.title: Judge’s rebuke of Trump official 'reads like draft articles of impeachment'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A federal judge has blocked Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr from accelerating the renewal review of ABC-owned broadcast licenses, finding that the network is likely to prove the agency retaliated against protected speech that angered President Donald Trump and Carr. item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has blocked Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr from accelerating the renewal review of ABC-owned broadcast licenses, finding that the network is likely to prove the agency retaliated against protected speech that angered President Donald Trump and Carr. The preliminary injunction is not a final judgment, and the FCC may appeal. But U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan’s conclusion was already blunt: “This is not a close case.”

Legal journalist Roger Parloff went further, writing on X that the opinion “reads like draft articles of impeachment.” That is his assessment, not the court’s ruling. AliKhan did not impeach Carr, find him liable, or issue a final verdict. What she did was document a sequence in which the official empowered to regulate broadcasters repeatedly acted in step with a president demanding punishment for an unfriendly network.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump demanded punishment; Carr controlled the machinery

ABC and its parent company, Disney, sued Carr and the FCC in August after the agency instructed ABC’s eight owned stations to seek license renewals years ahead of schedule. Broadcast licenses are not symbolic credentials. Their loss would threaten the stations’ ability to operate, giving the FCC enormous leverage over the speech of companies it regulates.

According to AliKhan’s opinion, Trump called for ABC’s licenses to be revoked 11 times over two years. Carr, she wrote, treated that rhetoric as “his marching orders.”

The chronology described by the court makes the institutional relationship difficult to disguise as ordinary administration. Carr directed the FCC’s Enforcement Bureau to investigate Disney’s employment practices and ordered another inquiry involving “The View.” Then, one day after Trump attacked a Jimmy Kimmel skit on social media, the commission began the early license-renewal process at Carr’s request.

AliKhan described the pattern as “call-and-response.” Trump publicly identified the target and demanded regulatory punishment; Carr possessed the authority to place that target under government scrutiny. The constitutional problem is not merely that the president complained about television coverage. It is that the chairman of an ostensibly independent regulator allegedly converted those complaints into official pressure backed by an “extreme, indeed existential” potential penalty.

The FCC’s explanation failed in court

The FCC argued that its treatment of ABC arose from a discrimination investigation rather than the network’s programming. AliKhan wrote that the explanation was not credible on the record before her.

That finding matters because bureaucratic retaliation rarely arrives labeled as retaliation. Government officials can invoke neutral-sounding procedures—employment investigations, expedited reviews, regulatory compliance—while the timing and public statements reveal whom the machinery is serving. Here, the judge considered Carr’s own words, Trump’s repeated demands and the sequence of agency actions.

Among those words was Carr’s warning to the network: “We can do this the easy way or the hard way.” Coming from the official overseeing licenses essential to ABC stations’ continued operation, that was not ordinary political criticism. It was regulatory pressure from an office capable of imposing the hard way.

AliKhan concluded that the FCC’s conduct created enough risk to chill “a broadcaster of ordinary firmness.” The First Amendment violation alleged by ABC therefore does not depend on the agency completing the punishment. A regulator can distort protected speech by making the cost of displeasing the president sufficiently clear.

An injunction, not an impeachment

Parloff argued that Carr’s conduct was knowing, “servile” and “gleeful,” and placed him high on his list of officials who should be impeached. He also characterized Carr’s alleged abuses as unusually flagrant and sadistic. Those descriptions belong to Parloff; the judicial finding at this stage is narrower.

The court granted ABC’s request only in part and issued a preliminary injunction, meaning AliKhan found the network likely to prevail on its First Amendment claim and entitled to protection while the litigation continues. Carr maintains that the lawsuit is “meritless” and says the accelerated review had nothing to do with ABC’s content. The FCC can challenge the order on appeal.

Still, the impeachment comparison draws its force from the conduct the opinion recounts. Congress entrusted the FCC chairman with public authority over communications infrastructure, not a mechanism for carrying out presidential vendettas against disfavored speakers. The alleged abuse is not confusion over where the constitutional line sits. It is the use of a regulator’s immense discretionary power in a pattern the judge found likely retaliatory—and the attempt to repackage that pattern as content-neutral enforcement.

For now, the injunction prevents Carr from advancing the early review. It also leaves the FCC with a problem larger than one halted proceeding: a federal court has found its official rationale unpersuasive and its chairman’s alignment with Trump’s demands sufficiently stark to threaten ABC’s First Amendment rights.

item.title: The threat to Trump’s retribution campaign is coming from his own government
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s campaign of retribution is colliding with federal judges, sworn testimony and the basic requirements of competent prosecution. In the case of former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, the administration’s own proceedings exposed an investigation pushed from the top of the FBI after Trump publicly attacked the two—and a federal magistrate dismissed the charges within two weeks, citing “rampant errors and misstatements.” That is the immediate obstacle to Trump’s proje
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s campaign of retribution is colliding with federal judges, sworn testimony and the basic requirements of competent prosecution. In the case of former FBI officials Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, the administration’s own proceedings exposed an investigation pushed from the top of the FBI after Trump publicly attacked the two—and a federal magistrate dismissed the charges within two weeks, citing “rampant errors and misstatements.”

That is the immediate obstacle to Trump’s project: not a lack of institutional power, but the evidentiary record created when his appointees try to convert presidential grievance into criminal cases.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A prosecution ordered from above

Floris and Benavides led the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force and participated in work examining possible foreign involvement in the 2020 election. The Trump administration had already fired them when the Justice Department targeted them again.

On Oct. 23, the office of U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro charged each former official with one count of making false statements to Congress. Prosecutors alleged that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee in 2023 about their roles in the FBI’s Hunter Biden investigations.

But testimony described by AlterNet, drawing on CNN’s reporting, showed that this was no ordinary case generated from the bottom up. FBI agent Bryan Witt testified that Director Kash Patel had personally instructed the bureau’s Kansas City field office to investigate Floris and Benavides for possible obstruction or conspiracy. Witt said he had never encountered such a directive from an FBI director.

Patel issued the order one day after Trump used a nationally televised speech to denounce the officials as “rogue bureaucrats” and accuse them of suppressing intelligence that China sought to help Joe Biden win in 2020. According to CNN’s account, FBI leadership supplied agents with potential charges and demanded continuing updates.

The sequence does not, by itself, prove that every allegation was invented. It does establish where the pressure originated: Trump named targets in public, Patel directed an investigation from headquarters, and federal agents were told to search for charges. Witt testified that most of those involved regarded the exercise as a “witch hunt.”

The case collapsed under scrutiny

Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui dismissed the charges after a hearing exposed how the investigation had been assembled. He faulted Justice Department lawyers for bringing a politically charged case riddled with errors and misstatements produced by its “slapdash” execution.

“If a high-profile case like this is so poorly executed, what can the public expect in the run-of-the-mill case with far less resources and oversight,” Faruqui wrote.

That question reaches beyond prosecutorial embarrassment. High-profile defendants can attract experienced counsel, press attention and a crowded courtroom. Floris and Benavides had fired FBI agents, former acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll and others present in solidarity at an early November hearing. Most people caught in the federal system do not arrive with that protection.

The administration had the power to fire these officials, investigate them, charge them and attach their names to alleged crimes. The dismissal checked the prosecution; it did not erase the punishment already imposed. Faruqui called the damage to their reputations “incalculable,” writing that they would remain associated with a politicized attack regardless of the case’s failure.

This is how state retaliation can produce consequences even when it loses in court. An indictment becomes a headline. Legal defense consumes money and time. Professional standing deteriorates. The government can fail to prove its case while still demonstrating its capacity to make targeted people suffer.

Fear is part of the institutional damage

Faruqui identified the warning delivered to the rest of the bureau: “They are one tweet away from being prosecuted by their own government.”

The danger he described was not confined to current employees. Politically driven investigations can shape who is willing to join the FBI, particularly its national-security work. “What sane person would join the FBI, particularly in the national security branch, under these circumstances?” he wrote, warning that the loss of capable agents and analysts would itself create a national-security risk.

That is the larger consequence of ordering law enforcement around presidential resentments. Agents learn that disputed investigative decisions may later be treated as potential crimes if a president needs enemies. Leadership learns that satisfying the White House can matter more than building a durable case. Prospective recruits learn that professional conduct offers no reliable protection from political targeting.

The administration’s failures also reveal the limits of the “weaponization” slogan Trump and his allies have used against their opponents. Here, the alleged weaponization is not an abstraction or a campaign grievance. A federal agent testified that Patel personally ordered the investigation; the order followed Trump’s televised attack; and a judge found the resulting prosecution so defective that he threw it out.

Retaliation checked, not dismantled

AlterNet reported that four people have so far succeeded with claims of vindictive prosecution by the Trump administration, citing Lawfare. They include Kilmar Ábrego García, whom the government sent illegally to a prison in El Salvador despite a judge’s explicit instruction, and a Russian-born Harvard scientist accused by the administration of smuggling clawed frog embryos into the United States.

Those cases differ substantially, and success in one does not establish the merits of another. What connects them is the role of courts in forcing the administration to account for actions taken against people it chose to pursue.

Judicial intervention has frustrated parts of Trump’s retribution campaign, but it has not removed the machinery that enabled it. Trump still commands the executive branch. Patel still leads the FBI. Pirro’s office still brought the charges. The institutional threat to the campaign is therefore narrow but real: when officials must testify, prosecutors must present competent evidence and judges are willing to examine the record, presidential vengeance can be exposed as a defective case rather than accepted as law enforcement.

For Floris and Benavides, that exposure came only after dismissal, public accusation and professional harm that Faruqui said they may never escape. The government lost the prosecution. It had already delivered the warning.

item.title: Top Clinton aide calls out Clinton, Obama and Biden over biggest blunders
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: William Galston, a former senior adviser to Bill Clinton, identifies three major Democratic failures: Joe Biden’s decision to seek a second term, Barack Obama’s handling of the recovery after the Great Recession, and Clinton’s support for admitting China to the World Trade Organization on highly accommodating terms. His criticism is notable because it reaches across three Democratic administrations—and because it exposes the limits of treating consequential exercises of presidential power as fai
item.content:encoded:
William Galston, a former senior adviser to Bill Clinton, identifies three major Democratic failures: Joe Biden’s decision to seek a second term, Barack Obama’s handling of the recovery after the Great Recession, and Clinton’s support for admitting China to the World Trade Organization on highly accommodating terms. His criticism is notable because it reaches across three Democratic administrations—and because it exposes the limits of treating consequential exercises of presidential power as failures of personal humility.

Galston told AlterNet that Biden still has not clearly acknowledged what he considers a “terrible mistake” with lasting national consequences. He faulted Obama for failing to accept greater responsibility for a painfully slow economic recovery and the social damage surrounding the country’s loss of manufacturing jobs. And he called China’s WTO entry near the end of Clinton’s presidency “a very large blunder,” albeit one based, in his assessment, on an honest judgment that proved badly wrong.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

These were not errors of tone. They were decisions and failures made by presidents who possessed enormous institutional authority. The people harmed by them did not need better apologies after the fact. They needed those holding power to make different choices while the choices still mattered.

Three presidents, three evasions

Galston’s sharpest criticism falls on Biden. While Biden has reportedly expressed regret about failing to address questions concerning his health more openly, Galston argues that this stops short of confronting the central decision: seeking another term. When AlterNet’s Matthew Rozsa said the country was still living with the consequences, Galston agreed and corrected his own use of the past tense.

The distinction matters. Regretting poor communication about one’s health is not the same as accepting responsibility for pursuing another four years in office. The first formulation makes the problem one of disclosure and political management. Galston’s formulation places agency where it belongs: on the incumbent president who decided to run.

His judgment of Obama is broader and more economic. Galston said he wanted the former president to accept more responsibility for the slow recovery after the Great Recession, which he believes contributed to Donald Trump’s election, as well as for the social consequences of manufacturing-job losses during the first decade of the century. That causal claim is Galston’s analysis, not an established finding presented in the interview. But it points toward a familiar political failure: governing elites treating headline recovery as sufficient while communities experience prolonged insecurity and institutional abandonment.

On Clinton, Galston turns to a decision made at the end of the administration in which he served. He said he was unsure whether Clinton had fully reckoned with the consequences of admitting China to the WTO under what Galston described as exceptionally accommodating terms. Calling the policy an honest miscalculation may explain its origins, but it does not reduce its scale. Good intentions do not redistribute the costs of a failed policy back onto the officials who designed it.

Penance is not accountability

The interview’s most revealing anecdote concerns George W. Bush. Galston recalled visiting the Bush Center and being shown a gallery of portraits Bush had painted of Iraq War veterans. As Bush described the subjects and what had happened to them, Galston interpreted the paintings as acts of personal penance—evidence that Bush regarded the war’s outcome and execution as more than a policy mistake.

That may illuminate Bush’s private conscience. It does not amount to public accountability for a war launched by his administration. Personal remorse and institutional responsibility occupy different categories. A president can feel anguish over the human consequences of his decisions without supplying a full public reckoning with how those decisions were made, justified and imposed.

The anecdote nevertheless fits Galston’s larger concern: leaders should acknowledge failure instead of manufacturing excuses or transferring blame. He invokes Dwight Eisenhower’s prepared acceptance of responsibility in case the D-Day invasion failed and John F. Kennedy’s admission of failure after the Bay of Pigs. But Galston also concedes that these examples may be remembered precisely because they were exceptional. His sense that responsibility-taking has declined is a judgment he says he cannot establish through rigorous historical analysis.

That caution is more useful than nostalgia. American political history does not offer a lost golden age in which presidents routinely confessed error and institutions reliably imposed consequences. The relevant question is not whether today’s leaders possess less admirable personalities. It is why the political system so often allows powerful officials to redefine major failures as communication problems, unforeseeable developments or unfortunate historical forces.

The convenient turn toward voters

Galston’s proposed remedy is electoral. He argues that voters should reward “peacemakers” and reject “warriors,” creating incentives for politicians to practice compromise and conciliation. If conciliatory candidates begin winning, he reasons, others will imitate them.

Political incentives plainly matter. But this diagnosis shifts much of the burden from officials who wield state power to voters choosing among candidates produced by parties, donors and institutions. Galston quotes George Bernard Shaw’s aphorism that democracy gives people what they deserve. In this context, the line risks turning democratic responsibility into a mechanism for laundering elite responsibility.

Voters did not personally negotiate China’s WTO terms. They did not control the pace or distribution of the post-recession recovery. They did not decide whether an incumbent president would seek another term. Presidents, senior advisers, party leaders and other powerful officials made or enabled those choices. Elections can punish them, but punishment after the damage is not the same as democratic control before it.

Conciliation also cannot substitute for judgment. Galston acknowledges that some conflicts involve principles that should not be compromised. That qualification is essential, because “political humility” becomes another form of evasion when it asks people bearing the costs of policy to reconcile themselves with those who imposed them. A politics that lowers the temperature while leaving the allocation of power untouched may be more decorous. It is not necessarily more accountable.

Galston’s criticism is strongest when he names the decisions presidents still resist confronting. It is weakest when the solution dissolves into a general appeal for voters to choose better temperaments. The three Democratic blunders he identifies were not produced by excessive partisan rhetoric alone. They came from concentrated presidential power, elite confidence and institutions willing to treat consequential judgment calls as errors whose architects could assess at their leisure.

item.title: Old friend trolls Trump with profane Nobel Peace Prize jab

item.content:encoded:
Geraldo Rivera answered Donald Trump’s campaign for a Nobel Peace Prize with a pointed alternative on Friday: give it to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Rivera, Trump’s friend since the 1970s, praised Zelenskyy’s leadership against Russia’s invasion, contrasted Ukrainian attacks on military targets with Vladimir Putin’s targeting of civilian infrastructure, and closed with an unmistakable rebuke: “F— Russia. Wake up President Trump. Slava Ukraini.”

The jab matters less as celebrity trolling than as an indictment from inside Trump’s long-standing social circle. Rivera’s message targeted the central distortion in Trump’s posture toward the war: the president treats the personal relationship he claims with Putin as an asset, while shifting responsibility for the conflict toward the mutual hostility between Putin and the leader of the country Putin invaded.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump turns aggression into a personality dispute

Rivera’s post followed an interview in which Zelenskyy criticized Trump’s “strange” relationship with Putin and expressed frustration with Washington’s handling of the war. Trump responded that the problem was that Zelenskyy and Putin “really hate each other.”

That formulation erases the defining asymmetry. Russia is the aggressor, Ukraine is resisting it, and Putin commands the forces attacking Ukrainian territory and infrastructure. Personal animosity may be real, but presenting it as the obstacle to peace converts a war of aggression into a quarrel between two difficult men. It is misdirection with institutional consequences because Trump controls the foreign-policy machinery of the United States; Zelenskyy does not.

Rivera rejected that frame. He described Zelenskyy as seeking “a just end to this war of Russian aggression” while leading Ukraine “with courage and brilliant innovation,” including strikes on distant Russian warships and military airfields. His comparison was explicit: Ukraine was hitting difficult military targets, while Putin was attacking civilian infrastructure and “other easy targets.”

The Nobel recommendation was therefore also a demand for moral and strategic clarity. Rivera was not merely praising Zelenskyy. He was telling Trump to identify the aggressor and use presidential power accordingly.

An administration fluent in Kremlin flattery

Trump’s language is not isolated from the conduct of his administration. Earlier in the same week, Jared Kushner—Trump’s son-in-law and special envoy in the peace negotiations—gave an interview lavishing praise on senior Russian figures. Kushner called Putin a “grand master of politics” and a “historic figure.” He described lead Russian negotiator Kirill Dmitriev as “an incredible friend” and Russian National Security Adviser Yuri Ushakov as “fantastic.”

That vocabulary reveals the administration’s orientation even without proving what motivates it. Officials entrusted with negotiating an end to Russia’s war are publicly admiring the political skill of the man directing it and celebrating relationships with his representatives. The warmth is conspicuous; the reported account contains no comparable tribute to the government resisting the invasion.

Dan Hoffman, a former chief of the CIA’s Moscow station, told Fox News on Friday that the administration’s approach had failed. He also challenged Trump’s repeated description of Putin as a friend: “Nations don’t have friends, typically. They have interests.”

That distinction is elementary but crucial. Trump personalizes statecraft around affinities, grievances and perceived loyalty. The United States, however, has interests and enormous leverage. Treating Putin’s favor as politically meaningful risks subordinating those interests to Trump’s fascination with personal relationships among powerful men.

The peace prize as presidential tribute

Trump has repeatedly promoted himself for the Nobel, claiming—with exaggeration, according to AlterNet—that he ended numerous wars. When he failed to receive the 2026 prize, he declared it “forever discredited” and said the decision placed an “indelible stain on Norway.”

His reaction went beyond wounded vanity. During his pressure campaign over Greenland earlier in the year, Trump texted Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre that because Norway had not awarded him the prize “for having stopped 8 Wars PLUS,” he no longer felt obliged “to think purely of Peace.”

The Nobel committee is independent of Norway’s government, but Trump’s message treated the award as something a foreign country owed him—and peaceful conduct as something he might condition on receiving it. That is not a peace doctrine. It is transactional coercion dressed up as personal injury.

Rivera’s nomination of Zelenskyy punctured precisely that conceit. Trump wants the honor attached to peacemaking while his administration praises the aggressor’s political mastery and describes the war through the supposed mutual hatred of its leaders. Rivera instead directed attention to the person leading the invaded country.

A friendship broken by the use of power

Rivera’s criticism carries history. He broke with Trump after Trump attempted to overturn the 2020 election, though he has alternated between defending and condemning his old friend during Trump’s second term. In recent months, the condemnations have become sharper.

Earlier in the year, Rivera compared Trump’s corruption to the conduct of a “mob boss.” In September, he criticized Trump’s attempt to put his own name on the Kennedy Center, saying, “There is no honor in that, only spite.” Later that month, he called Trump’s taxpayer-funded midterm advertisements attacking Democrats “unhinged” and unconstitutional.

Those disputes share a common feature: Trump’s use of public power for personal vindication, promotion or advantage. The Nobel fixation fits the pattern. So does his response to being denied it. He does not merely crave recognition; he speaks as though governments and institutions incur obligations when they fail to provide it.

Rivera’s profanity made the exchange easy to package as a troll by an old friend. But the substantive rebuke was more severe. A president with the power to shape Ukraine’s survival is framing an invasion as interpersonal hatred, while his emissary celebrates the invading regime’s leadership. “Wake up” was Rivera’s phrase. The reported record suggests the problem is not that Trump lacks information about which country invaded the other. It is what he chooses to center despite knowing it.

item.title: Conservative analyst exposes Trump’s troubling boardroom precedent
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump says he personally convinced Nvidia’s board to restore Jensen Huang as CEO after Huang resigned amid questions involving national security, alleged chip smuggling and extramarital affairs. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump says he personally convinced Nvidia’s board to restore Jensen Huang as CEO after Huang resigned amid questions involving national security, alleged chip smuggling and extramarital affairs. The intervention matters beyond one executive’s fate: according to the reporting, the president used the power of his office to influence who runs a corporation whose technology sits at the center of U.S. export policy—and whose shares Trump reportedly owns.

Brayden Myers, a financial policy analyst at the libertarian Reason Foundation, identified the precedent in a Friday analysis for the Washington Examiner. Corporate leaders answer to shareholders through boards, he argued, not to presidential preference. Once continued employment depends on White House approval, corporate governance begins to look less like governance than proximity management.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A board decision reversed after White House pressure

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 after acknowledging extramarital affairs, including one with a woman whom U.S. intelligence says Chinese intelligence recruited. Nvidia’s board brought in outside lawyers to investigate and announced on Nov. 17 that it did not plan to reinstate him.

The matter also extended beyond Huang’s personal conduct. Several House committees scheduled closed-door hearings with him as part of their investigation into alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips to China. Because those chips are highly sensitive components of U.S. export policy, Myers argued, Nvidia’s board had a duty to protect shareholders from potential legal and national-security exposure.

Then the Trump administration intervened. CNN reported that senior officials led by Vice President JD Vance lobbied Nvidia’s board over the weekend. On Nov. 23, the board said input from senior levels of the federal government had made it confident that Huang did not pose a national-security risk, although its investigation remained open.

Within hours, Trump supplied the bluntest account of what had happened: “I convinced them.”

That statement strips away any convenient fiction that the board simply reconsidered on its own. The reversal followed pressure from the administration, and the president publicly claimed responsibility for producing it. The board retained the formal authority to reinstate Huang, but the White House brought the institutional leverage.

Public authority, private holdings

Myers suggested Nvidia’s falling share price probably influenced Trump’s calculation. The Washington Post, meanwhile, reported that Trump owns between $13 million and $62 million in Nvidia stock.

The supplied reporting does not establish that Trump acted to increase the value of his holdings. It does establish an obvious conflict that cannot be waved away: a president with a reported multimillion-dollar financial stake in Nvidia intervened in a leadership dispute at Nvidia, then advertised his success when the board reversed course.

The administration itself was reportedly divided. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent favored an outside search for new leadership, according to the account. Trump and officials led by Vance instead pressed for Huang’s return. The faction with direct access to the board prevailed.

The market can price political access

Huang’s qualifications are not seriously in question. He led Nvidia for 33 years and made an early bet on artificial intelligence that helped turn the company into a corporate giant. Myers considers him probably the best candidate for the job.

But competence does not answer the governance question. An executive can be exceptionally valuable without being entitled to presidential rescue. Myers pointed to Apple’s success under Tim Cook as evidence that even a leader closely identified with a company is not literally irreplaceable.

More revealing is Myers’s suggestion that Nvidia’s share-price surge after Huang’s return may partly reflect a belief that he enjoys access to the administration. If investors value an executive not only for operating skill but also for his relationship with the president, political favor becomes a corporate asset. That is the incentive structure created when the White House makes itself an arbiter of boardroom leadership.

The consequences are widely distributed because Nvidia is a major holding in index funds and pension plans used by millions of Americans. Their savings are exposed not merely to Nvidia’s commercial performance, but potentially to a system in which presidential access affects corporate value.

The precedent runs in both directions

Trump intervened here to restore an executive. Myers’s warning is that the same asserted authority can be used to remove one. A future president could pressure a board to fire a leader who is politically inconvenient, and point to Nvidia as proof that presidential involvement in corporate succession has already been normalized.

“A company whose leadership is contingent on the president’s approval is not being held accountable by its shareholders but rather by their proximity to power,” Myers wrote.

That is the central issue, not whether Huang is talented or whether Nvidia’s stock recovered. The board had an open investigation, lawmakers were examining alleged chip smuggling, and the company had declared that Huang would not return. Senior administration officials applied pressure; the board changed its position; Trump claimed the result.

The danger in that sequence is concrete. It teaches corporate boards that the president’s wishes belong inside their deliberations—and teaches markets that access to him may be worth pricing into Americans’ retirement accounts.

item.title: MAGA melts down over car seat law they claim will 'kill the birth rate'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: California’s new child-passenger law does not require every teenager to ride in a booster seat until age 16. It requires children ages 8 through 15 to use one only when a standard seat belt fails a five-step fit test. Yet over Thanksgiving, prominent MAGA voices converted that safety standard into a lurid story about 16-year-old drivers trapped in booster seats—and then blamed it for suppressing the birth rate. item.content:encoded:
California’s new child-passenger law does not require every teenager to ride in a booster seat until age 16. It requires children ages 8 through 15 to use one only when a standard seat belt fails a five-step fit test. Yet over Thanksgiving, prominent MAGA voices converted that safety standard into a lurid story about 16-year-old drivers trapped in booster seats—and then blamed it for suppressing the birth rate.

The uproar began with Katie Miller, wife of White House chief of staff Stephen Miller. “The fastest way to kill the birth rate is mandating more car seats,” she wrote on X, arguing that car seats complicate motherhood through vehicle-width constraints, anchors and the difficulty of traveling with them.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That complaint contains a recognizable burden: transporting several children safely can be expensive and inconvenient. But Miller inflated a conditional fit requirement into a sweeping mandate and leapt from inconvenience to demographic collapse. The target was not the cost of raising children, the design of family policy or the economic choices available to parents. It was a seat-belt rule.

A fit test became a blanket mandate

Under the law as AlterNet describes it, children between 8 and 15 may use an ordinary seat belt whenever it fits properly under the five-step test. Age alone does not determine whether a booster is necessary; height and belt placement matter. Many older children will therefore qualify for regular restraints.

That distinction dismantles the most provocative image circulated by the law’s critics. A 15-year-old with a learner’s permit would not automatically be “confined” to a booster seat, as a New York Post opinion article suggested. Nor does the law create a general rule that 16-year-olds must use boosters, despite repeated conservative claims built around that premise.

Robby Starbuck, an America First-aligned host, mocked the idea of a short 16-year-old being strapped into a booster while licensed to drive and asked Gov. Gavin Newsom whether “mommy” should buckle the teenager in. But the scenario he attacked does not match the law summarized in the reporting. The joke works only after replacing the actual policy with an easier target.

The New York Post similarly called the measure “nonsensical” and folded it into the familiar charge that California is a “nanny state.” Others repeated the label, including one self-described space industrialist who called the state a “literal nanny state.” Repetition did the work that accuracy could not.

The burden is real; the demographic claim is not

Some participants offered a more grounded point. Palmer Luckey, founder of Oculus VR and ModRetro, suggested that automakers could design vehicles and options specifically for new mothers. That response at least identifies a material constraint and proposes that companies serve families better.

Jeremy Carl, a senior fellow at the right-wing Claremont Institute and former Hoover Institution research fellow, attacked CNN’s S.E. Cupp for questioning whether Miller was serious. Carl said anyone who had tried to fit three car seats into a standard vehicle or travel with several restraints would understand the complaint.

But experience with cramped cars does not establish Miller’s claim that booster-seat requirements are “the fastest way to kill the birth rate.” It establishes that American transportation and consumer products often make family life needlessly cumbersome. Turning that structural problem into an attack on a conditional safety rule lets more powerful actors disappear from view: governments deciding whether to support families, employers determining pay and leave, and industries deciding what kinds of households their products will accommodate.

The misdirection became clearer in Gabriel Syme’s nostalgic account of six children piling into a station wagon without seat belts. He contrasted that childhood with the time modern parents spend securing children and warned that leaving them unattended could bring arrest or family separation. Whatever legitimate questions exist about overcriminalization or burdens on parents, riding unrestrained in a station wagon is not evidence that restraint standards are malicious. It is evidence that earlier generations routinely accepted risks now governed by safety rules.

Culture-war arithmetic

The political maneuver is familiar: take a narrow regulation, exaggerate its reach, attach it to a genuine social anxiety and declare the state the enemy. Here, collapsing birth rates supply the anxiety. California supplies the villain. Parents supply the emotional leverage.

The result is an argument that sounds pro-family while refusing to examine the conditions that shape family decisions. AlterNet reported that much of the online response pointed instead to affordability. Rep.-elect Sara McGee chose ridicule, writing that she was thankful Katie Miller was not her mother. Others argued that anyone unable to manage a car seat should reconsider having children.

That last response is glib in the opposite direction. Car seats do impose costs and logistical demands, especially on larger families and people without roomy vehicles. Dismissing those burdens concedes useful territory to demagogues who exploit them. The sharper answer is that a burden can be real while the political claim constructed from it remains false.

Miller and her defenders could have argued for cheaper restraints, better vehicle design or greater material support for parents. Instead, they turned a seat-belt fit test into demographic sabotage. The law’s actual terms were inconvenient to that story, so the story proceeded without them.

item.title: The simple reason Trump has failed at passing any major laws
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s weakness as a domestic legislator is not mysterious, according to MIT political scientist Charles Stewart. Trump built a political career around commanding attention and humiliating opponents, but lawmaking requires something his performance-driven style does not reliably provide: partners who trust that compromise will not be repackaged as surrender. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s weakness as a domestic legislator is not mysterious, according to MIT political scientist Charles Stewart. Trump built a political career around commanding attention and humiliating opponents, but lawmaking requires something his performance-driven style does not reliably provide: partners who trust that compromise will not be repackaged as surrender. Stewart told AlterNet that Trump’s confrontational communication may mobilize an audience, yet it works poorly as a tool for assembling durable legislative coalitions.

That is a persuasive explanation for limited legislative effectiveness, though AlterNet’s headline goes further than the interview establishes. Stewart described Trump as “not particularly successful domestically, legislatively.” The supplied reporting does not inventory Trump’s record or substantiate the absolute claim that he has passed no major laws. The narrower conclusion is still politically revealing: occupying the presidency gives Trump enormous power, but spectacle alone cannot perform the institutional work of governing.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A negotiating strategy built for an audience

Stewart distinguished Trump’s approach from the conventional bargaining needed to move legislation through Congress. On divisive domestic questions such as health and social policy, lawmakers face entrenched partisan conflict. Agreements become more feasible when an issue divides each party internally, allowing a coalition to form across party lines. Stewart identified artificial intelligence and negotiations surrounding the Iran war as possible examples, although their visibility would make them unusual terrain for bipartisan bargaining.

Trump’s political language creates an additional obstacle. His aggressive, trolling style rewards confrontation in public, but negotiation depends on private assurances and some tolerance for mutual credit. Legislators asked to compromise with a president need reason to believe he will not portray their concession as weakness for the entertainment of his supporters.

The problem is not that Trump lacks communication skills. He has repeatedly demonstrated an ability to capture public attention. It is that attention and agreement are different political products. A message designed to dominate a news cycle can make accommodation more costly for everyone else, particularly when the president’s brand depends on identifying winners to celebrate and losers to ridicule.

That incentive structure places responsibility where it belongs. Congressional polarization constrains any president, but Trump chose and cultivated a style that compounds those constraints. He is not merely trapped by a dysfunctional institution. His public method can make that institution harder to operate.

Flattery is not a governing program

The limits of Trump’s approach help explain the recurring idea that political actors can secure his cooperation by appealing to his vanity. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed suggested letting Trump attach his name to a potential Medicare for All bill, an overture framed as a way for Democrats to subordinate partisan ego to a policy goal.

Stewart was skeptical. He characterized the suggestion as more likely an act of trolling or political messaging than a serious negotiating strategy. That judgment punctures an appealingly simple theory: that Congress can unlock sweeping reform by finding the correct compliment for the president.

Foreign leaders, Stewart said, have sometimes found that flattery can take them unusually far with Trump. But personal inducement is not a substitute for the interests, votes and procedural work required to enact domestic legislation. A flattering pitch might win attention. It does not automatically reconcile members of Congress whose parties, donors, constituencies and ideological commitments pull them elsewhere.

The historical example raised in the AlterNet interview—the failure of Richard Nixon and congressional Democrats to reach agreement on health policy in the early 1970s—also shows that credit-seeking and partisan ego long predate Trump. Yet reducing legislative conflict to wounded pride can misdirect responsibility away from the officials with the power to bargain, schedule votes and build coalitions. El-Sayed’s proposal may expose the absurdity of personality-centered government, but it does not dissolve the institutional conflict surrounding Medicare for All.

Publicity once served coalition-building

Presidents have always used performance. Theodore Roosevelt exploited the “bully pulpit” to rally public opinion, while John F. Kennedy adapted effectively to television. Ronald Reagan carried professional entertainment experience into politics and became a consequential legislator.

Stewart’s distinction is not between theatrical and sober presidents. It is between performance used to construct a governing majority and performance treated as the governing achievement itself.

Roosevelt appealed to progressive Republicans and voters who might otherwise support Democrats. Reagan, after serving as governor of California, surrounded himself with people who understood legislative mechanics and could translate presidential communication into political action. His record cannot be explained by charisma alone; he had acquired experience in what Stewart called the “small ball of politics,” and his administration employed people capable of doing that work.

Trump moved directly from reality television into the presidency without an intervening career in government. Stewart argued that this missing apprenticeship matters. Domestic legislation is difficult, detailed labor. Presidents do not enact bills by issuing commands or attracting coverage. They must manage factions, delegate to competent operators and offer potential allies a reason to accept the risks of cooperation.

The presidency cannot be run as a permanent taunt

AlterNet’s interview does not prove that Trump’s background as an entertainer caused every legislative failure, and Stewart did not claim that it did. Polarization, ideological conflict and divisions within Congress remain powerful constraints. Nor does the comparison with Reagan establish that political experience necessarily produces good policy; it establishes that experience can make a president more effective at imposing policy.

That is the sharper lesson. Legislative ineffectiveness should not be mistaken for harmlessness, just as legislative success should not be confused with public benefit. A president can wield executive and international power while struggling to build congressional majorities. But when domestic government does require cooperation, Trump’s signature tactic becomes a liability: the taunt that thrills spectators gives potential partners advance notice that they may become the next prop in the show.

Trump knows how to keep attention fixed on Trump. Stewart’s account suggests that he has been far less adept at converting that attention into the painstaking relationships through which major laws are made. The gap is not between entertainment and politics. It is between performing power and doing the work necessary to exercise it through Congress.

item.title: Comer Has a Stereotype. He Wants You to Hear a Verdict.
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: An investigation exists. Public proof of welfare fraud does not. James Comer’s rhetoric depends on blurring that distinction. item.content:encoded:
An investigation exists. Public proof of welfare fraud does not. James Comer’s rhetoric depends on blurring that distinction.

James Comer knows how to turn a conditional accusation into a declaration of guilt.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Discussing Representative Ilhan Omar on Newsmax, the House Oversight chairman predicted an indictment and announced: “They’ve got her on two fronts.”

Then came the familiar ingredients: immigration fraud and welfare fraud. A Somali-born Black Muslim congresswoman, her family, her citizenship, and public assistance—all bundled into a story whose conclusion the audience is invited to supply before seeing the evidence.

The existence of an investigation is real. Comer’s certainty is a political product.

What the records establish

Federal agents searched Omar’s Washington home on October 12, 2026, under a judicially authorized warrant. Grand jury subpoenas to relatives have been reported. These are consequential investigative actions. They establish that the government is pursuing a case; they do not establish that its allegations are true.

The unsealed filings show prosecutors submitted an affidavit, warrant attachments, and supplemental legal arguments. Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh requested a fuller explanation of probable cause, required changes to search procedures, and ultimately authorized the warrant. The record therefore contains evidence of judicial scrutiny—not a basis for declaring the judge corrupt simply because he signed it.

But the public cannot meaningfully audit the factual foundation. The underlying 67-page affidavit remains sealed. AP’s review found that the released documents did not disclose new details explaining the investigation or the search’s outcome.

That distinction matters. A judge evaluated material the public cannot see. His authorization is a legal act, not public access to the evidence supporting it.

A sweeping search is not a public demonstration of guilt

The visible filings describe a scope reaching back to 1980 and authorize seizure categories including records, phones, and electronic storage. Suspected offenses and important limiting language are redacted. Those omissions prevent an independent assessment of whether the breadth was justified. The timeline alone proves neither a legitimate evidentiary necessity nor an unlawful fishing expedition.

The judge’s insistence on protections for legislative material is significant. It shows a constitutional boundary being enforced. It cannot answer the separate question of whether the government’s underlying allegations withstand scrutiny.

We should resist both unsupported conclusions: that judicial authorization establishes an honorable investigation, or that the visible breadth establishes judicial corruption. Neither follows from the accessible record.

Comer practices no such restraint.

Where the evidence stops, the stereotype starts

Newsweek’s report on Comer’s appearance explicitly noted that he supplied no evidence backing his allegations. It also reported that Omar had not been charged and denied wrongdoing. His prediction was presented as a prediction—not confirmation from prosecutors of an impending indictment.

Yet “they’ve got her” communicates a completed evidentiary victory. It tells the audience the matter is settled while the supporting material remains unavailable.

“Welfare fraud” supplies an especially potent shortcut. The racist welfare-cheat trope casts Black people as fraudulent claimants on public resources. Attached to a refugee’s family history, it merges economic suspicion with suspicion of belonging: she came here improperly, took something improperly, and therefore never deserved to be here.

That is an analysis of the rhetoric—not a claim that the records prove Comer’s private motives. The mechanism is visible in what he asks his audience to accept without presenting evidence.

A separate inquiry into financial disclosures does not fill that gap. Investigating financial reporting is not proof of stealing public benefits. Treating every financial suspicion as interchangeable lets the accusation expand while its factual content disappears.

Accountability requires particulars

Public scrutiny should demand the suspected offense, reliable supporting evidence, and an explanation of why the search’s scope was necessary. Some information may remain sealed during an investigation. That does not entitle a congressional chairman to manufacture certainty from secrecy.

If prosecutors possess credible evidence, it must withstand the legal process. If they have stretched old suspicions into a politically directed investigation, that abuse demands exposure.

Until the evidence can be assessed, Comer has no warrant to sell guilt.

The accusation is new television. The stereotype is old machinery.

item.title: Trump relative exposes 'humiliating' mashed potato incident he never forgot
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Mary Trump says the mashed-potato incident her uncle never forgot began with five-year-old Donald Trump tormenting his younger brother Robert and ended when their older brother, Fred Jr., dumped a bowl of potatoes over Donald’s head. The family laughed. Decades later, Mary Trump argues, the episode helps explain the president’s fixation on humiliating others—but her family story supports a narrower conclusion more securely than a sweeping psychological diagnosis: Trump was already bullying someone smaller, and ridicule stopped him when parental authority did not.

A bully interrupted

In a Thanksgiving video posted to YouTube, Mary Trump described a family dinner at which Donald repeatedly harassed Robert while their mother, Mary Anne Trump, struggled to serve the meal. According to her account, he took pleasure in destroying things Robert valued, including gluing together his building blocks and dismantling his Tonka trucks.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Mary Trump said her grandmother pleaded and shouted but could not make Donald stop. Fred Jr., nearly eight years older than Donald, then chose a remedy that was forceful without being violent: He picked up a large bowl of mashed potatoes and emptied it onto Donald’s head.

“And you know what? It worked,” Mary Trump said.

The room initially fell silent, according to her telling, before the family—including Donald’s mother—began laughing. Donald’s sister later revived the story at family gatherings, including Thanksgiving and Christmas, turning the episode into recurring family lore.

The headline-ready object is the mashed potatoes. The consequential detail is the hierarchy: Donald was tormenting a younger child who could not stop him, ignoring a mother whose authority he rejected, and was finally checked by an older, stronger brother. The humiliation did not create the bullying described in the story. It interrupted it.

A family theory becomes a political diagnosis

Mary Trump, an author and clinical psychologist who has publicly opposed her uncle and his political agenda, interprets the dinner as a formative lesson. She said Donald concluded both that humiliation was something he must avoid and that it could be wielded as a weapon.

That is her psychological reading, not an independently established causal account. One childhood memory—even one repeatedly retold—cannot by itself explain an adult political career. Mary Trump’s interpretation also risks assigning too much power to the family’s laughter and too little to the conduct that preceded it. In her own account, the future president was already using domination as what she called a form of “self-soothing.”

She places that behavior within a broader family culture established by Fred Trump Sr. Her grandfather, she said, enjoyed humiliating people who were weaker and dependent on him. She argues that Donald’s motive differs: Where Fred Sr. allegedly took pleasure in degradation, Donald uses it defensively.

That distinction may matter clinically, but it offers little comfort politically. Whether humiliation is deployed for enjoyment or self-protection, the burden still falls on the chosen target. A president has access to institutions, audiences and loyal political actors that a five-year-old at a dinner table did not. The weapon, if Mary Trump’s theory is right, acquired vastly greater reach.

The limits of the origin story

Family anecdotes are irresistible because they compress a public figure into a single revealing scene. They can also misdirect responsibility. Explaining Trump’s behavior through a loveless upbringing, a domineering father or one embarrassing dinner can make his later conduct sound like the automatic expression of childhood damage.

It is not. Mary Trump’s account may illuminate a pattern, but it does not transfer agency away from the adult who repeats it or from the people and institutions that reward it. Childhood can shape a person without absolving the choices that person later makes with power.

The mashed-potato story is therefore less useful as a tidy origin myth than as an early illustration of a familiar structure: a stronger person targets someone weaker, ordinary authority fails to restrain him, and only an intervention carrying immediate social consequences makes him stop. Mary Trump remembers the humiliation. Her own account makes the unchecked cruelty that came first harder to ignore.

item.title: Trump ‘could absolutely’ be removed from office: polling guru
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet’s headline overstates Nate Silver’s argument. item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s headline overstates Nate Silver’s argument. Silver did not report that President Donald Trump is on a clear path to removal; he said Trump “could absolutely” be convicted by the Senate if his collapsing approval and the Nvidia scandal produced enough Republican defections. The obstacle is decisive: although Democrats won both chambers in the November 3 midterms, removing Trump would still require a two-thirds Senate vote, meaning a substantial bloc of Republican senators would have to abandon him.

Silver’s case, made Wednesday on Still Counting, rests on political deterioration rather than an announced impeachment drive. Prediction markets put the chance of Trump being impeached and removed before his term ends at roughly 25 percent—odds Silver called “entirely reasonable.” That is a market estimate, not a congressional count, and possibility is not momentum.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Nvidia turns party loyalty into a liability

The more consequential issue is the conduct Silver says could make removal plausible. On Monday, Nvidia’s board reinstated ousted CEO Jensen Huang after Trump pressured the company to restore him, according to AlterNet. Huang had reportedly had an affair with a woman widely believed to be a Chinese agent, while Nvidia faced questions about efforts to evade U.S. export controls.

Silver argued that if Trump was working to “profit off selling advanced chips to China,” removal would be warranted, calling such conduct “a profound betrayal of his base.” The conditional matters: the supplied reporting does not establish that Trump personally sought profit from chip sales. It does establish, as AlterNet reports it, that he used presidential pressure on behalf of Huang despite national-security concerns surrounding Huang and Nvidia.

That is where the story’s institutional stakes lie. A president can turn informal pressure into a material corporate outcome without waiting for Congress to legislate or an agency to act. Nvidia’s board made the reinstatement decision, but Trump reportedly applied the pressure that preceded it. Concentrating only on Huang’s personal exposure would misdirect attention from the public official wielding state power and the directors who yielded to it.

The political danger for Trump comes from his own coalition’s hostility toward China. An Economist/YouGov poll cited on the program found that 54 percent of Americans believed the affair definitely or probably compromised national security. Among Republicans, the figure was 61 percent. Those results measure public belief about the affair; they do not prove a security breach. But they show why Trump’s intervention could be unusually costly inside a party that has made confrontation with China central to its identity.

Republican criticism is not yet a removal coalition

Two Republican senators have publicly broken with the administration’s handling of the matter. Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton called the scandal “just the tip of the iceberg.” North Dakota Sen. Kevin Cramer said the possibility that a Chinese asset could extort Huang was sufficient reason not to rehire him.

Those statements puncture the appearance of party unanimity, but criticism is cheaper than conviction. Nothing in AlterNet’s report indicates that Cotton, Cramer or other Republican senators have committed to removing Trump. Silver’s broader theory is that Republicans who survived the midterms and face voters again in 2028 may fear being dragged down by an increasingly unpopular president.

Trump’s approval rating was 35.9 percent in Silver Bulletin’s average. Silver said that, if the decline continued at the same pace, it could reach roughly 29 percent by the end of the following year. That is an extrapolation, not a forecast carved into the calendar. Approval can stabilize or recover. Its immediate significance is leverage: elected Republicans become more willing to defy a president when loyalty looks electorally dangerous rather than politically compulsory.

Silver said that, were he a Democratic leader such as Hakeem Jeffries or Chuck Schumer, he would already be counting votes for a veto-proof two-thirds majority to impose tougher China export controls. That would test Republican senators on policy before asking them to take the far more drastic step of ending a presidency. It would also force Trump’s allies to choose publicly between the president and the China restrictions their party’s voters say they favor.

A constitutional possibility sold as a probability

One of Silver’s co-hosts, Malone, rejected the removal scenario outright, saying it was more likely that Marco Rubio or JD Vance would resign than that Trump would be impeached and convicted. That disagreement is the clearest description of the present situation: Trump’s vulnerability is no longer unimaginable, but the reported facts do not show that removal is approaching.

The headline’s teaser therefore resolves to a narrower claim. Trump “could absolutely” be removed because the Constitution permits it, Democrats control Congress, his approval is weak, and the Nvidia affair has drawn criticism from Republican senators and voters. Yet Democrats cannot do it alone, prediction-market odds are not Senate votes, and rebukes from Cotton and Cramer are not commitments to convict.

What has changed is the cost structure around Republican obedience. Trump reportedly spent presidential influence to secure a corporate reinstatement that most Republican respondents in the cited poll viewed as compromising national security. Whether that becomes an impeachable rupture depends less on Democratic outrage than on how many Republican senators decide Trump has become more dangerous to their careers than defying him.

item.title: Trump is on 'death’s door' and no one’s covering it: ex-MSNBC host
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Joy Reid’s claim is blunt but unproven: President Donald Trump “looks like he’s on death’s door,” she said Wednesday on Shannon Sharpe’s Club Shay Shay podcast. Reid offered no medical evidence that Trump is dying. Her substantive charge was about the press—namely, that journalists soften or ignore signs of decline in the 80-year-old president while having subjected Joe Biden to relentless scrutiny over his age and cognitive fitness. That distinction matters. Trump’s health cannot be diagnosed f
item.content:encoded:
Joy Reid’s claim is blunt but unproven: President Donald Trump “looks like he’s on death’s door,” she said Wednesday on Shannon Sharpe’s Club Shay Shay podcast. Reid offered no medical evidence that Trump is dying. Her substantive charge was about the press—namely, that journalists soften or ignore signs of decline in the 80-year-old president while having subjected Joe Biden to relentless scrutiny over his age and cognitive fitness.

That distinction matters. Trump’s health cannot be diagnosed from a podcast or his public appearance. The conduct of news organizations, however, can be examined. Reid alleged that Trump’s remarks are frequently edited into coherence and that visible signs of frailty receive little attention. Her criticism targets the institutions deciding what audiences see, what gets cleaned up and which presidential liabilities become sustained national stories.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The comparison Jake Tapper helped create

Reid singled out CNN’s Jake Tapper, co-author of Original Sin, the bestselling 2025 book about Biden’s cognitive decline and efforts by his White House to conceal it.

“Where’s Jake Tapper? Jake, where are you?” she asked.

The point was not that Biden deserved less scrutiny. A president’s capacity to perform the job is plainly legitimate news. Reid’s accusation is that the standard changed when a Republican returned to the White House: Biden’s deterioration became a major accountability story, while Trump’s age, appearance and often disjointed speech are treated less aggressively.

That allegation is more consequential than Reid’s “death’s door” flourish, which outruns the evidence presented. Trump’s health status remains a medical question. Whether editors repeatedly rescue his public statements from their original disorder is an editorial choice—one that can give audiences a more competent version of the president than the president himself supplied.

Editing can become political insulation

Reid said Trump’s statements are often “re-edited to seem coherent.” If broadcasters reduce wandering or confused remarks to polished excerpts without conveying their character, they are not merely shortening material. They may be changing the public’s understanding of how the president communicates and performs.

Trump’s age makes that choice especially salient. He turned 80 in June and was the oldest person ever sworn in as president. He also spent years attacking Biden’s mental fitness. A press corps that amplified those attacks but treats comparable questions about Trump as impolite or peripheral would not be maintaining neutrality. It would be preserving an asymmetry that Trump himself exploited.

Reid argued that the imbalance extends beyond Fox News. In her account, Democratic politicians face more demanding interviews, harder questions and stricter expectations, while Republicans routinely receive greater latitude. “There is no liberal media,” she said. “That is just not real.”

Reid is not a detached observer of that system. She formerly hosted The ReidOut in prime time on the left-leaning MSNBC, which canceled the program in early 2025. She now hosts The Joy Reid Show through YouTube, Substack and podcast platforms. That history does not settle her argument, but it does locate it: this is a former cable host accusing the national press—including institutions adjacent to her former employer—of applying its standards unevenly.

Petty scrutiny for Obama, deference for Trump

Reid contrasted Trump’s treatment with the coverage Barack Obama received. She recalled controversies over Obama wearing a tan suit, saluting while holding a coffee cup and presiding over the failed rollout of the Affordable Care Act website. Those incidents varied greatly in substance, but each became an occasion for extended judgment about Obama’s competence or respect for the presidency.

If Obama had used presidential power as Trump has, Reid argued, he “probably would have been impeached and convicted.”

“He’s black,” she added.

That is Reid’s interpretation, not a demonstrated counterfactual. But the comparison identifies how political misdirection works. Attention can be lavished on symbolic breaches by one president while far more consequential conduct by another is normalized through repetition. The distortion does not require journalists to endorse Trump. It requires only that they treat his abnormalities as familiar, convert his incoherence into usable clips and reserve their sharpest institutional scrutiny for politicians operating under stricter expectations.

Reid’s most defensible conclusion was therefore narrower than her most explosive line. “If the press covered Trump like they would have covered Obama or Biden, we might have a chance of a more educated public,” she said.

The public does not need reporters to pronounce Trump terminally ill. It needs them to show his remarks and conduct accurately, investigate credible questions about his fitness and apply the same evidentiary standard they used when Biden held power. Anything less turns editing, framing and selective intensity into political protection.
