item.title: Trump’s holiday rant has ex-MAGA fan calling for 25th Amendment
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s Thanksgiving post triggered fresh demands for his removal after he used the holiday to promote a false claim about Somali immigrants, allege political manipulation of economic data, advertise his proposed White House ballroom and threaten undocumented immigrants with permanent expulsion. Breck Worsham, described by the Daily Beast as a former “MAGA stalwart,” responded by saying he would be thankful for “a 25th Amendment action.” But the officials with the constitutional power to
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s Thanksgiving post triggered fresh demands for his removal after he used the holiday to promote a false claim about Somali immigrants, allege political manipulation of economic data, advertise his proposed White House ballroom and threaten undocumented immigrants with permanent expulsion. Breck Worsham, described by the Daily Beast as a former “MAGA stalwart,” responded by saying he would be thankful for “a 25th Amendment action.” But the officials with the constitutional power to begin that process—Vice President JD Vance and Trump’s Cabinet—gave no indication in the reporting that they would do so.

A presidential message built around targets

Trump published the more than 400-word post from his Mar-a-Lago resort, moving among grievances without abandoning a consistent political method: identify a population with little institutional power, depict it as predatory or undeserving, and place the president at the center of an imagined campaign of national retribution.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

He called for the expulsion of nearly the entire Somali population in the United States, relying on the false assertion that only 2 percent of Somalis work rather than receive government assistance. The demand was not merely another insult buried in a rambling social-media post. It paired false economic information with collective punishment based on national origin.

Trump also alleged that officials deliberately suppressed economic-growth figures before the midterm elections. AlterNet’s account does not identify whom he accused or report evidence supporting the charge. Presented as Trump’s allegation, it fits a familiar maneuver: unfavorable or inconvenient information becomes proof that unnamed officials secretly manipulated the system against him.

The president then praised the ballroom he wants to construct at the White House, claiming presidents had sought such a venue for more than 150 years. The boast sat alongside a sarcastic Thanksgiving message aimed at “murderers, drug dealers, and criminals of all shapes, sizes, and colors, who illegally entered our country.” He said he hoped they would enjoy life in their own countries and concluded, “We will miss you dearly, but you will never be back.”

That language collapses undocumented immigrants into violent criminals and treats deportation as a punchline. The misdirection is useful: migrants become the menace, while the president exercising the immense power of the federal government casts himself as the aggrieved party.

Calls for removal meet the officials protecting his tenure

Worsham was not alone in invoking constitutional removal. Commentator Mehdi Hasan wrote, “25th Amendment this guy. Seriously.” Mary Trump, the president’s estranged niece, directed her response at the party sustaining his power: “Hey, Republicans—is there any line you’re willing to draw, or is this ok with you, too?” Conservative commentator Bill Kristol called on the next Congress to impeach Trump quickly.

Mary Trump’s question identifies the institutional issue more accurately than the spectacle of one presidential post. Trump can publish the message, but Republican officials decide whether it carries consequences. Their authority—not the outrage of former supporters or commentators—determines whether condemnation becomes action.

Section 4 of the 25th Amendment does not operate through public revulsion. Vance and a majority of the Cabinet would have to declare Trump unable to discharge the duties of the presidency. If Trump disputed that declaration, keeping him from resuming power would require two-thirds votes in both the House and Senate. Impeachment would likewise depend on Congress.

The removal demands therefore expose a hard distinction between alarm and power. Those calling for action can describe the conduct; the people positioned to act are members of an administration and party whose power depends on Trump remaining president.

A second removal controversy in one week

The Thanksgiving post followed another episode earlier that week. On Monday, Trump shared an AI-generated image depicting Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang with blood on his face and holding a red bra. The image had been altered from the photograph of Trump after the 2024 assassination attempt in Butler, Pennsylvania. That post also produced calls for Trump’s removal, according to AlterNet.

Two eruptions in a week may intensify questions about Trump’s conduct, but repetition does not lower the constitutional threshold. The vice president, Cabinet and Congress remain the actors capable of converting concern into an official proceeding.

For now, the clearest result is not that Trump faces imminent removal. It is that he again used the presidency’s platform to circulate falsehood, stigmatize immigrants and recast executive aggression as personal grievance—while the officials empowered to restrain him remained, in AlterNet’s account, conspicuously outside the story.

item.title: Rumors swirl after Trump and Melania clocked in unusual walking pattern
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet’s evidence establishes only this: Melania Trump attended the Trump family’s Thanksgiving gathering at Mar-a-Lago and, in footage posted by actress and real estate consultant Amber Carey Gitter, walked well behind Donald Trump on the way to the dining room. It does not establish why she kept her distance, what the couple’s relationship is like, or whether the spacing meant anything at all. The “rumors” were social-media speculation built around a few seconds of choreography. That distinc
item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s evidence establishes only this: Melania Trump attended the Trump family’s Thanksgiving gathering at Mar-a-Lago and, in footage posted by actress and real estate consultant Amber Carey Gitter, walked well behind Donald Trump on the way to the dining room. It does not establish why she kept her distance, what the couple’s relationship is like, or whether the spacing meant anything at all. The “rumors” were social-media speculation built around a few seconds of choreography.

That distinction matters because a story about presidential power was reduced to amateur marital interpretation. Viewers were invited to diagnose a marriage from a walking pattern while the gathering itself displayed something more concrete: the presidency, the Trump family and the family’s private Florida club occupying the same stage.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A procession becomes a personality test

The footage showed Melania Trump behind other relatives, including Tiffany Trump and several grandchildren, rather than entering beside the president as she often has at public appearances. Her father, Viktor Knavs, was also present. According to the report, family members arranged themselves at the dining-room entrance so Melania stood beside him while diners applauded Donald Trump.

Online observers supplied the rest. One suggested Melania might be avoiding her husband. Another expressed sadness that Trump no longer walked with her; a reply rejected sympathy on the ground that she was “raking it in.” Others mocked the scene as “central casting” or asked whether Trump was “shaking down guests.”

Those comments reveal what the video cannot. They show an audience primed to read every physical gap as evidence of estrangement, coercion or financial calculation. None of those explanations is established by the footage. Treating them as news launders conjecture through repetition: anonymous interpretation becomes “rumors,” and the existence of rumors becomes the development.

The earlier footage proves no more

The Thanksgiving clip followed another scrutinized appearance at the White House’s annual turkey pardon. There, Donald and Melania Trump walked hand in hand, but observers described the interaction as stiff. The president appeared rigid, moved her hand abruptly and pulled her forward toward the audience; one viewer compared their movement to a tug-of-war.

That footage may support a narrow description of awkward public body language. It does not convert the later distance at Mar-a-Lago into a confirmed pattern with a known cause. A couple can look uncomfortable without the public learning why. Precision requires stopping where the evidence stops.

The stronger political observation is not a diagnosis of Melania Trump’s feelings. It is that presidential image management creates these scenes in the first place: staged entrances, applause, family placement and ceremonial gestures designed for cameras. When the performance looks strained, the same machinery that manufactures intimacy invites viewers to hunt for rupture.

The business story is real, but separate

AlterNet also connected the speculation to Melania Trump’s recently released television series. The report said the program debuted at sixth place on Amazon before falling on the platform’s charts. Forbes described its premiere as muted and reported that Amazon had spent a combined $75 million on rights and marketing for the series and the documentary film preceding it.

That is a concrete commercial story: a sitting first lady’s global celebrity was converted into an expensive Amazon media property that, according to the reported chart performance, did not sustain commensurate audience interest. It raises legitimate questions about how proximity to presidential power is packaged and monetized.

But the show’s weak performance does not explain where Melania Trump walked at Thanksgiving. Placing the two facts side by side encourages readers to construct a causal or emotional narrative the reporting cannot support. The same problem applies to questions about Barron Trump’s absence from the footage: viewers asked where he was, but the supplied reporting provides no answer.

The result is a piece framed around a mystery it cannot solve. Donald Trump’s entrance at his own club, surrounded by relatives and applauding diners, is visible. Melania Trump’s distance is visible. Her reason is not. The honest answer to the headline’s insinuation is therefore unsensational: she walked behind him, and everyone claiming to know why was guessing.

item.title: The Cheese That Broke the Free Market
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: How a humble Brazilian culinary innovation exposes the contradictions of capitalism, protectionism, regulation, and the relentless pursuit of corporate profitability. There is something almost comical about using a glass of requeijão to challenge the foundations of modern capitalism. Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself: ☕ Buy us a coffee And yet, here we are. I recently came across a Brazilian video titled “ Por Que o Requeijão Só Existe no Brasil? ” (“Why Does Requeijão
item.content:encoded:
How a humble Brazilian culinary innovation exposes the contradictions of capitalism, protectionism, regulation, and the relentless pursuit of corporate profitability.

There is something almost comical about using a glass of requeijão to challenge the foundations of modern capitalism.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

And yet, here we are.

I recently came across a Brazilian video titled “Por Que o Requeijão Só Existe no Brasil?” (“Why Does Requeijão Only Exist in Brazil?”). What initially appeared to be an interesting documentary about Brazilian culinary history turned out to contain the ingredients for a much broader economic discussion.

For those unfamiliar with it, Brazilian requeijão is a smooth, creamy dairy product made by melting fresh curds with dairy fat and emulsifying salts. It is neither American cream cheese nor the Portuguese product that shares its name. It has its own texture, flavor, manufacturing process, and culinary applications.

In Brazil, it is practically a household institution. We spread it on bread, put it on pizzas, stuff pastries with it, incorporate it into sauces, and use it in countless other dishes.

It is relatively inexpensive, versatile, commercially successful, and technologically straightforward to manufacture.

In other words, it is precisely the kind of product that free-market capitalism should enthusiastically embrace.

So why hasn't it conquered the world?

And why, in the country where it succeeded, are manufacturers increasingly interested in selling us something that merely looks like it?

When Necessity Was the Mother of Innovation

The history of Brazilian requeijão begins not in a corporate boardroom but in the practical difficulties of agricultural life.

Before refrigeration became widely available, preserving milk in Brazil's tropical climate was a considerable challenge. Rural communities developed techniques to transform perishable milk into products that could be stored and transported more easily.

Fresh curds were separated from the whey, washed, and cooked with dairy fat, producing what would become traditional Brazilian requeijão, including the firmer varieties known as requeijão de corte.

The objective was straightforward: make better use of an available resource and prevent waste.

There was no marketing department attempting to manufacture demand. There was no venture capital firm demanding exponential growth. There was a problem, and people developed a solution.

In 1911, the Italian immigrant couple Mário and Isaíra Silvestrini created Catupiry in Lambari, Minas Gerais, helping establish another chapter in the history of Brazilian dairy products.

Decades later, in Poços de Caldas, businessman Moacyr de Carvalho Dias, affectionately known as Xixo, and his team developed the creamy requeijão that Brazilians recognize today.

Accounts of its development describe hundreds of experiments culminating in the celebrated formula number 606.

The objective was not to imitate an existing American or European product. It was to create something with its own characteristics, using the resources and knowledge available locally.

And it worked.

Chemistry in the Service of Consumers

The technological challenge was not insignificant.

Milk proteins, particularly casein, form structures influenced by calcium. Heating cheese does not automatically transform it into a stable, homogeneous cream. Under unsuitable conditions, water and fat separate, leaving behind an unpleasant mass.

Emulsifying salts such as sodium citrate and phosphates help modify those protein structures, allowing the proteins to retain water and emulsify fat more effectively.

European cheese manufacturers had already employed this chemistry in processed cheeses. Brazilian manufacturers adapted it to fresh curds, creating a different kind of product.

The result was a mild, creamy, spreadable cheese that did not require months of maturation.

This matters economically.

Traditional aged cheeses require time, controlled storage conditions, substantial quantities of milk, and capital that remains immobilized while the product matures.

Requeijão, by contrast, can be manufactured through a much shorter production cycle. Its higher moisture content also contributes to a greater finished-product yield, although the dairy fat added during manufacturing must be included in any honest comparison of production costs.

None of this means that requeijão is inherently superior to Parmesan, Gruyère, or Cheddar. They are different products serving different culinary purposes.

But where a creamy, spreadable dairy product is desirable, requeijão represents a compelling alternative.

It is an example of chemistry and industrial engineering being used to deliver something genuinely useful to consumers.

Remember that distinction. We will return to it.

The Packaging That Refused to Become Garbage

There was another innovation associated with the commercialization of requeijão: its packaging.

Instead of treating the container as something destined for the garbage, manufacturers sold the product in glass cups that could subsequently be used as ordinary drinking glasses.

Generations of Brazilians grew up drinking water, juice, coffee, and other beverages from former requeijão containers.

Long before corporations discovered that they could put green leaves on their logos and call themselves environmentally responsible, Brazilian households were practicing a perfectly functional form of packaging reuse.

The consumer bought a dairy product and received a reusable glass as part of the transaction.

No sustainability subscription.

No premium environmental surcharge.

No corporate campaign explaining how buying more products would somehow save the planet.

Just a useful container that remained useful after fulfilling its original purpose.

The packaging delivered value beyond the contents.

It was not necessarily the most profitable arrangement imaginable for the manufacturer, but it was certainly a practical one for the consumer.

The Free Market, in Theory

According to the familiar narrative of free-market capitalism, a business identifies an opportunity, develops a product, and introduces it to consumers.

If the product is good, affordable, and useful, consumers buy it. Competitors recognize the opportunity and develop alternatives. Competition encourages improvements, reduces prices, and rewards innovation.

Everybody wins.

Brazilian requeijão appears to satisfy many of these conditions.

It offers potential manufacturing efficiencies, a short production cycle, multiple culinary applications, and demonstrated consumer acceptance in a substantial domestic market.

One would expect international dairy companies to recognize the opportunity, introduce the product into their markets, and let consumers decide whether they like it.

After all, isn't that supposed to be the entire point of a free market?

Instead, outside Brazil, requeijão remains largely a specialty product.

Brazilian expatriates frequently seek it out in stores catering to their communities, sometimes paying considerably more than they would at home.

Having lived in the United States for years, I am familiar with the peculiar experience of discovering that something entirely ordinary in one country can become an expensive specialty product in another.

But requeijão is particularly interesting because there is no obvious technological reason why American or European manufacturers could not produce it themselves.

The chemistry does not cease to function when it crosses the equator.

American cows are not fundamentally incompatible with Brazilian dairy engineering.

The manufacturing equipment is not a closely guarded national secret.

In fact, as far back as June 2000, Pesquisa FAPESP reported that a dairy company in Houston, Texas, had entered into an agreement with Brazil's Federal University of Viçosa to establish a production line for Brazilian dairy products, including requeijão.

The technology was available. Someone had already recognized the commercial opportunity.

And yet, more than two decades later, requeijão has not become an ordinary fixture of American supermarkets.

When Reality Doesn't Fit the Regulatory Schema

Part of the explanation may lie in the regulatory systems governing food production and international trade.

The Brazilian video argues that requeijão falls between established American categories of dairy products.

There is some substance to this argument, although the situation is more nuanced than the video suggests.

American food regulations establish specific standards of identity for numerous products, including cream cheese, processed cheese, and processed cheese spreads.

These standards define permissible ingredients, manufacturing characteristics, moisture content, fat content, and other requirements.

Brazilian requeijão does not necessarily fit neatly into these categories.

The traditional American standard for pasteurized processed cheese spread, for example, establishes a maximum moisture content of 60%, whereas the Brazilian technical regulation allows creamy requeijão to contain up to 65%.

The Brazilian manufacturing process also differs from conventional processed cheese manufacturing.

As a software developer, I recognize this problem immediately.

Imagine designing a database to accommodate every product currently available in a particular market.

You create tables, categories, constraints, validation rules, and relationships.

Then someone arrives with a perfectly legitimate product that your database cannot accommodate.

The product is not defective.

The schema is incomplete.

Unfortunately, institutions sometimes respond to this situation by demanding that reality conform to their schema rather than updating the schema to accommodate reality.

That is not necessarily malicious. Regulatory frameworks are created at particular moments in history to address particular circumstances. They inevitably reflect the products, technologies, and commercial practices familiar to their authors.

But when those frameworks are unnecessarily difficult to navigate or update, they can become obstacles to subsequent innovation.

It is worth emphasizing that American regulations do provide mechanisms for selling foods under appropriate descriptive names when no established standard applies.

Requeijão is not categorically prohibited merely because it cannot be called cream cheese.

The problem, therefore, is not a demonstrated legal impossibility. It is the potential accumulation of classification difficulties, compliance costs, unfamiliar terminology, commercial uncertainty, and barriers to distribution.

Each obstacle might be manageable individually.

Together, they can make introducing a new product considerably less attractive.

Protectionism: The Free Market With an Asterisk

Then there is the less romantic reality of international agricultural trade.

The United States, despite its historical enthusiasm for preaching the virtues of free markets, maintains tariff-rate quotas for several categories of imported dairy products.

These mechanisms allow specified quantities of products to enter under preferential tariff conditions, with different rates applying beyond those quantities.

Other agricultural markets, including the European Union, also maintain their own systems of trade restrictions and agricultural protections.

Some restrictions serve legitimate sanitary purposes. Others serve economic objectives, including protecting domestic producers from foreign competition.

Those are not interchangeable justifications.

Preventing contaminated food from entering a country is consumer protection.

Making a safe, competitive foreign product artificially expensive to protect an established domestic industry is protectionism.

One addresses a public health risk. The other addresses a commercial threat.

And that is where the ideological contradiction becomes apparent.

If international competition is supposedly good for consumers, why should an efficient foreign product face artificially imposed disadvantages merely because domestic manufacturers might find it inconvenient?

If a Brazilian manufacturer can deliver an affordable, desirable dairy product to American consumers, the theoretical free market should welcome the competition.

The actual market, however, is shaped by trade policy, historical relationships, established industries, distribution networks, and political influence.

To be clear, the existence of dairy protectionism does not establish that requeijão specifically has been targeted by domestic manufacturers or their lobbyists. Demonstrating that would require evidence about its precise tariff classification, import conditions, and relevant industry activities.

But the broader mechanisms are real.

And they complicate the comforting fiction that international markets are simply neutral arenas in which the best products compete on equal terms.

A market does not need to formally prohibit competition to make competition economically unattractive.

The Market Cannot Reject What It Has Never Been Offered

Another possible explanation is consumer preference.

Americans are accustomed to cream cheese. Europeans have their own established dairy traditions. Introducing an unfamiliar Brazilian product would require marketing, distribution, refrigerated shelf space, and consumer education.

Those are legitimate commercial considerations.

But there is a circularity here that deserves attention.

Manufacturers may decline to introduce requeijão because consumers are unfamiliar with it. Consumers remain unfamiliar with requeijão because manufacturers decline to introduce it.

Eventually, its absence from the market is interpreted as evidence that there is no demand for it.

But there is an important difference between consumers rejecting a product and consumers never being given a meaningful opportunity to choose it.

The market cannot discover consumer preferences when the available choices are determined in advance by manufacturers and distributors.

Requeijão's success in Brazil does not guarantee that it would succeed elsewhere. Cultural preferences are real, and not every successful domestic product translates into an international success.

Nevertheless, the Brazilian experience demonstrates that the product is capable of achieving widespread consumer appeal.

Its international potential remains a commercial proposition worth testing, not something that can be dismissed merely because it is unfamiliar.

Meanwhile, Back in Brazil…

Here is where the story becomes particularly absurd.

While a genuinely innovative and relatively affordable Brazilian dairy product struggles to achieve mainstream international distribution, manufacturers in Brazil have discovered another opportunity.

They can make something cheaper than requeijão.

Not by improving the manufacturing process.

Not necessarily by reducing energy consumption, improving logistics, or developing a more efficient method of utilizing milk.

But by replacing some of the ingredients that make requeijão what it is.

Dairy fat can be substituted with cheaper vegetable fat. Starches can be employed to thicken mixtures and reproduce the appearance of a creamy dairy product.

The resulting product may resemble requeijão.

It may be packaged like requeijão.

It may occupy the same supermarket shelf as requeijão.

It may even feature photographs of the same appetizing bread, pizza, or pastry.

But it is not necessarily requeijão.

Brazil's Portaria 359 of September 4, 1997, implementing a Mercosur technical standard, defines the identity and composition of requeijão and its varieties.

Products containing ingredients that place them outside the applicable standard cannot legitimately be marketed under the same unqualified product designation.

Consequently, consumers encounter products described as mistura de requeijão e amido, especialidade láctea, or cobertura culinária, among other designations.

There is nothing inherently wrong with manufacturing such alternatives.

A properly identified, affordable substitute might be useful to someone operating on a limited budget. Different formulations may also have legitimate culinary applications.

The problem begins when the marketing depends on the consumer failing to appreciate the distinction.

When the packaging communicates “requeijão” more effectively than the legally required product designation communicates “something else,” the manufacturer may technically comply with labeling requirements while undermining their very purpose.

The label informs.

The packaging misdirects.

And the consumer is expected to reconcile the contradiction.

Two Uses of the Same Science

Consider the difference between the original innovation and the subsequent imitation.

The original manufacturers employed chemistry to transform agricultural resources into a genuinely new product.

A manufacturer producing a cheaper imitation may employ chemistry to reproduce the appearance and certain functional characteristics of that product while reducing its manufacturing cost.

Both require technical knowledge.

Both involve experimentation.

Both may be described in a corporate presentation as innovation.

But they are not necessarily delivering the same kind of value.

In the first case, reducing costs through technological innovation can benefit consumers by making a desirable product more affordable.

In the second, reducing costs by substituting ingredients can benefit consumers if the savings are passed on, the alternatives are clearly identified, and buyers understand the trade-offs.

However, when those substitutions primarily increase margins while marketing preserves the perceived value of the original product, the economic objective is different.

The company is no longer competing primarily by making a better product.

It is competing by making a less expensive product sufficiently resemble an existing one.

There is a fundamental difference between engineering a better product and engineering a cheaper product that consumers will mistake for a better one.

The former creates value.

The latter, when built on misleading consumer expectations, extracts it.

The Supermarket Has Become a Terms of Service Agreement

Requeijão is hardly an isolated example.

Brazilian consumers have become increasingly familiar with products that resemble condensed milk but are actually dairy mixtures.

Elsewhere, consumers encounter chocolate-like confectionery, cheese substitutes, frozen desserts that do not qualify as ice cream, and fruit-flavored beverages containing remarkably little fruit.

Again, the mere existence of these alternatives is not the problem.

The problem is the growing necessity of conducting a miniature forensic investigation every time we go grocery shopping.

What precisely is this product?

What ingredients have been replaced?

Has its composition changed since the last time I purchased it?

Is this the same product in a redesigned package, or a different product in a deliberately familiar package?

What does the small print say?

The supermarket has become a physical manifestation of a software Terms of Service agreement.

The seller presents an attractive proposition, while the actual nature of the transaction is buried in information that the buyer is technically able, but not always practically equipped, to examine.

And when the consumer discovers that the product is not what they expected, the response is predictable:

“You should have read the label.”

Apparently, the burden of maintaining an honest commercial transaction belongs primarily to the party with the least information about the product.

The manufacturer knows exactly what it is selling.

The consumer is expected to figure it out.

Economists call this information asymmetry.

The rest of us might reasonably call it a lousy shopping experience.

The Contradiction at the Heart of the Market

Put these two sides of the requeijão story together.

Outside Brazil, a genuine innovation may encounter regulatory friction, trade barriers, unfamiliar consumer preferences, and distribution systems that discourage its introduction.

Inside Brazil, where the innovation has already earned widespread consumer recognition, manufacturers can exploit that recognition to market cheaper substitutes.

One side of the market can discourage a new product from competing against established ones.

The other can reward manufacturers for exploiting the reputation of an established product.

Neither outcome necessarily maximizes consumer welfare.

Both, however, can be consistent with rational corporate behavior.

And that is the systemic problem.

Corporations are not inherently rewarded for producing the best possible product. They are rewarded for producing commercially successful products.

Sometimes those objectives align.

Sometimes they do not.

A company can create something genuinely useful and make a healthy profit from it. It can also improve its profitability by reducing quality, limiting competition, exploiting consumer inertia, or taking advantage of information asymmetries.

The financial statement does not contain a separate column distinguishing profits earned through genuine innovation from profits earned through the exploitation of consumer confusion.

Revenue is revenue.

Profit is profit.

The balance sheet is remarkably indifferent to how either was obtained.

This does not mean that capitalism cannot produce innovation. Requeijão itself is evidence that commercial enterprise can accomplish exactly that.

It means that innovation is not the only behavior that markets reward.

Nor is consumer welfare the automatic consequence of every commercially rational decision.

Regulation Is Not the Enemy

It would be tempting to conclude that the solution is simply to eliminate regulations and allow the free market to operate without interference.

But the requeijão case demonstrates why that conclusion is inadequate.

The same kind of regulatory mechanism that can become an obstacle to introducing unfamiliar products can also protect consumers against misleading substitutions.

Brazil's standard of identity gives the word “requeijão” a meaning that manufacturers cannot legitimately redefine at their convenience.

Without such a standard, a manufacturer could potentially replace substantial portions of the original ingredients and continue selling the resulting product under the same designation, subject only to general labeling and consumer protection rules.

The consumer would have even less certainty about what they were purchasing.

The appropriate distinction is not between regulation and deregulation.

It is between regulation that serves a legitimate public purpose and regulation that creates unnecessary barriers or primarily serves established commercial interests.

A sensible regulatory framework would accommodate genuine innovation without compromising food safety, facilitate fair competition, require meaningful disclosure, and prevent manufacturers from exploiting consumer confusion.

It would protect the consumer's ability to choose, rather than merely protect the manufacturer's ability to sell.

That distinction should be fundamental to any discussion of economic freedom.

Freedom for the seller is not the entirety of a free market.

The buyer must also have the freedom to make a genuinely informed decision.

A Glass Half Empty

In the middle of the twentieth century, Brazilian dairy manufacturers experimented with hundreds of formulations to create a product that was affordable, versatile, and appealing to consumers.

They packaged it in a container that remained useful after the product was consumed.

They combined agricultural knowledge, industrial chemistry, entrepreneurship, and practical engineering to create something that became part of everyday Brazilian life.

That is what economic innovation can look like.

Today, the same product provides an opportunity to examine a very different set of economic incentives: the protection of established markets, the difficulty of introducing unfamiliar products, the exploitation of consumer recognition, and the pursuit of margins through ingredient substitution.

The irony is almost perfect.

Brazilian manufacturers once used chemistry to transform an agricultural limitation into a valuable product.

Now, chemistry can be used to transform cheaper ingredients into something that resembles that product.

Meanwhile, consumers elsewhere may never encounter the original at a price that would allow it to compete fairly against their established alternatives.

The free market promises that better ideas will compete, consumers will choose, and innovation will prevail.

The actual market offers no such guarantees.

It rewards whatever generates an acceptable financial return, whether that means creating something better, defending an existing market, or making something worse without losing too many customers.

The humble glass of requeijão illustrates the distinction beautifully.

Once, it represented the ingenuity of people trying to make something useful out of what they had.

Today, it also represents the ingenuity of businesses trying to discover how much they can remove from a product before consumers stop buying it.

And we are still expected to call both processes innovation.

That is the systemic error.

Sources and further reading

  • Por Que o Requeijão Só Existe no Brasil? — Original video

  • Instituto Brasil a Gosto — Requeijão Spread

  • Folha de S.Paulo — Seu Xixo e o famoso requeijão cremoso de copo

  • Pesquisa FAPESP — Brazilian Cream Cheese Spread in the United States, June 2000

  • Brazilian Ministry of Agriculture — Portaria 359/1997

  • 21 CFR § 133.179 — Pasteurized Process Cheese Spread, 2025 edition

  • 21 CFR § 101.3 — Identity Labeling of Food in Packaged Form

  • 21 CFR § 102.5 — General Principles of Food Product Naming

  • USDA — Dairy Import Licensing and Tariff-Rate Quotas

item.content:encoded:
How artificial intelligence is separating discovery, verification, and understanding—and why mathematics is confronting a problem software engineering has been living with for decades.

I recently came across a cartoon shared by Erik Meijer on LinkedIn, illustrating the apparent difference between mathematicians and computer scientists when confronted with artificial intelligence.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

On one side, a mathematician stands beside a mountain of paper representing 17 million lines of Lean code proving the Riemann Hypothesis.

“We can never understand that as humans. Ban AI!”

On the other side, computer scientists stand beside an even larger mountain representing 51 million lines of C++ code in Chrome.

“We can never understand that as humans. Bring on the AI!”

It is an amusing observation, but beneath the humor lies a fundamental philosophical question about the nature of human knowledge.

Does humanity need to understand something to know it?

Until recently, that question might have sounded like an exercise in academic philosophy. Artificial intelligence is rapidly turning it into a practical problem.

Seventeen Million Lines of Mathematics

On November 20, 2026, mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, developed in collaboration with Anthropic’s Claude.

For those unfamiliar with the Riemann Hypothesis, it is one of the most significant mathematical problems in history. First formulated in 1859, it concerns the distribution of the zeros of the Riemann zeta function and has profound implications for our understanding of prime numbers.

It has resisted mathematicians for 167 years.

The proposed proof was released not as a conventional mathematical paper, but as approximately 17.4 million lines of Lean, a formal mathematical proof language and verification system, distributed across 175,187 files.

Independent verification efforts have since reported successful checks of the formal proof.

Formal verification, of course, is distinct from the Clay Mathematics Institute’s process for officially recognizing a solution to a Millennium Prize Problem. That process remains separate.

But consider the extraordinary situation we find ourselves in.

We have a mathematical proof that independent verification systems have accepted, yet whose original implementation is far beyond what any individual human could reasonably read and comprehend in its entirety.

The formal mathematics has passed its verification.

Human understanding is still catching up.

Mathematics Has Entered the Refactoring Era

What happened next should amuse anyone who has spent a significant portion of their professional life developing software.

Mathematicians started refactoring the proof.

Within days, researchers working with AI had produced substantially smaller versions of the original formalization. Human-readable mathematical expositions also began appearing, attempting to extract the underlying reasoning from the enormous collection of machine-generated formal statements.

Any experienced software developer recognizes this process immediately.

Make it work. Establish that it works. Simplify it. Identify unnecessary complexity. Extract reusable components. Make it comprehensible to the next person who has to deal with it.

The difference is that, instead of refactoring an enterprise resource planning system, mathematicians are refactoring a proposed solution to one of the most important mathematical problems of the last two centuries.

And the original result does not become less valid simply because the subsequent implementation is more elegant.

Elegance is desirable. Correctness is indispensable.

They are not synonymous.

The Tyranny of Human Comprehension

For much of human history, our ability to discover things was closely tied to our ability to understand them.

A mathematician had to construct a proof. An engineer had to design a machine. A programmer had to write an algorithm.

The act of creation produced understanding as a natural consequence.

Artificial intelligence is disrupting that relationship.

A system can now generate a solution that exceeds the cognitive capacity of the person requesting it, even when that person possesses the expertise necessary to define the problem and evaluate the result.

This is uncomfortable because we have traditionally conflated three distinct intellectual activities:

  • Discovery: Finding a solution to a problem.

  • Verification: Establishing that the solution is correct.

  • Comprehension: Understanding how and why the solution works.

Historically, these activities were deeply intertwined because humans performed all three.

There is, however, no fundamental law of mathematics, physics, or epistemology requiring them to occur in a particular order—or to be performed by the same intelligence.

AI is making that separation increasingly consequential.

We can discover something, establish its validity, and only afterward begin the process of understanding it.

That represents a significant change in how humanity acquires knowledge.

Software Developers Have Been Here Before

As a software developer, I find the controversy particularly fascinating because our profession abandoned the expectation of complete human comprehension decades ago.

Consider what happens when I write a relatively simple C# application.

I rely on the .NET runtime, the operating system, database engines, networking libraries, cryptographic implementations, device drivers, compilers, firmware, and processor microcode.

I have not personally inspected every line of those implementations.

Neither has anyone else.

Yet nobody seriously argues that I am incapable of developing reliable software because I cannot explain every transistor-level operation occurring between my application issuing a database query and the database returning its results.

The entire history of software engineering is a history of progressively surrendering the need to understand implementation details in exchange for higher levels of abstraction.

We moved from machine code to assembly, from assembly to higher-level languages, from procedural programming to frameworks, and from manually implementing common functionality to consuming libraries.

At every stage, we surrendered some degree of intimate knowledge while gaining productivity and expressive power.

AI-assisted development is another step along that trajectory, albeit with a significant difference: generated implementations are not necessarily as predictable or as thoroughly validated as established libraries.

That difference deserves engineering attention. It does not invalidate the trajectory.

Management Still Wants the Punch Card

As I have argued before, there is a growing contradiction in the software industry.

Management wants developers to use artificial intelligence to increase productivity. Simultaneously, it expects those developers to possess the same intimate knowledge of every line of generated code that they would have possessed had they written it manually.

These expectations become increasingly incompatible as the scale of AI-generated software grows.

Writing code manually provides an intrinsic understanding of its structure. You remember why you made certain decisions, why you introduced a particular abstraction, and why you avoided a seemingly obvious alternative.

That knowledge is acquired through the act of creation.

When AI generates the implementation, acquiring that knowledge becomes a separate activity.

And asking AI to generate thousands of pages of documentation does not magically restore it.

Documentation nobody reads is not institutional knowledge. It is noise with headings.

The solution is not to prohibit AI or demand that developers manually reproduce everything AI generates.

The solution is to recognize that software development increasingly involves managing the relationship between discovery, verification, and comprehension.

We need to develop better mechanisms for establishing correctness, better abstractions for containing complexity, and better tools for understanding systems that exceed our individual cognitive capacities.

Insisting that developers return to an earlier model of intellectual labor is not quality assurance.

It is nostalgia masquerading as professional responsibility.

The Great Irony: Mathematics Is Better Equipped Than Software Engineering

Here is where the cartoon becomes particularly ironic.

Mathematicians actually possess something that most software developers would dearly love to have: a mechanism capable of formally establishing the logical correctness of an enormous artifact.

Lean is not simply running mathematical unit tests.

Its proof-checking kernel verifies that the formal derivation follows from the accepted axioms and inference rules of the system.

Provided the theorem has been correctly formulated and the verification mechanism is sound, its acceptance offers a guarantee that ordinary software testing cannot match.

I can write a million unit tests for a software application.

I can achieve 100 percent code coverage.

I can subject it to automated security analysis, integration testing, and millions of hours of real-world usage.

None of that establishes that the application is free of defects.

Testing can demonstrate the presence of errors. It generally cannot demonstrate their complete absence.

Formal verification can establish specific properties under explicitly defined assumptions. Software engineering can use formal methods, too, but applying them to large, general-purpose applications remains considerably more difficult than ordinary testing.

The mathematician standing beside 17 million lines of Lean code therefore has a significant advantage over the software engineer standing beside 51 million lines of C++.

The mathematician has a much stronger mechanism for establishing that the artifact satisfies its stated purpose.

The software engineer, comparatively speaking, has a collection of tests and varying degrees of confidence.

Perhaps mathematicians should be considerably less afraid of AI than software developers.

This Is Not Entirely Unprecedented

Humanity has encountered earlier versions of this problem.

The computer-assisted proof of the Four Color Theorem in 1976 generated controversy precisely because portions of its verification depended on computational work that humans could not practically reproduce by hand.

Modern experimental science routinely relies on instruments, statistical models, and computational systems whose complete operation no individual researcher understands.

Civilization itself is built upon distributed knowledge.

No individual knows how to construct a modern civilization from scratch.

We collectively know how to produce semiconductors, manufacture pharmaceuticals, generate electricity, construct aircraft, and operate global telecommunications networks.

Individually, we understand fragments.

What makes AI different is the possibility of accelerating this phenomenon beyond the rate at which human beings can absorb and organize the resulting knowledge.

Previously, our collective understanding was distributed among human minds, institutions, and accumulated records.

Now, we are beginning to produce intellectual artifacts whose correctness can potentially be established before their underlying reasoning has been absorbed into human knowledge.

The Emerging Comprehension Debt

Software developers are familiar with the concept of technical debt.

I would suggest that artificial intelligence is introducing another category: comprehension debt.

Comprehension debt is the gap between what we have established to be correct and what we understand sufficiently to explain, modify, generalize, or reproduce.

A formally verified mathematical proof can accumulate comprehension debt.

A functional AI-generated software application can accumulate comprehension debt.

A scientific discovery supported by strong experimental evidence can accumulate comprehension debt.

The existence of that debt does not invalidate the achievement.

But neither should we pretend that the debt does not exist.

Understanding remains essential for identifying incorrect assumptions, adapting solutions to changing circumstances, communicating knowledge, and making further discoveries.

If a mathematical proof contains a genuinely new technique, its value extends beyond the theorem it establishes. Understanding that technique could unlock dozens of other mathematical problems.

Likewise, understanding a software implementation allows us to modify it intelligently rather than blindly regenerating it every time requirements change.

The mistake is treating comprehension debt as evidence that the original achievement should never have occurred.

Debt can be managed. It can be reduced. It can even be an acceptable temporary consequence of progress.

But, like technical debt, comprehension debt becomes dangerous when it accumulates without recognition or management.

A software company that generates millions of lines of code without investing in verification and understanding is not necessarily becoming more productive. It may simply be accumulating liabilities faster than its engineers can identify them.

Similarly, a mathematical community that accumulates formally verified results without extracting their underlying techniques risks establishing an enormous catalog of truths while failing to capitalize on their intellectual significance.

The efforts to simplify and explain the Riemann Hypothesis proof are an excellent illustration of humanity beginning to pay down that debt.

The End of Human Intelligibility as a Prerequisite

There is a certain anthropocentrism underlying the insistence that knowledge must be immediately intelligible to human beings before it can be considered legitimate.

The universe is under no obligation to be comprehensible to the human brain.

Mathematical truths do not become true because we understand them.

Physical phenomena do not wait for humanity to develop an adequate theoretical framework before occurring.

Our cognitive limitations are characteristics of our species, not characteristics of reality.

If artificial intelligence can help us discover mathematical truths that we can independently verify but cannot yet comprehend, then rejecting those discoveries solely because they exceed our immediate understanding would be an extraordinary act of intellectual self-sabotage.

This does not mean abandoning skepticism.

It means redirecting skepticism toward the appropriate questions.

Is the result correct? Are the assumptions valid? Is the verification mechanism trustworthy? Have we actually solved the problem we intended to solve?

Those are legitimate concerns.

Whether the result fits comfortably within the intellectual capacity of a single human being is a different question altogether.

We must not confuse the limitations of the observer with the validity of the observation.

Conclusion: Discovery First, Understanding Later

For centuries, humanity’s capacity to discover was largely constrained by its capacity to reason.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to loosen that constraint.

We may increasingly encounter a world in which discovery happens faster than comprehension, where solutions precede explanations, and where the work of scientists, mathematicians, and engineers involves not only producing new knowledge but also making independently established knowledge accessible to human minds.

That is not the end of human intellectual activity.

It is a transformation of its purpose.

Perhaps the mathematicians in the cartoon should take a lesson from the software developers.

And perhaps software developers should take a lesson from the mathematicians about the importance of formal verification.

Neither profession needs to abandon understanding.

Both need to abandon the assumption that understanding every implementation detail is a prerequisite for progress.

For much of human history, discovery and understanding were inseparable companions.

We are entering an era in which we can increasingly discover, verify, and then understand.

The frontier of human knowledge no longer needs to coincide with the frontier of human comprehension.

And that may be one of the most profound consequences of artificial intelligence.

Sources and Further Reading

  • Associated Press — Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI

  • Michael Rubinstein, University of Waterloo — Alpöge/Claude proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis

  • Riemann Atlas — The Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

  • The Riemann Hypothesis and GRH for Dirichlet L-functions: A readable account of the Lean proof

  • Cairn Commons — Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proved? Status on November 27, 2026

  • Clay Mathematics Institute — Riemann Hypothesis

item.content:encoded:
The Supreme Court can leave a constitutional protection on the books and still take away the lawsuit that gives it teeth.

Kekai Watanabe says he asked to go to a hospital after other inmates beat him in a federal prison in Honolulu. According to his lawsuit, a prison nurse told him to stop being a “cry baby” and refused. Watanabe kept asking for medical attention. For months, he says, he received only over-the-counter pain medication. About seven months after the beating, he was diagnosed with a fractured tailbone.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

On November 9, the Supreme Court heard his case. The justices were deciding whether the law lets him seek damages from the nurse. A ruling against him could end that claim before a court ever determines whether the nurse violated the Constitution. The case is Nielsen v. Watanabe. It’s the part of LegalEagle’s Supreme Court preview that deserves its own headline.

Same Constitution, different badge

Congress gave people a way to sue for violations of federal rights committed under state authority. The statute, now known as 42 U.S.C. § 1983, generally covers state and local officials acting in that capacity. Congress never enacted a comparable, generally applicable statute for constitutional violations committed under federal authority. So the badge can determine which lawsuit you’re allowed to bring.

In 1971, the Supreme Court filled part of that gap in Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents. It let a man sue federal narcotics agents for damages over an allegedly unconstitutional search and arrest. The Court later recognized two more such claims, one for sex discrimination by a congressman and one for unconstitutional medical treatment in federal prison. That last case, Carlson v. Green, involved a prisoner who died after officials allegedly delayed and mishandled treatment for a severe asthma attack. His estate could sue the officials personally under the Eighth Amendment even though it could also pursue a tort claim against the United States.

That’s the step that comes before qualified immunity. Qualified immunity can shield an official from damages even when a cause of action exists. Bivens asks whether you have that cause of action to begin with. You can lose at the second door. Watanabe is still arguing over the first.

How to overrule a case without saying so

In 2022, Egbert v. Boule made it extraordinarily difficult to extend Bivens. If a claim differs meaningfully from the three cases the Court has already recognized, even one adequate reason to leave the decision to Congress can foreclose a damages remedy. An administrative grievance process can count in that analysis even if it gives the claimant no damages. Under that rule, a great deal turns on what judges consider a meaningful difference.

So what counts? Asthma versus a broken bone? Hours versus months? Death versus survival? The Ninth Circuit concluded that Watanabe’s claim was materially the same as Carlson. Both involved alleged deliberate indifference to a federal prisoner’s serious medical needs. The nurse’s lawyers argued that the differences matter. They also offered a broader theory under which developments since 1980 could foreclose even a claim on Carlson’s own facts.

Justice Elena Kagan put the question directly to the nurse’s lawyer: “overrule Carlson without saying you’re overruling Carlson?” He conceded that his broader argument gets “essentially that result.” The Justice Department went further. It urged the Court to declare Carlson obsolete or expressly overrule it, while offering a fact-specific ruling as a fallback. Justice Brett Kavanaugh pressed the other way, asking why the Court should pull the precedent out from under Congress when Congress had legislated against that backdrop for decades. Those were exchanges at oral argument. As of November 27, the Court had issued no ruling.

The government has a serious argument about who should decide when federal officials face personal liability. It also points to a route that can compensate some prisoners: a tort claim against the United States under the Federal Tort Claims Act. But that claim depends on the applicable tort law and the statute’s exceptions. A grievance can ask the prison to fix a problem. A court order can address ongoing harm. Each can matter. In Carlson, the Court held that the tort remedy and the constitutional claim against individual officers could coexist. The government is asking the Court to undo that choice.

Congress wrote the rule. Who gets to enforce it?

The same question comes up under a different body of law in Crowther v. Board of Regents of the University System of Georgia, scheduled for argument on November 30. A former art professor and a former women’s basketball coach sued the university system for sex discrimination in employment. Title IX prohibits sex discrimination in federally funded education programs. In Cannon v. University of Chicago, the Supreme Court recognized an implied private right to sue under Title IX. In Jackson v. Birmingham Board of Education, it held that a coach could sue under Title IX for retaliation after he complained about sex discrimination against his team. Now the Court has to decide whether employees can use Title IX to sue for discrimination in their own employment. Eight federal appeals courts have said yes. Three, including the Eleventh Circuit in Crowther, have said no.

Title VII separately provides a route for employment discrimination claims, with its own procedures and deadlines. The question in Crowther is whether Title IX supplies a route of its own. A ruling for the university system would close that route to employees bringing this kind of claim, even though the underlying prohibition on sex discrimination would remain in federal law.

We already have an example of what that distinction can mean. In 2025, South Carolina excluded Planned Parenthood from its Medicaid program. A patient, Julie Edwards, challenged the exclusion under Medicaid’s provision allowing beneficiaries to obtain covered care from any qualified provider willing to treat them. In Medina v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic, the Supreme Court ruled 6–3 that this provision did not unambiguously confer an individual right enforceable through § 1983. Federal officials could still police compliance with the funding condition. Edwards lost her ability to enforce that provision through her own § 1983 lawsuit.

Watanabe, Crowther, and Medina involve three different legal questions. One concerns a judge-made remedy for constitutional violations by federal officials. One concerns a private action implied from a civil rights statute. One concerns whether a Medicaid provision creates an individual right that an existing civil rights statute can enforce. Put them side by side and ask who bears the cost when a court insists that enforcement belongs elsewhere. It’s the prisoner waiting for care, the employee bringing a discrimination claim, and the patient trying to keep her provider.

Congress can write an express constitutional damages remedy for misconduct by federal officers. It can say exactly who may sue under Title IX. If the Court believes those decisions belong to Congress, Congress owns the consequences of leaving them unresolved. And when the Court takes a remedy people have had for decades and narrows it to the point of disappearance, the Court owns that decision too.

The next time someone tells you a ruling left your rights intact, ask what you can do on Monday morning. Who can you sue? What can a judge order? And if the answer is that an agency may act, Congress may someday legislate, or your injury was too different from the one a court recognized forty-six years ago, ask who benefits from making you wait

Sources:

  1. Cornell Legal Information Institute, Nielsen v. Watanabe case summary
  2. LegalEagle, The Supreme Court Is About to Change EVERYTHING!, discussion at 18:26
  3. U.S. Supreme Court, Nielsen v. Watanabe, November 9, 2026 oral argument transcript (PDF)
  4. 42 U.S.C. § 1983, civil action for deprivation of rights
  5. U.S. Supreme Court, Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022), opinion (PDF)
  6. U.S. Supreme Court, Carlson v. Green, 446 U.S. 14 (1980), opinion (PDF)
  7. U.S. Supreme Court, Nielsen v. Watanabe, docket No. 25-417
  8. 28 U.S.C. § 2680, exceptions to the Federal Tort Claims Act
  9. 20 U.S.C. § 1681, Title IX’s prohibition on sex discrimination
  10. U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, Crowther v. Board of Regents, November 7, 2024 opinion
  11. U.S. Supreme Court, Crowther v. Board of Regents, question presented (PDF)
  12. U.S. Supreme Court, Crowther v. Board of Regents, docket No. 25-183
  13. U.S. Supreme Court, Medina v. Planned Parenthood South Atlantic, June 26, 2025 opinion (PDF)

item.content:encoded:
How Thailand manufactures the economic segregation it claims to be fighting.

“THAT is the illegal service they are worried about?”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That was one of the comments underneath a video discussing the arrest of a Chinese barber in Bangkok. Given Thailand’s international reputation for sex tourism, and the considerably more serious problem of child sexual exploitation, the comment practically writes itself.

But beneath the dark humour lies something considerably more interesting: a government creating the very conditions it subsequently uses to justify its restrictions.

And it all begins with a haircut.

The Great Bangkok Barbershop Bust

In November 2026, Thai immigration police conducted an undercover operation against a thirty-year-old Chinese national operating a private barbershop from a rented apartment in Bangkok.

His customers booked appointments through an application. They knocked on his door, were admitted, received their haircuts and paid for the service. A man’s haircut cost 800 baht.

The police sent an undercover officer posing as a customer and arrested the barber while he was cutting someone’s hair.

Apparently, Bangkok could sleep soundly that night.

The authorities had neutralized the threat of unauthorized hairstyling.

What particularly angered some Thai people, however, was that the barber served exclusively Chinese customers, refusing entry to Thai nationals.

On the surface, that sounds discriminatory. Imagine a business operating in your country and refusing to serve you because of your nationality.

Now imagine that your government prohibits the person operating that business from practising his profession because of his nationality.

Suddenly, the story becomes considerably more complicated.

Discrimination With a Government Seal of Approval

Thailand maintains a list of 27 occupations strictly reserved for Thai nationals, with another 13 subject to conditional restrictions.

Among the prohibited occupations are hairdressing, wood carving, gem polishing, street vending, tour guiding, secretarial work and traditional Thai massage.

This is not merely a licensing requirement.

A Chinese barber could possess thirty years of professional experience, internationally recognized qualifications, impeccable hygiene standards, sufficient capital to establish a business and legal permission to reside in Thailand.

None of those qualifications would entitle him to practise his profession under the ordinary occupational rules.

His exclusion is not based on competence, professional standards, public safety or consumer protection.

It is based on nationality.

Calling this economic protectionism does not change its underlying mechanism. Protectionism describes the intended economic outcome; discrimination describes the means through which that outcome is pursued.

The two are not mutually exclusive.

Manufacturing the Enemy

The video raises an interesting possibility regarding the barber’s refusal to serve Thai customers.

What if it wasn't motivated by contempt for Thai people?

What if it was motivated by self-preservation?

Every unfamiliar customer represented a potential informant. Opening his establishment to the general public increased the likelihood of being reported to immigration authorities.

Indeed, an undercover officer posing as a customer was precisely how the police caught him.

We cannot know the barber’s actual motivation without hearing from him. His exclusionary customer policy may have had other explanations. But the incentives created by the legislation are unmistakable.

The government prohibits foreigners from practising certain professions. Those who continue practising are driven underground. Underground businesses have an incentive to restrict access to trusted communities. Their secrecy and exclusionary practices subsequently reinforce public suspicions about foreigners.

Those suspicions can then be invoked to justify maintaining or expanding the original restrictions.

The government creates the conditions for segregation and then points to segregation as evidence that its restrictions are necessary.

It is a textbook self-fulfilling prophecy.

The Myth of the Zero-Baht Business

The video also discusses a phenomenon known in Thailand as the “zero-baht business.”

The term describes foreign-operated businesses whose economic activities supposedly remain entirely within their own national communities, leaving Thai citizens without any share of the proceeds.

There are legitimate concerns surrounding foreign investment, commercial rents, tax evasion and the displacement of local businesses. These deserve serious economic analysis.

But consider the supposedly isolated Chinese barbershop.

The barber rented premises in Bangkok. He presumably consumed electricity and water, purchased food, required transportation and incurred ordinary living expenses.

Unless he had somehow managed to establish an entirely self-sufficient Chinese sovereign territory inside a Bangkok apartment, the assertion that his business contributed absolutely nothing to the Thai economy requires considerably more evidence than the nationality of his customers.

Money does not acquire a nationality simply because of the passport held by the person spending it.

Furthermore, if the concern is that clandestine businesses fail to pay taxes, perhaps making their legal registration categorically impossible is not the most effective solution.

An underground business cannot readily declare its income, register its activities, advertise publicly or participate openly in the formal economy without exposing itself to prosecution.

The government has established an incentive against the very economic integration it ostensibly desires.

Protection From Competition

The conventional justification for reserving occupations for nationals is the protection of domestic workers.

That objective is understandable. Governments have legitimate interests in preventing labour exploitation, protecting wages and ensuring that local workers are not unfairly displaced.

But there is a fundamental difference between protecting workers from unfair competition and protecting them from competition altogether.

If a foreign barber is undercutting local businesses by violating minimum-wage legislation, enforce the wage legislation.

If he is evading taxes, enforce the tax legislation.

If his establishment fails to comply with hygiene regulations, enforce the hygiene regulations.

If wealthy foreign investors are distorting the commercial property market, address the mechanisms through which that distortion occurs.

None of these problems inherently requires determining the nationality of the person holding a pair of scissors.

There is also a neglected party in this discussion: the customer.

Chinese residents of Bangkok may prefer a Chinese-speaking barber for perfectly ordinary reasons. Communicating how one wants one's hair cut is considerably easier when both parties speak the same language.

By prohibiting that barber from operating legally, the government restricts not only his economic freedom but also the choices available to his prospective customers.

Imagine the Law in Reverse

Imagine a Thai national moving to another country.

She obtains legal residency and decides to establish a business providing traditional Thai massage, a skill she learned in Thailand and perfected over decades.

Now imagine that her adopted country declares that only its own nationals may provide that service.

Her qualifications are irrelevant. Her experience is irrelevant. Her willingness to pay taxes is irrelevant.

She is forbidden from practising a traditional art originating in her own country because she was born on the wrong side of a national border.

The discriminatory nature of such a restriction becomes considerably easier to recognize when the nationalities are reversed.

A consistent principle of fairness should survive that reversal.

The Difference Between Law Enforcement and Public Safety

This brings us back to the original comment.

Thailand has a documented history of commercial sexual exploitation of children associated with international tourism. This is not a victimless regulatory offence. It is a devastating violation of fundamental human rights.

Thai authorities do investigate and prosecute such crimes, and a single barbershop raid does not establish the country's overall law enforcement priorities.

Nevertheless, the juxtaposition illustrates an important distinction between illegality and harmfulness.

Something can be illegal without being inherently harmful. Something can be profoundly harmful while remaining inadequately investigated or prosecuted.

Legislation determines what constitutes an offence. It does not automatically establish the moral legitimacy of criminalizing that conduct.

The fact that the Chinese barber violated Thai law is not, in itself, a defence of that law.

Otherwise, every discriminatory statute ever enacted would become immune to criticism simply by virtue of having been enacted.

The Systemic Error

The fundamental problem here is not uniquely Thai.

Governments across the world frequently create artificial barriers to participation in society, punish people who circumvent those barriers and subsequently cite their clandestine behaviour as evidence that they cannot be trusted to participate openly.

The excluded become suspicious because they are excluded.

Their attempts to survive outside the system become the justification for keeping them outside it.

Meanwhile, the original policy escapes scrutiny because the consequences it produces are attributed exclusively to the people subjected to it.

Thailand’s Chinese barber offers a particularly mundane illustration of this mechanism.

There were scissors. There was a chair. There was a customer. There was a mutually agreed price.

There was no allegation in the reported arrest that the haircut was dangerous, fraudulent or involuntary.

The haircut wasn't illegal because of what was being done.

It wasn't illegal because of how it was being done.

It was illegal because of who was holding the scissors.

item.content:encoded:
AlterNet’s supplied text does not establish that Donald Trump tried to silence any companies, let alone thousands of them, or that the alleged effort was connected to an impending Democratic takeover. It contains only a string of names and phrases, without a reported action, date, institution, policy, quotation, or result.

A claim without a reported event

The headline points toward a consequential abuse-of-power story: a president using federal authority to suppress corporate speech before control of government changes hands. But none of the facts required to report that story appears in the material provided.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The text does not identify the companies, the government body involved, the mechanism supposedly used against them, or the Democrats said to be taking over. Nor does it explain what “silence” means in this context—censorship, regulatory pressure, contractual restrictions, litigation, or something else.

Names are not evidence

A list that includes George Conway, Noam Chomsky, Kayleigh McEnany, Melania Trump, Paul Krugman, Lindsey Graham, Ivanka Trump, Eric Trump, and others cannot support the headline merely by association. Turning that debris into a narrative would require inventing connections, motives, and events that the supplied reporting does not contain.

The headline’s central claim therefore remains unresolved. On this record, there is no standalone news event to re-report and no factual basis for assigning responsibility, tracing institutional power, or assessing consequences. A sharp political argument cannot substitute for the missing story without becoming fabrication.

item.title: Legend Bob Woodward levels Trump with a chilling comparison
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Bob Woodward’s comparison was blunt: President Donald Trump’s reported initiation of war against Iran resembled the conduct of tyrants who designate an enemy and attack without having been attacked themselves.
