item.content:encoded:
Bob Woodward’s comparison was blunt: President Donald Trump’s reported initiation of war against Iran resembled the conduct of tyrants who designate an enemy and attack without having been attacked themselves. Speaking with CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, Woodward called Trump “the aggressor” and argued that Iran had provided no provocation for the war. His indictment was not that Trump had used impolite rhetoric or broken diplomatic convention. It was that the president wielded the United States’ military power to begin a conflict merely because his administration opposed another government.

“The best thing a president can do is stop wars, prevent wars,” Woodward said. Instead, he argued, Trump had done the reverse: “He actually started a war against Iran.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The comparison was about aggression, not personality

Woodward did not defend Iran’s government, which he described as an unfavorable regime. He rejected the more consequential sleight of hand: treating hostility toward that regime as sufficient cause for war.

“For the United States to say, ‘well, we’re just starting a war because we don’t like what you’re doing,’” Woodward said, is “exactly what tyrants do.” He described the authoritarian formula plainly: declare another country the enemy, then use that declaration to justify attacking it.

That distinction matters because governments routinely attempt to collapse it. A state can be repressive without having attacked the United States. American officials can oppose its conduct without possessing an unlimited mandate to launch a war. When those separate propositions are fused, the targeted government’s character becomes a substitute for evidence of necessity, and presidential preference becomes a substitute for public justification.

Woodward invoked Russian President Vladimir Putin as a point of comparison while noting Trump’s friendliness toward him. But the sharper charge concerned Trump’s own exercise of power. Woodward was not alleging guilt by association. He was arguing that initiating an unprovoked war is itself the relevant authoritarian conduct, regardless of what its architect calls the enemy.

Congress still controls the money

Woodward predicted that the Iran war would leave a lasting stain on Trump’s record. “I know lots of former presidents, late presidents who would be twirling in their graves” at a commander in chief beginning a war without an attack or provocation, he said.

Presidential legacy, however, is the least immediate consequence. Wars are sustained by institutions, appropriations and legislators willing to keep supplying both. AlterNet reported that Robert Malley, who served as a Biden administration special envoy to Iran, and foreign-policy historian Stephen Wertheim were already urging Democrats to end the war after taking the majority in January. In a New York Times essay, they described that decision as an early test of whether Democrats had understood the electorate and intended to honor its message.

That framing puts responsibility where it belongs. Democrats cannot condemn Trump’s voluntary war as an abuse while treating its continuation as an inherited condition beyond their control. If they possess the votes or leverage to restrict funding, their choice is whether to use institutional power—not whether to issue sufficiently grave statements about the president’s behavior.

Republican support for financing the war was also showing strain, according to AlterNet. Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson of Wisconsin acknowledged that the GOP’s preferred reconciliation route carried political costs because Democrats were threatening a government shutdown if Republicans proceeded.

Johnson’s complaint is revealing. He described Democratic resistance as a “downside” of reconciliation, shifting attention from the war Republicans sought to finance to the confrontation required to stop them. That is standard Washington misdirection: the exercise of power by those sustaining violence is treated as ordinary governance, while resistance becomes the disruption.

Woodward’s warning therefore reaches beyond one brutal comparison. Trump may have initiated the conflict, as Woodward charged, but Congress determines whether the machinery keeps running. The next consequential judgment will not come from former presidents imagined turning in their graves. It will come from living lawmakers deciding whether an unprovoked war is intolerable—or merely inconvenient to defund.

item.title: The most historic blow yet to Trump and MAGA
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet identifies Scott Colom’s election as the most historic blow yet to Donald Trump’s MAGA movement: Mississippi voters chose the state’s first Black senator in 145 years, breaking a line of exclusion stretching back to Blanche Kelso Bruce’s departure from office in 1881. item.content:encoded:
AlterNet identifies Scott Colom’s election as the most historic blow yet to Donald Trump’s MAGA movement: Mississippi voters chose the state’s first Black senator in 145 years, breaking a line of exclusion stretching back to Blanche Kelso Bruce’s departure from office in 1881. The result matters not because one election dismantles Trumpism, but because a Black candidate won power in a state where white authorities spent generations using law, violence and electoral machinery to keep Black citizens from exercising it.

Colom’s victory formed part of what AlterNet describes as a Democratic “blue tsunami” in the midterm elections, propelled by anger over affordability, corruption and the Trump regime’s cruelty. Black voters—and Black women especially—were central to that rejection. Treating their role as incidental would reproduce a familiar distortion: political coverage lavishes attention on voters who wander away from democracy and occasionally return, while regarding the people who consistently oppose authoritarian politics as background scenery.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A victory measured against organized exclusion

Colom will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Bruce served during Reconstruction, from 1875 to 1881. That gap was not an electoral accident. At least 226 Black Americans held public office in Mississippi during Reconstruction, according to the account, before nearly all were driven out as Reconstruction ended and white supremacy consolidated control across the South.

The machinery changed over time, but its purpose remained recognizable. Terror and apartheid gave way to racist gerrymandering, voter suppression and other efforts to dilute or nullify Black political power. Colom’s election therefore represents more than demographic symbolism. It is an instance in which voters overcame institutions designed to make outcomes like his less likely.

That is the sharper answer to the headline’s superlative. The blow to MAGA is not merely that a Democrat won. It is that multiracial political power asserted itself in a place central to the construction of white rule—and did so against a movement whose electoral strength depends heavily on racial grievance, exclusion and the preservation of hierarchy.

AlterNet reports that Colom received 70 percent of the vote and carried Forrest County, named for Confederate general and first Ku Klux Klan grand wizard Nathan Bedford Forrest, as well as Jefferson Davis County, named for the Confederacy’s president. Those victories do not cleanse the names or erase the histories. They demonstrate that inherited symbols of white power do not possess an eternal claim on the voters living beneath them.

Mississippi’s wealth and violence were political systems

Mississippi’s racial order was never simply a collection of private prejudices. It was an economic and governmental system. In 1860, between 35 and 50 percent of white families in Mississippi, Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina enslaved Black people. The human beings held as property were valued, in present-day terms, at trillions of dollars—more than the railroads, factories and banks combined.

That wealth depended on a deliberate contradiction: Black labor, knowledge and creativity were indispensable, while Black humanity was denied whenever recognition threatened white ownership and control. The later exclusion of Black officeholders served the same political economy. Keeping Black citizens from governing helped protect the distribution of wealth and authority built through their exploitation.

The violence enforcing that order was concrete. Civil-rights organizers James Chaney, Andrew Goodman and Michael Schwerner were kidnapped and murdered in Mississippi in June 1964. Journalist Thomas Ricks described the state that summer as the site of a “small civil war.” Between June 15 and September 15, the movement recorded more than six known murders, 80 beatings, 35 shootings, 35 church bombings and 30 other bombings.

Those were not mysterious eruptions of social tension. White attackers committed the violence to defend a racial regime, while government institutions had repeatedly permitted or enforced the conditions that made such terror effective. Calling Colom’s election historic without naming that structure would reduce history to atmosphere and obscure who exercised power against whom.

The voters treated as political scenery

Kimberlé Crenshaw and Tim Wise, writing in The Nation, argue that the political press rewards inconsistency with attention. Voters who defect and return become the story; Black voters who recognized Trumpism early and opposed it election after election are treated as an unremarkable constant.

That habit does more than produce shallow campaign narratives. It shifts political agency away from the people doing the durable work of defeating authoritarian candidates and toward constituencies whose susceptibility to right-wing appeals is endlessly indulged as an economic or cultural puzzle. Black voters become a resource to be harvested, while white grievance is granted the status of a national emergency.

AlterNet characterizes the midterm result as a repudiation of MAGA led in substantial part by Black voters. That does not mean every vote carried the same motivation, nor does an election settle the endurance of Trump’s movement. It does mean the coalition opposing it cannot be honestly described while its most reliable members are relegated to a footnote.

The right benefits from that erasure. If Black political leadership disappears from the account, working-class conflict can again be narrated as a contest between supposedly authentic white voters and everyone else. The economic interests shared across racial lines then remain subordinate to resentment, allowing political and economic elites to retain power while directing anger downward.

Colom’s promise rejects MAGA’s governing proposition

Before Colom delivered his November 4 victory speech at Tougaloo College, his daughters, ages 8 and 9, recited the Pledge of Allegiance before an American flag. Several miles away in Jackson, white supremacist Byron De La Beckwith assassinated civil-rights organizer Medgar Evers in 1963.

The proximity gives the moment its force, but sentiment should not obscure the underlying contest. The question is whether citizenship carries equal political substance or whether it remains conditional on race, gender and inherited position. MAGA politics has repeatedly mobilized voters around the fear that greater equality for others constitutes dispossession for them.

Colom answered that politics with a plain account of public obligation. Addressing those who voted for him, those who opposed him and those who did not vote, he promised to treat their children as he would want his own children treated, their parents as he would want his treated, and their future as he would want his own.

That is universalism stated as a governing commitment, not the counterfeit populism that identifies vulnerable groups as the cause of material insecurity while leaving concentrated power undisturbed. Colom did not promise domination by a different constituency. He promised equal regard from an office whose history shows how long Mississippi denied Black citizens even the opportunity to make such a promise.

The burden now is institutional, not spectral. Being the first Black Mississippian elected to the Senate in 145 years gives Colom symbolic weight, but symbolism neither governs nor protects itself. His victory broke a barrier built by identifiable systems of white power. What follows will depend on whether political institutions honor the equal citizenship voters asserted—or begin constructing the next mechanism for containing it.

item.title: Americans can’t afford to just 'move on' again
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Americans cannot afford another official return to “normal” that leaves abuses of power intact. The argument advanced in AlterNet is that Democrats’ next turn in power should link economic relief to accountability: investigate corruption, establish facts, and pursue criminal cases where evidence supports them. Political scientist Joshua Zingher’s warning is blunt: Donald Trump learned from escaping substantial consequences after his first term, and future officials will study the same lesson unl
item.content:encoded:
Americans cannot afford another official return to “normal” that leaves abuses of power intact. The argument advanced in AlterNet is that Democrats’ next turn in power should link economic relief to accountability: investigate corruption, establish facts, and pursue criminal cases where evidence supports them. Political scientist Joshua Zingher’s warning is blunt: Donald Trump learned from escaping substantial consequences after his first term, and future officials will study the same lesson unless misconduct carries a real cost.

That is the article’s strongest case. Its weakest is the attempt to turn a strategic dispute into a hunt for a Democratic “fifth column.” Skepticism about investigations can reflect cowardice, opportunism or bad judgment without proving that critics secretly want authoritarianism—or that they want Democrats to fail. Accountability requires evidence and due process. So does an accusation of betrayal.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Affordability and corruption are not competing agendas

The supposed choice facing congressional Democrats is between lowering household costs and investigating wrongdoing. Incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries has rejected that separation in his rhetoric about “the cost of corruption,” a phrase that treats corruption as material governance rather than an abstract offense against etiquette.

That connection matters. Officials who exploit public authority for private benefit do not operate in a sealed moral compartment. Their decisions determine who receives government favors, who bears regulatory costs and whether public resources serve citizens or insiders. Investigating those arrangements can therefore expose economic harms as well as legal ones.

Zingher told AlterNet’s John Stoehr that Democrats should begin by pursuing corruption “on all fronts.” He pointed to alleged misconduct involving Trump’s cryptocurrency activities, Nvidia and congressional stock trading, though the interview does not establish criminal liability in any of those matters. His proposal is to investigate first, explain the evidence publicly and prosecute only conduct that can be shown to violate the law.

That distinction is essential. A government that manufactures charges against opponents is practicing political persecution. A government that declines to enforce the law against powerful people is practicing selective impunity. Treating those two abuses as equivalent protects officeholders by making any attempt at accountability appear vindictive.

The lesson Washington chose not to learn

Zingher expects pressure on Democrats to “move on” if they win the presidency in 2028. He sees a precedent in 2021, when many Democrats wanted relief from the first Trump administration and a restoration of ordinary government. In his account, the pursuit of normalcy did not secure normal government. It left intact the expectation that Republicans could regain power without facing durable institutional restraints.

“Normalcy is a privilege,” he told AlterNet. His point is less nostalgic than procedural: stable government depends on officials believing that constitutional and legal limits will be enforced even after the immediate crisis has passed.

Zingher argues that Trump interpreted the limited punishment following his first term as permission. That is an inference about Trump’s lesson, not a documented admission from him, but the institutional incentive is plain. When misconduct produces political turbulence but few lasting consequences, the next officeholder has little reason to regard restraint as mandatory.

Accountability cannot guarantee deterrence. It can, however, change the calculation. Investigations can expose mechanisms of abuse; legislation can close opportunities revealed by those inquiries; prosecutions supported by admissible evidence can demonstrate that public office does not confer personal immunity. Zingher also invokes the Supreme Court’s reasoning in Trump v. United States as an obstacle to restoring that principle.

A case must come before a prosecution

The interview becomes more troubling when it shifts from investigating reported corruption to “building the case for prosecutions in 2029 against people like Hegseth.” No specific offense by Pete Hegseth is identified in the supplied account. Naming a future defendant before presenting the alleged crime reverses the standard Zingher otherwise says Democrats must uphold.

He correctly notes that the public must be convinced officials committed actual crimes and are not being punished for their politics. But that obligation begins with the investigators themselves. Congress can uncover facts, refer evidence and write laws. Prosecutors must still make independent charging decisions based on conduct and proof, not a party’s promised timetable.

The same discipline applies to the article’s denunciation of left-wing critics. Stoehr describes some self-identified progressives as bad actors who use affordability politics to help Democrats fail and advance themselves. Zingher calls a small authoritarian-left faction “fellow travelers with Trump.” The report establishes that both men hold those views; it does not establish the motives they assign to an undefined group.

“Fifth column” is not analysis unless the alleged coordination or disloyalty is demonstrated. Used loosely, it turns dissent into subversion and reproduces the authoritarian habit the article condemns: replacing an argument about conduct with a declaration that inconvenient people are internal enemies.

The damage is not confined to Washington

AlterNet also places immigration at the center of the consequences. Drawing on an essay by Cory Doctorow, Stoehr argues that two years of enforcement and fear drove documented and undocumented immigrants from the United States, depriving an aging country of workers, families and future citizens. He contends that many will build their lives elsewhere rather than return.

That harm, as described, cannot be repaired by a congressional hearing or a change in tone. People who have fled, relocated their families or abandoned plans do not automatically reverse those decisions when an administration changes. The state can halt an abusive policy faster than it can restore the trust the policy destroyed.

This is where the argument against “moving on” becomes concrete. The issue is not whether Democrats should spend their time punishing enemies instead of lowering prices. It is whether they will identify how public power was used, repair what remains repairable and impose lawful consequences where evidence warrants them.

Democrats will eventually lose power again; that is not failure but the ordinary condition of electoral government. What they leave behind will matter more than the duration of their control. If they substitute revenge for law, they validate the machinery of persecution. If they substitute relief and ceremony for enforcement, they preserve a different privilege: the right of powerful officials to wait out public outrage and try again.

item.title: Top economist predicts war inside both parties —and who will win it
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump and the Republican Party suffered a sweeping defeat in the 2026 midterms, but voters did not settle the fight over what comes next. They moved it inside both major parties. Economist Richard Wolff predicts sustained conflict between entrenched party organizations and insurgent factions demanding a break with the economic and political arrangements those organizations protect. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump and the Republican Party suffered a sweeping defeat in the 2026 midterms, but voters did not settle the fight over what comes next. They moved it inside both major parties. Economist Richard Wolff predicts sustained conflict between entrenched party organizations and insurgent factions demanding a break with the economic and political arrangements those organizations protect. His wager is that the emerging left will ultimately gain the advantage—not simply because its prominent figures are younger, but because a broader constituency is increasingly willing to challenge capitalism, concentrated wealth and Washington’s confrontation with China.

That is a forecast, not an election result. Yet it identifies a struggle that the usual left-center-right sorting obscures. Democratic leaders are not passive referees waiting to discover what voters want. They control donor relationships, campaign money, consultants and institutional support. Their “center” is therefore not merely an ideological position. It is a structure of power with contracts to award, careers to preserve and donors to satisfy.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The machinery behind the Democratic “center”

In an interview with AlterNet, Wolff argued that policy disputes—including sharp disagreements over Israel and domestic programs benefiting workers—do not fully explain the Democratic establishment’s resistance to figures such as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, Reps. Rashida Tlaib and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Sen. Bernie Sanders.

The more fundamental conflict, in his account, concerns control of the party’s operating system. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries represent an organization built around recurring relationships with large donors and specialized campaign firms. Party leaders raise money, decide how to distribute it and repeatedly hire the same political professionals. Insurgent candidates threaten more than a policy platform; they threaten the people and institutions that decide which platforms receive money, legitimacy and protection.

Wolff described this as a contest between “old” and “young,” while explicitly separating those categories from biological age. The old politics is a comfortable rotation of party control in which personnel change but the underlying arrangements remain tolerably stable for those running them. The new politics begins from the judgment that this stability has failed much of the country.

That distinction matters because calls for Democrats to “move to the center” often disguise an institutional demand as electoral common sense. The people defining the center are frequently the same people whose authority, donor networks and vendors would be disrupted by a leftward shift. Their preferred position conveniently preserves their power.

Two parties, two insurgencies—and no moral equivalence

Wolff expects continuing internal warfare in both parties. Trump had to displace the Bush-era Republican establishment to remake the GOP around himself; Sanders, Ocasio-Cortez, El-Sayed and others are fighting the Democratic establishment from the left.

The structural similarity ends there. One insurgency captured a party through Trump’s personal authority and right-wing politics. The other is pressing for universal health care, redistribution and a less militarized foreign policy. Treating both merely as expressions of voter dissatisfaction would erase the substance of what each faction intends to do with power.

Still, Trump’s success exposed a vulnerability shared by both party establishments: institutions that reproduce themselves through donors, consultants and managed succession can appear formidable until a faction mobilizes voters whom the old leadership has ceased to represent. Wolff traces that destabilization back to the economic crisis of 2008 and argues that Trump accelerated it.

His forecast that the left will inherit the future rests partly on a generational change in political permission. A growing group of voters and candidates, he said, no longer treats socialism as unspeakable or capitalism as exempt from judgment. If an economic system produces unacceptable results, they are prepared to question, constrain or change it. That does not prove the left will prevail. It does explain why establishment attempts to restore the pre-Trump routine may fail: the taboos that protected that routine are weakening.

“Trumpcare” and the limits of presidential vanity

The most provocative tactical proposal in the interview came from El-Sayed, not Wolff: Democrats could offer Trump a robust Medicare for All program and let him call it “Trumpcare.” Wolff endorsed trying the gambit, speculating that Trump’s attachment to his name might make him receptive.

The idea is deliberately transactional. If branding a universal program around the president could secure health coverage for millions of people who lack it or cannot afford it, Wolff argued, the label would matter less than the institution created.

But the proposal also reveals how deformed federal policymaking becomes when access to medical care is imagined as dependent on flattering one powerful man. It substitutes an appeal to presidential ego for the ordinary work of assembling durable legislative power. Wolff cited Trump’s reported shift in language about El-Sayed—from “lunatic jihadist” to something resembling “smart young man”—as a reason not to dismiss the tactic outright. At most, that suggests Trump’s posture may be mutable. It does not establish that he would support Medicare for All, much less preserve a sufficiently robust version through negotiation and implementation.

The suggestion is worth understanding as an opportunistic route through an existing concentration of power, not as evidence of an alliance. A president’s vanity may create an opening; it is no foundation for a health-care system.

China and the policy class that knows only escalation

Wolff’s economic argument begins with a changed international reality: the United States now faces a peer economic competitor in the People’s Republic of China. He contends that current leaders have no experience managing the American economy under those conditions and that Washington’s decades-long effort to contain China has failed.

His proposed alternative is negotiation with Chinese President Xi Jinping over economic and ecological coexistence. He criticized military pressure in the region, including the Seventh Fleet’s presence and Washington’s fixation on Taiwan, warning that continued friction between heavily armed nuclear powers risks escalating toward war.

That is a political break not only with Republicans but also with a Democratic foreign-policy establishment that routinely presents confrontation as prudence and negotiation as weakness. Wolff calls his alternative a peace policy. Whether a majority of Americans would support it, as he predicts, remains his assessment. The institutional obstacle is clearer: a foreign-policy apparatus organized around military primacy is unlikely to surrender that framework merely because it has become more dangerous or less effective.

Redistribution versus managed deprivation

Wolff’s second priority is income and wealth inequality. He rejects endless economic growth as the central objective and argues that the United States already produces enough; the political question is who receives the gains.

He placed two reported developments side by side. One headline anticipated Elon Musk becoming the first trillionaire. In the same week, according to Wolff, Vice President JD Vance said with pride that 750,000 families had been removed from Medicaid because they did not qualify. Wolff called the prospect of further enriching the world’s wealthiest person “obscene.”

The juxtaposition captures a governing choice too often laundered into separate stories about innovation and eligibility. Vast private accumulation is celebrated as success, while the removal of families from public health coverage is presented as administrative discipline. The state is not absent from either outcome. It enforces the ownership arrangements that enable extreme fortunes and sets the rules determining who may receive medical assistance.

Wolff expects the Democratic left to build a program around redistribution, pointing to Mamdani and the incoming Los Angeles mayor as early signs. That program would collide directly with the donor-centered machinery he described. Party leaders cannot plausibly champion a serious transfer of wealth and power downward while remaining structurally dependent on those who possess both.

The coming Democratic battle, then, is not a seminar about whether the party should turn left, right or center. It is a contest over who controls the party’s resources and whose material interests its policies will serve. Wolff predicts the left will win because economic conditions and political attitudes are changing beneath the establishment. The midterms may have created the opening. They did not remove the officials, donors and contractors positioned to close it.

item.title: Joe Rogan blurts out Republicans’ most 'stupid' failure with Trump

item.content:encoded:
Joe Rogan’s blunt diagnosis of the Republican Party’s midterm losses was that it broke promises, pursued policies its voters did not support and then expected partisan loyalty to protect it from consequences. The “stupid” failure was not merely losing. It was assuming voters would keep rewarding the party after Donald Trump departed from the agenda he sold them.

Rogan’s criticism matters because he was not a detached observer of Trump’s return to power. He endorsed Trump and helped carry his appeal to a large audience of young men. Now, according to reporting cited by AlterNet, he is describing political backlash among the very voters Republicans treated as dependable.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The coalition was not a blank check

“You can't just [mess] … everything up and expect to keep winning,” Rogan said during Wednesday’s episode of The Joe Rogan Experience. He cast the Republican defeat as a predictable response from voters who believed Trump had abandoned his commitments: “This is not what you ran on. This is not what you promised. This is not what we signed up for.”

The discussion with former Navy SEAL and podcast host Jocko Willink centered on the Iran war and affordability concerns. Rogan’s argument was straightforward: Republicans exercised power, produced outcomes that angered voters and were punished at the ballot box.

That explanation assigns responsibility where it belongs. Voters did not force the Trump administration to pursue the Iran war described in the report, and they did not compel Republicans to neglect affordability. The administration chose its course; the party defended or enabled it. Blaming electoral defeat on disloyal supporters would reverse that chain of agency.

Rogan said he personally knew Republicans in formerly deep-red Texas who voted Democratic throughout the ballot. He attributed their defection partly to anger over the party’s handling of unreleased files involving Jeffrey Epstein, the convicted financier who had been Trump’s longtime friend. That is anecdotal evidence, not a measurement of Texas voters. But it captures the political danger for a movement built on promises of disclosure and institutional combat: its supporters may eventually notice when secrecy survives the transfer of power.

Accountability, newly rediscovered

“If your team does stupid things … you break a bunch of promises,” Rogan said, voters are “supposed to vote it out.” He argued that defeat should force a party to reconsider its candidates and policies.

That is conventional democratic accountability, delivered as a revelation because partisan politics increasingly treats it as betrayal. Rogan’s complaint exposes the weakness in the team-sport model Republicans have relied upon: a governing party cannot endlessly substitute identity, grievance and loyalty for material results.

His comments also place him in an awkward but revealing position. Rogan helped validate Trump for listeners Trump needed, lending personal credibility to a candidate whose coalition depended heavily on distrust of established institutions. He is now telling that audience that the administration failed to deliver what it advertised. The criticism does not erase his role in selling the original promise, but it does show that the coalition’s media allies cannot fully control what happens when governing choices collide with expectations.

Losing attention after losing confidence

The electoral backlash described by Rogan accompanies broader signs of political deterioration. CNN polling analyst Harry Enten said Trump and the Republican Party had reached levels of unpopularity comparable to those associated with Harry Truman and George W. Bush, two deeply unpopular presidents in the history of modern polling.

Enten also reported that Google searches for Trump had fallen to their lowest point of his second term, while nearly three-quarters of Republicans surveyed lacked confidence that he could fulfill his agenda. Search activity does not measure approval, but in conjunction with the polling it suggests a problem beyond ordinary opposition: even Republican voters increasingly doubt Trump’s ability to produce the results he promised.

Enten called “becoming irrelevant” the outcome Trump likely fears most and said Americans were losing interest in him. That may be more politically damaging than another cycle of outrage. Trump has long converted attention into power, keeping supporters and opponents fixed on his performance even when policy receded from view. A public that no longer expects delivery—and no longer feels compelled to watch—offers him less to work with.

Rogan’s outburst is therefore less a dramatic break with Trump than a belated description of the transaction Republicans thought they could evade. They asked voters to judge the party by its promises, took power, and governed in ways that Rogan says violated those promises. The losses were not inexplicable. They were the bill.

item.title: Businesses are flying blind into a historic El Niño —thanks to Trump
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: An unusually powerful El Niño is colliding with a federal government that has dismantled or degraded parts of the public climate-information system businesses use to prepare for extreme weather. item.content:encoded:
An unusually powerful El Niño is colliding with a federal government that has dismantled or degraded parts of the public climate-information system businesses use to prepare for extreme weather. NOAA forecasters identified the danger months in advance, but Trump administration cuts have made the more detailed data needed to estimate losses, protect workers and reinforce supply chains harder to obtain—especially for smaller firms that cannot buy private substitutes.

The result is not simply less climate research. It is a transfer of risk: Washington saves money by withdrawing a public service, large corporations purchase replacements, and smaller suppliers and consumers absorb more of the damage.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A historic warning, followed by disappearing data

NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center had forecast a very strong El Niño since spring 2026. Its October update placed the probability that the event would become the strongest since records began in 1950 at 83 percent, with conditions likely to persist into early 2027.

That advance notice matters. Retailers, farmers, food processors and transportation companies can use it to increase inventories, arrange backup suppliers and reroute shipments before drought, flooding or severe storms interrupt production. El Niño patterns in North America are associated with Pacific storms as well as fires, floods and droughts, and historically strong events have imposed trillions of dollars in global economic costs.

But a broad forecast is not a substitute for the observation networks, historical records and regular analysis needed to decide where, when and how to prepare. Those resources have been steadily weakened.

NOAA stopped updating its Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters database in May 2025 and retired it after data through 2024. The database had tracked the cost of major American weather disasters for more than four decades, giving researchers and businesses a historical foundation for estimating future losses and economic disruption.

The federal government also shut down Climate.gov in 2025. Its El Niño blog has not been updated since June of that year. National Climate Assessments were removed from government websites, while staffing shortages led the National Weather Service to reduce weather-balloon launches at several locations, depriving forecast models of observations used in daily prediction.

These losses come as expensive disasters grow more common. The United States averaged fewer than five billion-dollar disasters annually during the 1980s; it now experiences more than 20 a year, even after adjusting for inflation. The totals in 2023 and 2024 were the highest recorded.

The administration cut the tools, not the exposure

The Trump administration has defended the cuts by pointing to administrative expense and possible errors in predictive models. Models are imperfect. Eliminating public data does not correct that imperfection; it leaves decision-makers with less information while the physical and economic hazards remain.

That distinction exposes the misdirection in the administration’s rationale. The relevant choice is not between flawless federal forecasts and wasteful ones. It is between a shared information system—available to businesses and researchers regardless of wealth—and a fragmented market in which access depends increasingly on the ability to pay.

Public weather intelligence runs quietly through the economy. Companies use current and near-current information to plan inventories, improve crop yields, select transportation routes and keep employees out of dangerous conditions. Insurers use it to price commercial coverage and handle claims. Risk Management Solutions, a catastrophe-modeling company owned by Moody’s, uses NOAA hurricane data in its models. Walmart maintains specialists and technology dedicated to monitoring weather threats to its supply chain.

The federal retreat does not make those needs disappear. It creates customers for private providers such as WindBorne Systems, Sofar Ocean, Tomorrow.io, Black Swift Technologies and Saildrone, which sell specialized observations and forecasting services.

Private data can replace some lost capacity for companies with sufficient budgets. It cannot reproduce equal access. Major retailers and insurers can pay subscription fees; local farmers, independent truckers and small suppliers often cannot. Those businesses occupy precisely the vulnerable links where a failed harvest, closed road or unsafe workplace can begin a much larger disruption.

Some scientists have tried to preserve the abandoned public work. The researchers behind NOAA’s El Niño blog moved their effort to a nonprofit, and another nonprofit has continued the disaster-database project. That salvages expertise, but it also reveals the institutional choice: functions once supported by the federal government are now dependent on private organizations to survive.

Consumers receive the bill later

Weather shocks rarely appear at the checkout counter on the day they occur. They move through farms, factories, warehouses and freight networks before emerging as shortages and higher prices months later.

The pattern is already visible. Extreme weather in the Americas, including Florida, helped push U.S. orange-juice prices to a record in fall 2024; prices remained elevated after Hurricanes Helene and Milton damaged Florida groves. A Pacific Northwest heat dome harmed Christmas-tree farms in 2021 and added an estimated 5 to 10 percent to prices that year. Poor rainfall in West Africa more than doubled cocoa prices in 2024, with the effects still reaching American consumers as U.S. chocolate prices rose 14 percent in 2026.

Suvrat Dhanorkar, a Georgia Institute of Technology operations-management professor writing in The Conversation, warned that diminished federal climate information could produce cascading failures across companies and supply chains before reaching consumers as inflation. That is not a claim that better data can prevent every crop failure or storm closure. It can, however, give businesses time to reduce foreseeable losses.

The 2026 El Niño has already disrupted crops and supply chains internationally, including through a delayed monsoon season in India. Its arrival during the erosion of American climate infrastructure turns the coming months into a test the Trump administration chose to make harsher: not whether weather intelligence has value, but who can still afford it after the government withdraws it from everyone else.

item.title: The unspoken reason Trump and MAGA are trying to erase history
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s campaign against disfavored accounts of American history serves a clear political function: it strips the public record of the evidence needed to understand how racial conquest, concentrated wealth and attacks on organized labor produced present-day inequalities. But AlterNet’s headline promises an “unspoken reason” that its interview does not actually establish. The reporting documents Trump’s effort to control historical interpretation and offers Bob Hennelly’s argument for why
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s campaign against disfavored accounts of American history serves a clear political function: it strips the public record of the evidence needed to understand how racial conquest, concentrated wealth and attacks on organized labor produced present-day inequalities. But AlterNet’s headline promises an “unspoken reason” that its interview does not actually establish. The reporting documents Trump’s effort to control historical interpretation and offers Bob Hennelly’s argument for why that effort benefits entrenched power; it does not produce evidence of a concealed MAGA strategy or admission.

That distinction matters. Trump’s administration has targeted the Smithsonian and other federally supported museums, weakened the Department of Education, sought to cancel academic grants and stigmatized accounts of exploitation as “woke” or “DEI,” according to AlterNet. Those are concrete exercises of presidential power. The administration is not merely entering a scholarly disagreement. It is using control over institutions and funding to narrow what the country is permitted to say about itself.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Government control disguised as neutrality

Alan Dershowitz, a former Trump attorney, supplied the administration’s defense in an earlier interview with AlterNet. Museums and schools, he argued, should not promote the view that the United States “was created by slavery” or is “a terrible country.” Because the Smithsonian is part of the state, he said, the administration was entitled to tell it what it could not do.

That formulation does not remove ideology from public history. It gives the executive branch authority to define ideology—and then to suppress whatever falls outside its approved national story. The maneuver is familiar: describe contested evidence as partisan, present state censorship as neutrality and treat patriotic reassurance as the absence of politics.

It also substitutes a caricature for the scholarship being attacked. Examining slavery’s role in the nation’s development is not the same as declaring the country irredeemably terrible. By collapsing those positions, defenders of the administration can avoid the historical question and prosecute the emotional offense of making some Americans uncomfortable.

Hennelly, the WBAI executive and author of Stuck Nation, called Dershowitz’s analysis ahistorical because it begins too late. He traced the underlying system to the Catholic doctrine used to legitimize European dominion over Indigenous people, territory and resources in the Americas. In his account, Indigenous dispossession and slavery were not marginal departures from an otherwise untouched political economy. They helped construct it.

His “cracks in the foundation” metaphor is useful precisely because it rejects two convenient evasions: that acknowledging structural damage requires condemning every part of the country, or that later generations can safely ignore defects they did not personally create. A building does not become sound because its current occupants deny responsibility for pouring the foundation.

The history that makes exploitation legible

Hennelly’s larger case is that suppressing this history harms many of the working people whom MAGA politics claims to represent. Colonial labor systems differed—enslaved labor, indentured servitude and independent farming existed alongside one another—but industrialization increasingly organized capital on a scale individual workers could not match. Unions became a counterweight.

That history explains why labor rights were won collectively and why employers and allied politicians have repeatedly tried to dismantle them. Hennelly said union representation has historically raised pay by roughly 15 to 20 percent and frequently secured benefits unavailable to nonunion workers. He contrasted union density of about one-third of the workforce after World War II with roughly 10 percent today, while putting public-sector membership near 30 percent.

The decisive actors in that decline were not workers who somehow forgot the virtues of solidarity. Political and corporate leaders changed the balance of power. Hennelly pointed to President Ronald Reagan’s firing of 13,000 striking air traffic controllers in the early 1980s. The controllers had raised concerns about overstretched infrastructure, working conditions and inadequate investment. Reagan’s action demonstrated that the federal government would use its authority to break a major labor confrontation, strengthening employers far beyond that dispute.

This is where sanitized history becomes materially useful. If Americans learn labor decline as an impersonal trend, no one has to answer for weakening unions. If they learn it as a succession of decisions made by presidents, employers and lawmakers, falling worker power stops looking inevitable.

Division protects the people already in charge

Hennelly’s argument also exposes the trap in presenting racial history and class politics as rival explanations. Slavery generated wealth through racial domination; later employers accumulated power by limiting workers’ ability to act together. The mechanisms are not identical, but erasing either one makes the other harder to understand.

That is the political benefit of reducing historical education to a fight over whether individual white Americans should feel guilty. It redirects attention from institutions to personal grievance. Workers are encouraged to experience an account of exploitation as an insult to their identity instead of asking who gained wealth, who wrote the rules and who still holds leverage.

Hennelly applied the same analysis to health care before COVID-19. Unions and public-health workers, he said, warned that a system organized around profit and executive compensation had failed to maintain basic reserves such as N95 masks. He argued that the resulting lack of preparation contributed to mass death during the pandemic. His point is not that history mechanically repeats itself. It is that institutions repeatedly reward extraction while treating investment in workers and public capacity as expendable.

The same conflict appears in his discussion of data centers and immigration enforcement in 2026. Hennelly described communities confronting resource-intensive development backed by wealthy technology interests, including more than 300 proposed data centers in Texas that he said threatened water quality. He also cited violent ICE apprehension tactics unfolding in local neighborhoods and invoked Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis as ordinary people willing to accept personal risk in response.

Some of Hennelly’s electoral interpretation goes beyond what the interview demonstrates. He suggested that Texas ranchers concerned about water consequently voted for Democrats, but the supplied reporting does not establish that chain of causation. Nor does the interview prove that a unified labor awakening explains recent electoral upheaval. Those claims remain his analysis, not reported findings.

A motive inferred, not uncovered

The strongest conclusion supported by the article is narrower—and more damning—than its teaser. Trump is using federal authority to discipline museums, education and research that challenge a celebratory national narrative. Hennelly argues that the histories under attack teach Americans how power was accumulated and how collective action can contest it. Erasing those lessons predictably benefits political and economic actors whose position depends on people misunderstanding the origins of their own precarity.

What AlterNet does not establish is that Trump or MAGA officials privately chose historical whitewashing for the specific purpose of concealing labor history. Calling that motive “unspoken” turns an evidence-grounded interpretation into the promise of a revelation the interview never delivers.

No secret explanation is required to recognize the power play. An administration that decides which parts of the national record are too offensive for public institutions is not protecting Americans from ideology. It is asserting the state’s authority to make official innocence—and the political obedience that innocence demands—a condition of public memory.

item.title: Trump welcomes Thanksgiving with reckless posting tirade
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump marked the first minutes of Thanksgiving by attacking a New York Times reporter who had challenged the president’s preferred account of his intervention at Nvidia. The post was more than a holiday grievance spree. item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump marked the first minutes of Thanksgiving by attacking a New York Times reporter who had challenged the president’s preferred account of his intervention at Nvidia. The post was more than a holiday grievance spree. It showed Trump using the presidency’s platform to demand personal credit for favorable developments, assign every setback to political enemies and punish scrutiny with insults rather than answers.

At about 12:47 a.m., Trump targeted national security reporter David E. Sanger over an article examining the market consequences of Trump’s role in Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia’s chief executive. According to reporting cited by AlterNet, Nvidia shares initially rallied after Huang’s reinstatement but had fallen nearly 11 percent since Tuesday. Trump did not address that reversal. He called Sanger a “lowlife” who writes what his bosses tell him to write.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A presidential intervention with unanswered consequences

Earlier in the week, Trump claimed that he had personally pressured Nvidia’s board to restore Huang as CEO. Huang had resigned after acknowledging multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy reportedly involved in moving valuable artificial-intelligence chips into China despite export controls.

That is not an ordinary corporate personnel dispute. It implicates national security, enforcement of technology restrictions and the president’s use of federal influence on behalf of a powerful company’s leadership. Subsequent reports, according to AlterNet, found that Trump had been briefed on the situation months earlier but did not act then.

Trump nevertheless treated the immediate stock rally following Huang’s return as proof of his intervention’s success. When the gain evaporated, he blamed the market decline on a Democratic “blue wave” in the midterm elections. The allocation of responsibility was perfectly asymmetrical: the president owned the rise, while voters and Democrats owned the fall.

Sanger’s reported observation—that Trump regularly claims surging markets while rejecting responsibility for declines—identified the maneuver Trump’s response tried to bury. Trump’s post did not rebut the account of Nvidia’s falling share price or explain why he pressed for Huang’s reinstatement. It redirected attention toward the reporter’s character and Trump’s catalogue of alleged triumphs.

A wall of boasts in place of an answer

Trump listed what he described as the successful closure of the border, historic crime figures, record tax and regulatory cuts, an unmatched naval blockade, the destruction of Iran’s naval and air forces, a “ONE DAY WIN” against Venezuela and success resolving what he called an “Obama caused mess in Iowa.” He also claimed to have settled eight wars and restored unprecedented respect for the United States.

These were assertions embedded in a personal attack, not a response to the Nvidia reporting. Their political function was distraction through volume: replace a specific question about presidential judgment with so many sweeping claims that scrutiny becomes a contest over the entire Trump mythology.

The choice of target also clarified the power relationship. Sanger is a journalist whose work can be criticized. Trump is the president, commanding the executive branch and wielding a public platform capable of directing mass hostility toward named individuals. Calling a reporter corrupt or controlled by unnamed bosses allows Trump to portray unwelcome reporting as illegitimate without confronting its substance.

Credit without accountability

Trump extended the same logic to the election results and Americans’ retirement savings. “I wasn’t on the Ballot,” he wrote, claiming that the outcome would have been different had he been a candidate and that the stock market and “your 401-k’s” would be “BOOMING.”

The statement converts two setbacks—a poor election for his party and a market downturn—into evidence of his own indispensability. Voters are cast as having produced economic damage by failing to ratify Trump’s political project, while Trump remains entitled to credit for hypothetical prosperity that did not occur.

That is the central story behind the Thanksgiving posting. A president intervened in the leadership of a strategically important technology company, celebrated the market’s initial reaction and then lashed out when a reporter documented the reversal. The insults and unrelated boasts were not explanations. They were an attempt to make accountability itself look like partisan misconduct—and to ensure that, in Trump’s telling, power brings limitless credit but never responsibility.

item.title: Wall Street’s Three Stooges: The AI Economy and the Twenty-Dollar Bill
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Artificial intelligence may be the technological revolution of our lifetime. The financial machinery built around it, however, increasingly resembles a vaudeville routine. There is an old Three Stooges routine that, in retrospect, might be one of the finest explanations of modern American capitalism ever committed to film. Help fuel the work. item.content:encoded:
Artificial intelligence may be the technological revolution of our lifetime. The financial machinery built around it, however, increasingly resembles a vaudeville routine.

There is an old Three Stooges routine that, in retrospect, might be one of the finest explanations of modern American capitalism ever committed to film.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Moe finds a twenty-dollar bill. Larry taps him on the shoulder and reminds him that he owes him twenty dollars. Moe acknowledges the debt and hands him the bill.

Curly then reminds Larry that he owes him twenty dollars. Larry hands him the bill.

Finally, Moe reminds Curly that he owes him twenty dollars. Curly hands the bill back to Moe.

Three transactions. Sixty dollars in payments. One twenty-dollar bill.

And Moe ends up exactly where he started.

The remarkable thing about this little routine is that the Three Stooges actually accomplished something economically useful: they extinguished sixty dollars in outstanding debt using twenty dollars in available liquidity.

Now imagine the same routine performed by Silicon Valley’s biggest corporations, with Wall Street providing the laugh track.

The Magnificent Seven and the Twenty-Dollar Bill

In Brazil, we have a traditional children’s game called Escravos de Jó. The participants sit in a circle, passing objects from one person to another in rhythm with a song.

Watching the financial relationships developing around the artificial intelligence industry, I cannot help but be reminded of that game.

Except that instead of children passing stones around a table, we have multibillion-dollar corporations passing enormous bags of money around an increasingly interconnected financial ecosystem.

A semiconductor manufacturer invests billions in an artificial intelligence company.

The artificial intelligence company commits billions to purchasing computing capacity from a cloud provider.

The cloud provider purchases billions in processors from the semiconductor manufacturer.

The semiconductor manufacturer announces unprecedented demand for its products.

The cloud provider announces unprecedented demand for its infrastructure.

The artificial intelligence company announces unprecedented investment in its future.

Wall Street celebrates all three announcements.

Stock prices soar. Analysts revise their projections. Executives congratulate themselves. Financial journalists proclaim the dawn of a new economic paradigm.

And somewhere in the middle of this corporate choreography, the same capital has effectively financed several different transactions.

This is a simplified illustration of circular financing, not an allegation that every major technology company is engaged in fraudulent accounting. The transactions can be perfectly legitimate. The processors are real. The computing capacity is real. The infrastructure being built is real.

What remains uncertain is whether the demand ultimately supporting all this investment is sufficient and sustainable independently of the companies financing it.

That is a rather important distinction.

The Problem Begins When Someone Actually Needs to Spend the Money

Let us return to the Three Stooges.

Moe has his twenty-dollar bill back. Everyone has settled their debts. Everything is wonderful.

Then the landlord knocks on the door.

Each of the three owes twenty dollars in rent.

Suddenly, the three men have sixty dollars in external obligations and only twenty dollars between them.

They can pass that bill around the room as many times as they like. They can announce strategic partnerships, establish joint ventures, issue press releases and hire McKinsey to produce a magnificent PowerPoint presentation.

They are still forty dollars short.

That is the problem with confusing the circulation of money with the creation of wealth.

Artificial intelligence requires enormous amounts of physical infrastructure. Data centers require land, concrete, steel, transformers, cooling systems, networking equipment and electricity. Semiconductor manufacturing requires sophisticated machinery, raw materials and highly specialized labor.

Employees need salaries. Creditors expect interest payments. Construction companies expect to be paid.

The electric utility does not accept market capitalization as payment.

Eventually, the money has to leave the circle.

And when it does, it must be replenished by genuine economic activity capable of generating sufficient cash.

That cash can come from customers, from profitable existing businesses, from additional investors or from borrowing. But the latter two cannot indefinitely substitute for a commercially sustainable operation.

At some point, somebody has to make money rather than merely raise it.

Market Capitalization Is Not Money

One of the most peculiar affectations of modern financial journalism is its habit of treating market capitalization as though it were an enormous bank account.

A company supposedly “loses” a hundred billion dollars on Monday and “gains” a hundred and fifty billion dollars on Tuesday.

Where did the money go? Where did it come from?

In many cases, nowhere.

Suppose a corporation has one billion outstanding shares trading at one hundred dollars each. Its market capitalization is one hundred billion dollars.

Investor confidence deteriorates, and the share price falls to seventy dollars.

Thirty billion dollars in market capitalization has evaporated.

Yet the corporation has not necessarily lost thirty billion dollars in cash. Its factories are still there. Its employees are still working. Its intellectual property remains intact.

What changed was the price investors were willing to pay for its shares.

Market capitalization is a valuation, not a measurement of accumulated cash or productive capacity. It incorporates expectations about future profitability, growth, risk and, increasingly, the collective enthusiasm of investors.

Or, to dispense with the sophisticated financial terminology: vibes.

This does not mean stock market valuations are economically irrelevant. They influence borrowing costs, investment decisions, acquisitions, retirement savings and the ability of corporations to raise capital.

That is precisely what makes speculative valuations so dangerous.

An entirely subjective reassessment of future prospects can produce very real consequences in the present.

The Load-Bearing CEO

On November 23, 2026, Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang had been reinstated as its chief executive officer following his resignation earlier that month.

Nvidia’s shares surged 31.5%. The Nasdaq gained approximately 6.5%. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%.

Nearly a trillion dollars in Nvidia’s market capitalization was restored in a single trading session.

Had Nvidia invented a revolutionary processor overnight?

Had it constructed another semiconductor fabrication facility? Had its productive capacity increased by nearly one-third? Had artificial intelligence suddenly become dramatically more profitable for its customers?

No.

A man had returned to his office.

A YouTube creator discussing the incident coined a particularly appropriate expression: a “load-bearing CEO.”

In software engineering, we have a considerably less amusing term for this phenomenon: a single point of failure.

We spend enormous amounts of time designing critical systems specifically to eliminate single points of failure. We introduce redundancy, failover mechanisms, backups and alternative execution paths because we understand that individual components can and eventually will fail.

A system whose continued operation depends entirely on one irreplaceable component is a badly designed system.

Apparently, Wall Street considers this an investment strategy.

If the departure of one executive can contribute to a widespread financial panic, and his return can restore hundreds of billions of dollars in valuations, we should be examining the fragility of the financial ecosystem rather than merely celebrating the executive’s return.

The existence of a load-bearing CEO is not simply a testament to the individual’s brilliance. It is an indictment of the architecture surrounding him.

We Have Seen This Movie Before

The comparison with the 2008 financial crisis is tempting, although the underlying mechanisms are not identical.

Before 2008, financial institutions accumulated enormous exposure to interconnected financial instruments whose values depended on assumptions about the housing market.

Those instruments were packaged, repackaged, divided and distributed throughout the financial system. Institutions that appeared to have diversified their investments had, in reality, accumulated exposure to many of the same underlying risks.

When those assumptions failed, the apparent diversification offered far less protection than anticipated.

The contemporary artificial intelligence ecosystem presents a different but troubling form of interconnected exposure.

A semiconductor manufacturer finances a company that consumes computing capacity. A cloud provider builds infrastructure in anticipation of that consumption. An AI developer commits to purchasing infrastructure on the assumption that its own customer base will eventually justify the expenditure.

Each participant’s success becomes increasingly dependent upon the success of the others.

If anticipated demand fails to materialize, the consequences need not remain confined to one company.

The AI developer may reduce its computing commitments. The cloud provider may find itself with excess capacity and outstanding construction debt. The semiconductor manufacturer may experience declining orders.

The investors who thought they had diversified their portfolios across several different technology companies may discover that they had effectively made several variations of the same bet.

Correlated financial exposure masquerading as diversification.

Sound familiar?

Artificial Intelligence Is Not the Bubble

I want to make something abundantly clear: this is not an indictment of artificial intelligence.

I am a software developer who uses artificial intelligence professionally, extensively and daily. I have experienced firsthand the extraordinary productivity gains that these technologies can deliver.

I do not need a Wall Street analyst to convince me that artificial intelligence has practical economic value.

But there are four fundamentally different propositions that the financial establishment seems determined to treat as interchangeable:

  • Artificial intelligence is a revolutionary technology.

  • Artificial intelligence can dramatically increase productivity.

  • Artificial intelligence companies can become sustainably profitable.

  • Artificial intelligence companies are worth their current valuations.

The first two can be entirely true while the last two turn out to be spectacularly wrong.

We witnessed precisely this phenomenon during the dot-com bubble.

The Internet did not stop working when the bubble burst. Its usefulness did not suddenly disappear. Its potential to transform commerce, communication and society was not imaginary.

What collapsed was the speculative financial structure that had been erected around it.

Wall Street had correctly identified a revolutionary technology and then proceeded to lose staggering amounts of money by incorrectly valuing the businesses attempting to commercialize it.

Recognizing the technological revolution did not make every investment in it intelligent.

Artificial intelligence is no exception.

When the Music Stops

Unlike many of the companies that populated the dot-com bubble, today’s technology giants possess enormous established businesses capable of generating substantial cash.

Microsoft sells software and cloud services. Alphabet sells advertising. Amazon operates an enormous retail and cloud computing empire. Meta generates advertising revenue. Nvidia sells actual processors.

This provides the industry with considerable financial resilience.

But resilience is not immunity.

The question is whether the returns generated by artificial intelligence will ultimately justify the enormous capital expenditures being undertaken to support it.

If they do, much of this investment may prove extraordinarily profitable.

If they do not, the existence of profitable legacy businesses will not magically transform bad investments into good ones. It will simply determine how much financial punishment those corporations can absorb before they are forced to reconsider their commitments.

And, as usual, the consequences will not necessarily be confined to the executives who authorized those commitments or the investors who enthusiastically encouraged them.

Workers, pension funds, ordinary shareholders, contractors and communities dependent upon promised infrastructure projects may find themselves paying for decisions they never participated in making.

We have seen that movie before, too.

The danger is not that artificial intelligence will turn out to be useless.

The danger is that Wall Street will have once again taken something genuinely useful, inflated its financial expectations beyond what the underlying economics can sustain, and confused the resulting speculative frenzy with the creation of durable wealth.

Moe, Larry and Curly understood that circulating twenty dollars could settle sixty dollars in debts.

Wall Street appears determined to convince itself that circulating twenty dollars can create sixty dollars in wealth.

At least the Three Stooges knew they were performing a comedy.

The real test begins when the landlord knocks on the door.

References

  • Load Bearing CEO — YouTube

  • Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang as President, CEO and Board Director — November 23, 2026

  • Nvidia’s SEC Form 8-K concerning Huang’s reinstatement

  • US stocks surge after Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia’s CEO — Associated Press

item.content:encoded:
Sean Hannity, not Donald Trump, is emerging as the Republican gatekeeper to watch ahead of 2028. According to AlterNet’s account of a Washington Post profile, the longtime Fox News host plans to interrogate the party’s leading presidential contenders and decide whom to support—an endorsement Hannity portrays as potentially decisive even as Trump’s popularity declines.

That does not make Hannity the party’s formal leader, and the reporting cannot establish four years early who will determine the nomination. It does reveal something more concrete: Republican aspirants are expected to seek approval from a television personality whose power comes from commanding a loyal audience, enforcing ideological boundaries and offering favored politicians sustained protection.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The primary before the primary

Washington Post writer Timothy Bella calls the approaching competition “the Hannity Primary.” Hannity intends to question each major contender, testing not only conservative credentials but electoral viability.

“You could be the perfect conservative, but if you don’t have the ability to win a race, why would I support you?” Hannity said. That formulation places him in the role of strategist and validator, not merely commentator. Candidates must satisfy his definition of conservatism and persuade him that they can convert it into power.

Hannity presents his endorsement as a hard-won seal of approval. Recalling 2016, he described “very long, late-night, deep conversations” with Trump and said he warned the candidate: “If you don’t convince me, I’m not going to vote for you, and I will not support you. Period.”

This account conveniently casts Hannity as a discerning evaluator rather than what he became: one of Trump’s most dependable media advocates. But the distinction matters less than the access itself. Hannity had prolonged private conversations with a presidential candidate, then used one of cable television’s most influential platforms to champion him.

Advocacy packaged as judgment

Hannity’s power is built on the collapse of any meaningful boundary between political coverage and political sponsorship. His Fox program remained among cable news’s five highest-ranked shows even when the network’s broader standing suffered, according to AlterNet. That audience gives him something party officials cannot easily replicate: repeated access to Republican voters inside a trusted partisan environment.

Stephen A. Smith put the relationship bluntly: “I don’t think Trump would have become president without Sean.” Smith described Hannity as relentlessly protective of the people he supports, willing to erect “a ton of brick walls” between them and their critics.

Dan Bongino, identified in the report as a radio host and former FBI deputy director, offered a more qualified assessment. Trump “would have been fine on his own,” he said, but Hannity’s early support helped launch what became the MAGA movement—a political project Bongino said many people hope will survive Trump.

Neither comment proves that Hannity single-handedly produced Trump’s victory. They do, however, describe a media figure acting as political infrastructure: selecting allies, amplifying them and shielding them once selected. Hannity’s influence does not depend on holding office because elected Republicans depend on reaching the audience he has cultivated.

Loyalty without accountability

The substance of Hannity’s record matters as much as the size of his platform. AlterNet notes that he remained beside Trump through repeated controversies, including Trump’s questioning of election legitimacy when results went against him.

Hannity’s response to criticism is not reconsideration but self-exoneration. “We’ve been vindicated more times than I can count,” he told the Post. He treats that asserted record as the source of his credibility and, therefore, as the reason candidates seek his backing.

Fox host Laura Ingraham praised Hannity’s ability to understand people’s needs and navigate politics and culture, calling him both an analyst and an entertainer. That combination is precisely what makes his role politically potent. Entertainment supplies intimacy and loyalty; analysis supplies the appearance of independent judgment. The endorsement then arrives carrying both.

Hannity’s claim that a 2028 candidate cannot prevail without him remains a boast, not an established fact. His retrospective certainty—“I felt Donald Trump could win, and I was not wrong”—also turns one correct political judgment into a sweeping claim of authority.

Still, Republican contenders who submit to the “Hannity Primary” will help make the boast real. The power here is not mystical and does not belong to Hannity alone. It is produced by candidates who treat a cable host as a necessary broker, a network that supplies the platform and a party whose voters have been trained to receive political advocacy as news analysis. Trump may eventually leave the stage. The machinery that promoted and protected him is already auditioning replacements.

item.title: Young Republicans sound off on Trump and GOP at Texas meeting: 'Grow up'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Young Republicans meeting at a Texas brewery after the GOP’s 2026 midterm rout reached an unsparing conclusion: Donald Trump and his party had helped engineer their own defeat through broken promises, economic detachment, personal fealty and behavior several attendees described as childish. Their advice—“grow up”—was directed not at wayward voters but at the people who held power and squandered it.
