item.content:encoded:
The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact offers states a way to ensure that the presidential candidate who receives the most votes nationwide wins the White House—without formally abolishing the Electoral College. AlterNet reports that Democratic gains in governorships and state legislatures have created a realistic path for the compact, nearly 20 years after Maryland became its first member. But the mechanism remains contingent: it takes effect only when participating states control at least 270 electoral votes, depends on those states honoring their commitments, and could face a court challenge.

The proposal is less a repeal of the Electoral College than an attempt to neutralize its capacity to overrule the electorate. States joining the compact agree to award their electors to the national popular-vote winner, regardless of which candidate finishes first within their borders. Once the participating bloc reaches the 270 electoral votes required to elect a president, its combined votes would guarantee victory for the national winner.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That is the loophole: using the states’ authority over electors to change the outcome produced by the Electoral College without amending the Constitution.

Maryland opened the route in 2007

Maryland joined the compact in April 2007, when Democratic Gov. Martin O’Malley signed it into law. O’Malley told AlterNet that former Indiana Sen. Birch Bayh, then living on Maryland’s Eastern Shore, had urged him to act.

According to O’Malley, Bayh argued that states did not have to wait for a constitutional amendment to address presidential elections in which the popular-vote winner lost. Maryland could move first and invite other states to follow.

O’Malley did not expect a rapid transformation. Governors and legislatures face crowded agendas, he said, and a proposal like the compact can “fall off the plate” unless a governor makes it a priority. That explanation also identifies where the relevant power sits: not with voters acting nationally, because the United States does not conduct presidential elections as a single national contest, but with state officials who determine how their electoral votes are allocated.

Nearly two decades of incremental progress reflect the compact’s basic political difficulty. Every participating state must agree to bind its electoral power to a national result, but the agreement has no effect until the coalition is large enough to decide the presidency.

The Electoral College’s failures are not historical curiosities

Five presidents have taken office without winning the popular vote: John Quincy Adams in 1824, Rutherford B. Hayes in 1876, Benjamin Harrison in 1888, George W. Bush in 2000 and Donald Trump in 2016. The clustering of two such outcomes in the modern era turned what defenders can describe as an antique irregularity into a present political problem.

The 2016 result is central to AlterNet’s framing. Trump won the presidency through the Electoral College despite losing the national popular vote. Had an operative compact controlled at least 270 electors, the national popular-vote winner would instead have received the decisive electoral majority.

That history exposes the misdirection embedded in familiar descriptions of the Electoral College as merely “indirect.” Its consequence is not procedural quaintness. It can transfer the presidency to a candidate rejected by more voters than their opponent, giving state boundaries and electoral arithmetic more authority than the national vote count.

The system also concentrates campaign power in competitive states. The compact would replace that winner-take-all map with one decisive measure: the total number of votes each ticket receives nationwide.

A workaround is not the same as abolition

O’Malley described the compact as a way to “retire” an institution that “no longer serves.” At another point, he said the Electoral College would cease to exist once enough states pledged their electors to the popular-vote winner. That is politically understandable shorthand, but it overstates what the compact formally does.

The Electoral College would remain in the Constitution. Electors would still cast the votes that legally select the president and vice president. The compact would change how participating states instruct those electors, converting the institution into the vehicle for enforcing the national result rather than defeating it.

Nor does the plan require a majority of states, as O’Malley suggested in the interview. The threshold described by AlterNet is electoral, not geographic: states controlling at least 270 of the country’s 538 electoral votes. A coalition could therefore activate the compact without including most states, provided its members possessed a majority of electors.

That distinction matters because the proposal does not remove state power from presidential elections. It organizes enough states to use that power differently.

The plan’s leverage is also its vulnerability

The compact avoids the formidable process of amending the Constitution, but that shortcut creates its own exposure. AlterNet notes that the arrangement relies on participating states acting in good faith and could be struck down by the courts.

Those risks are not incidental. A mechanism designed to prevent the losing candidate from gaining power would face its greatest pressure precisely when it changed an election’s apparent state-by-state result. Officials would be required to award electors according to the nationwide count even if another candidate carried their own state. The compact’s mathematical guarantee therefore depends on its legal and political commitments surviving the moment when they become consequential.

Still, the proposal identifies the institution responsible for the distortion and the officials capable of changing it. Voters did not design a system in which the national runner-up can become president, and they cannot repair it through a single nationwide vote. State governors and legislators possess the operative authority. Maryland used that authority in 2007; the remaining question is whether enough states will do the same to reach 270—and whether the resulting agreement can withstand the first election it determines.

item.title: Trump's GOP was built by a 1964 book about treason
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: John Stormer’s 1964 book None Dare Call It Treason did not single-handedly build Donald Trump’s Republican Party. It supplied something more durable: a conspiracy narrative that cast government, organized labor, civil-rights movements and an increasingly assertive middle class as parts of the same subversive project. AlterNet columnist Thom Hartmann argues that wealthy conservatives used that framework to turn resistance to economic equality into a defense of the nation—and that Trump inherited
item.content:encoded:
John Stormer’s 1964 book None Dare Call It Treason did not single-handedly build Donald Trump’s Republican Party. It supplied something more durable: a conspiracy narrative that cast government, organized labor, civil-rights movements and an increasingly assertive middle class as parts of the same subversive project. AlterNet columnist Thom Hartmann argues that wealthy conservatives used that framework to turn resistance to economic equality into a defense of the nation—and that Trump inherited the political machinery it produced.

The important history is not a straight line from one paperback to one president. It is the construction of a movement that taught voters to fear relatively powerless groups while corporations, wealthy donors and Republican officials exercised the institutional power to rewrite tax law, weaken unions and dismantle public programs. Stormer’s book helped popularize the accusation. The people financing conservative politics converted it into policy.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Treason as a marketing strategy

Stormer alleged that communists had infiltrated the State Department and were preparing to surrender the United States to the Soviet Union. Hartmann recalls receiving the book at age 13 from his Republican activist father, who had obtained it through Barry Goldwater’s 1964 presidential campaign.

That story of internal betrayal drew on an older conservative hostility toward mass political participation. Hartmann traces it to Russell Kirk’s 1951 book The Conservative Mind and Kirk’s admiration for Edmund Burke, who argued that tradesmen should not be permitted to rule. In Hartmann’s reading, Kirk treated an empowered middle class as a source of disorder and regarded firm class hierarchy as the basis of social stability.

The social movements of the 1960s gave that argument new targets. Black Americans challenged segregation and police violence. Women demanded control over their lives. Students resisted the Vietnam War and the draft. Gay people organized openly. Union workers fought to protect their wages as inflation accelerated during the 1970s.

Conservative organizers grouped those distinct struggles under labels such as communism, socialism and moral decline. That was political misdirection with a material beneficiary. Students, minorities and workers did not control federal tax policy or corporate investment. Wealthy donors and elected officials did. By presenting demands for rights and economic security as evidence of national subversion, the movement made hierarchy look like patriotism.

Reagan turned the argument into government policy

Ronald Reagan’s election converted the conservative campaign against “socialism” into an assault conducted through the state itself. His administration cut the top marginal tax rate from 74 percent to 25 percent, according to Hartmann, while imposing or expanding taxes that reached Social Security benefits, unemployment income and tips. It also ended deductions for interest on consumer, automobile and student debt.

Reagan’s attack on the Professional Air Traffic Controllers Organization carried the same distributional logic into the workplace. He fired striking air traffic controllers, demonstrating that the federal government would use its authority against organized labor. Hartmann writes that union membership fell from roughly one-third of the workforce when Reagan entered office to about 10 percent by the end of the Reagan and George H.W. Bush presidencies; private-sector membership is now around 6 percent.

The decline cannot honestly be described as workers simply losing interest in unions. Employers gained leverage because political leaders changed the consequences of resisting them. When government withdrew support for labor rights, companies acquired more power to suppress organizing, hold down wages and retain a larger share of the wealth workers produced.

Trade policy reinforced that shift. Hartmann connects the Reagan and Bush administrations’ work on the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the North American Free Trade Agreement to Bill Clinton’s later support for NAFTA and the World Trade Organization. Companies could move manufacturing abroad, reducing labor costs and weakening unions. Democratic participation in that program matters because it deprived workers of a major-party alternative while preserving the economic settlement conservatives had built.

Hartmann attributes a $79 trillion transfer from working people to the wealthy since 1981 to this broader policy regime. He also argues that weakened unions sharply reduced workers’ incomes and that the retreat from publicly supported higher education helped produce more than $1.6 trillion in student debt. Those are his causal claims, but the political mechanism he identifies is clear: public policy increased insecurity, and that insecurity disciplined workers and students who might otherwise challenge concentrated power.

A private infrastructure sold public power as the enemy

Reagan’s familiar claim that government was the problem did not mean Republicans intended to stop using government. They used it aggressively—to cut taxes for the wealthy, break a federal union, alter financial incentives and narrow the public sector’s capacity to restrain private power.

The anti-government message required its own well-funded institutions. Hartmann describes conservative billionaires building think tanks and media networks throughout the 1970s and 1980s. Reagan accelerated Rupert Murdoch’s citizenship, ended the Fairness Doctrine, and conservative investors helped place Rush Limbaugh and similar hosts on more than 1,500 radio stations. Hartmann says billionaire-backed organizations including the Heritage Foundation subsidized right-wing broadcasters; Fox News later extended the model.

The product was not small government. It was government made less responsive to workers and more useful to capital, accompanied by a media system that called assistance to ordinary people socialism while treating corporate privilege as economic freedom.

That framing became so dominant that Clinton declared the era of big government over and moved to end welfare “as we know it.” The conservative victory was therefore larger than a sequence of Republican elections. Its assumptions constrained Democratic governance as well.

Trump captured the anger and protected its cause

By 2016, the economic order created by those policies had generated a pool of justified resentment. Trump directed that resentment away from the institutions that had accumulated wealth and toward the people with the least authority to reverse the damage.

He also campaigned against parts of the bipartisan economic consensus. Hartmann notes that Trump promised to restore jobs, reject free-trade policy, raise taxes on the rich, expand access to affordable health care and make college more affordable. Those pledges allowed him to pose as an adversary of the system that produced him.

Hartmann calls the promises lies. The sharper point is that Trump recognized the political market created by decades of wage pressure, deindustrialization and debt. He offered workers the language of economic revolt while leading a party built to protect wealth from redistribution. The old conservative maneuver survived intact: identify real injury, substitute a weaker culprit and leave the commanding institutions undisturbed.

Hartmann’s account becomes more contested when it turns to Russia. Citing a 2021 Guardian report and former Soviet intelligence officer Yuri Shvets, he writes that the KGB cultivated Trump during a 1987 visit to Moscow and celebrated Trump’s subsequent newspaper advertisements criticizing U.S. support for NATO and Japan as an “active measure.” Shvets described Trump as an asset. That is an allegation attributed to Shvets, not a fact established merely by Trump’s later alignment with positions advantageous to Moscow.

The distinction matters because Hartmann’s larger argument does not require a secret master narrative. Trump’s rise can be understood through visible institutions and documented political choices: conservative donors financed an ideological apparatus; Republican administrations weakened labor and shifted taxes; Democratic leaders preserved key parts of that settlement; and Trump exploited the resulting anger.

The conspiracy concealed the governing project

Hartmann closes by reversing Stormer’s accusation. The danger, he argues, was not communists hidden inside the State Department but a wealthy president prepared to attack unions, threaten protesters and align the United States with authoritarian governments.

His language sometimes outruns the case he presents. He calls Trump an “agent” of Russia and describes contemporary developments in sweeping terms that the column does not separately establish. Those assertions should not be smuggled into the historical argument as settled findings.

The stronger indictment is already in the record Hartmann assembles. Conservatives spent decades telling Americans that civil rights, feminism, labor power, public education and economic regulation were stages on the road to tyranny. Under cover of that panic, political leaders redistributed power upward. Trump did not invent the deception. He inherited a party trained to call equality subversion, hierarchy freedom and the beneficiaries of dispossession its victims’ only protectors.

item.title: Whistleblower relishes prospect of Trump watching 'it all come undone'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Miles Taylor, a former Trump-era Department of Homeland Security chief of staff, believes Donald Trump may spend his remaining years watching investigations destroy the public image he prizes. But the more consequential part of Taylor’s argument is not his satisfaction at that prospect. It is his prediction that Republicans may finally restrict presidential power—not because Trump abused it, but because a future Democratic president could inherit it.

Speaking Tuesday on Joyce Vance’s podcast, Taylor described political accountability as uniquely threatening to Trump, whom he portrayed as more invested in the “court of public opinion” than the court of law. Trump feared losing Congress, Taylor argued, because congressional power can turn investigations into a sustained public record of misconduct.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Litigation as narrative warfare

Taylor said he witnessed Trump explain this approach inside the Oval Office. According to Taylor, Trump told aides that suing someone could be useful regardless of the merits: the target might settle, suffer reputational damage and become trapped inside a narrative created by the lawsuit.

“It doesn’t matter if you end up winning in a court,” Taylor recalled Trump saying. “You basically create a public narrative.”

That account describes litigation not primarily as a means of resolving a legitimate grievance, but as leverage—a way for a powerful person to impose costs and manufacture appearances. Taylor said Trump carried the same philosophy into government, applying it to domestic policy, foreign affairs and the law itself.

The distinction matters. A president commands institutions capable of doing far more damage than a private litigant. When government power becomes another instrument for gaining leverage over enemies, the cost is borne not merely by Trump’s chosen targets but by the public institutions bent to serve him.

Taylor contended that a “waterfall of investigations” has now turned Trump’s method against him by damaging the public narrative he worked to control. That is Taylor’s forecast, not a reported conclusion about the investigations’ outcomes. Political exposure can impose costs, but it is not interchangeable with legal findings or institutional restraint.

A revenge fantasy obscures the institutional question

Taylor’s most vivid remarks concerned Trump’s age, health and legacy. He speculated that Trump would spend the rest of his life watching “it all come undone” and said the president might not live long enough to see the bricks removed from his ballroom. Taylor predicted the structure would eventually come down and called it the prospective “eulogy of his political career.”

That is the remark behind the headline’s promise that a whistleblower relishes Trump’s downfall. It is also the least politically useful part of the interview. Speculation about whether an aging president will survive to witness a building’s demolition converts an argument about public power into a fantasy of personal torment. However satisfying Taylor may find that image, mortality is not accountability, and architectural revenge is not reform.

Taylor made a more substantive accusation when he called Trump a “thief” who had stolen from taxpayers and abused the public trust. Those are Taylor’s characterizations. His proposed remedy was congressional action exceeding even the post-Watergate reforms: laws and rules designed to prevent another president from exploiting the same openings.

Republicans may act when the power changes hands

Taylor said the argument that resonates privately with elected Republicans is not that Trump’s alleged abuses are intolerable on their own. It is that a Democratic successor could use the same authority.

He pointed to presidential actions including eliminating federal agencies unilaterally, pursuing enemies and moving billions of dollars between federal accounts illegally. Taylor predicted Republicans would become intensely interested in closing those avenues during the final months of 2028, when the prospect of a Democratic president exercising them could become immediate.

If Taylor is right, that timetable exposes the governing incentive plainly. Republicans would tolerate expansive executive power while Trump wields it, then rediscover constitutional limits when their opponents might inherit it. That is not a principled rejection of abuse. It is an attempt to reserve impunity for one’s own side.

The enduring question is therefore larger than whether Trump suffers reputational humiliation. Congress can investigate, legislate and restrict executive authority. Republicans, in Taylor’s account, may possess both the votes and the institutional incentive to act. What they lack until power threatens to change hands is the will.

A ballroom may eventually disappear. The powers Trump used will remain available unless Congress closes them—and reform adopted only at the moment of partisan transfer would confirm that lawmakers understood the danger all along.

item.title: Family member exposes Trump’s 'egregious' crimes in broad daylight
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Mary Trump, the president’s niece, has accused Donald Trump of using presidential influence to help restore Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive while holding and personally trading Nvidia stock. item.content:encoded:
Mary Trump, the president’s niece, has accused Donald Trump of using presidential influence to help restore Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive while holding and personally trading Nvidia stock. Her allegation is explosive but not established by the facts AlterNet reports: she offered no details about Trump’s trades, purchase prices or timing. What is established is a serious conflict of interest. Trump publicly claimed credit for pressuring Nvidia’s board into a decision that reportedly sent shares up 36 percent—an outcome from which he stood to benefit as a shareholder.

The distinction matters. Mary Trump called the conduct criminal and described it as “so obvious, so egregious, so in your face” that Republicans should no longer ignore it. But an accusation from a relative, however emphatic, does not prove a crime. The documented scandal is already substantial without inflating it: a president with a personal financial stake says he intervened in a corporation’s leadership, then boasts about the result.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Presidential pressure, private exposure

Trump told CNBC that his intervention was crucial to Huang’s reinstatement and that Nvidia’s board would not have acted without him. Asked why the board had reversed course after people close to it reportedly said Huang would not return, Trump said he had spoken with Huang and “convinced” the directors.

That account places the president—not Nvidia employees, ordinary investors or some faceless “market”—at the center of the decision. Nvidia’s share price had fallen amid reports about Huang’s conduct and the company’s workplace culture. It then rose 36 percent following the announcement of his return. Trump owned Nvidia shares and had said he handled his own trading.

Mary Trump argues that her uncle bought at depressed prices after Huang resigned, then used the presidency to engineer Huang’s comeback and profit from the rebound. AlterNet reports that she did not provide the transaction records or other specifics needed to substantiate that sequence. Her claim should therefore remain what it is: an allegation. Trump’s admitted intervention and financial interest, however, do not depend on her theory.

A functioning ethics regime would treat that combination as an urgent question: Did the president use public authority in a way that affected his own portfolio? Trump instead presented his leverage over Nvidia’s board as evidence of effectiveness. The brazenness does not prove Mary Trump’s criminal allegation, but it does reveal an administration in which the boundary between presidential power and private wealth is treated as optional.

National security rhetoric meets corporate access

Huang’s restoration also lands inside a dispute over technology exports and China. According to AlterNet, U.S. officials suspect the chief executive of Megaspeed—someone with whom Huang has a relationship—of spying for China. Huang is expected to face a public Senate hearing and two days of questioning by three House committees over possible export violations and chip smuggling.

Lawmakers from both parties have challenged the administration’s position. Nebraska Republican Rep. Don Bacon said the government cannot proclaim an “AI war” while sending the country’s most advanced chips to China. Oregon Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden said Huang’s reinstatement demonstrated that “our national security is for sale.” Republican Sen. Tom Cotton, who chairs the Senate Intelligence Committee, called the controversy “just the tip of the iceberg.”

Those statements do not establish Huang’s culpability or prove that Trump intervened because of his stock holdings. They do expose the contradiction surrounding the administration’s conduct. If Nvidia’s leadership and export practices raise genuine security concerns, the president’s personal intervention in the company’s governance demands more scrutiny, not less. “National security” cannot credibly serve as the administration’s justification for controlling technology flows while the president uses his office to shape the leadership of a company in which he invests.

Oversight meets a White House warning system

Mary Trump placed the Nvidia episode alongside other potential conflicts involving the president’s circle. She cited Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, whose sons now operate Cantor Fitzgerald, the firm he formerly led. She also pointed to Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin’s inquiry into whether Donald Trump Jr.’s venture-capital firm, 1789 Capital, benefited from advance knowledge of federal contracts. These are separate matters, and the reporting does not establish wrongdoing in either one. Their relevance is institutional: political power, regulatory authority and family financial interests repeatedly occupy the same space.

The White House has also moved to tighten its control over information reaching Congress. On Nov. 20, Trump signed an executive order requiring federal contractors to notify the White House before answering congressional inquiries. Mary Trump characterized the order as unprecedented and intended to silence companies.

Whatever motive ultimately emerges, the mechanism is plain. Contractors approached by lawmakers must first alert the very executive branch Congress may be attempting to investigate. That gives the White House advance notice of oversight and creates an obvious deterrent for companies weighing whether to cooperate freely. It is not merely an administrative procedure; it rearranges the information balance in favor of the institution already holding executive power.

Democrats were preparing to investigate further when they took control of Congress on Jan. 3, AlterNet reported. Huang’s scheduled testimony offered one immediate test. The central question was not whether Mary Trump’s outrage could substitute for evidence—it could not—but whether Congress would obtain the trading records, communications and corporate testimony needed to determine what happened.

Trump has already supplied the starting point himself: he owned the stock, personally traded it and claimed that Nvidia’s board restored Huang because he intervened. The unanswered question is whether lawmakers will treat that admission as evidence requiring investigation, or allow presidential boasting to become another means of placing misconduct beyond consequence.

item.title: Trump’s boardroom power grab exposes the GOP’s big con: historian
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s intervention in Nvidia’s leadership fight exposed the fraud beneath the Republican Party’s free-market branding: corporate independence remained sacred only until the president wanted a particular executive restored. According to AlterNet, Trump assured Nvidia’s board that the government would not punish the company if it reinstated Jensen Huang, who had been removed after allegations of an extramarital affair with a woman believed to have ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia retu
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s intervention in Nvidia’s leadership fight exposed the fraud beneath the Republican Party’s free-market branding: corporate independence remained sacred only until the president wanted a particular executive restored. According to AlterNet, Trump assured Nvidia’s board that the government would not punish the company if it reinstated Jensen Huang, who had been removed after allegations of an extramarital affair with a woman believed to have ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia returned Huang to the top job. Historian Heather Cox Richardson argues that the episode reveals an economy increasingly governed by access to one man, not by neutral rules.

An assurance that carried an implied threat

The reported message to Nvidia’s directors matters because of who delivered it. When a president tells a company that the government “wouldn’t punish” it for making his preferred choice, the promise cannot be separated from the power to punish. Richardson writes that the board appeared to fear federal retaliation. That is not a free market functioning without government interference; it is a private company making a personnel decision under the shadow of presidential authority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump publicly dismissed the national-security concern surrounding Huang’s return. He told CNBC’s Eamon Javers that the Justice Department had “exonerated” Huang. But Maggie Haberman of The New York Times reported that Trump had retreated from his claim by Tuesday evening, saying instead that advisers were examining the intelligence. CNN’s Aaron Blake, meanwhile, reported that Attorney General Todd Blanche had avoided specifying what investigations were actually underway.

Those accounts leave the administration’s factual basis unclear while making its political action plain. Trump intervened before his government offered a stable public explanation of what it had examined, what it had concluded, or what remained under review. The certainty applied to the desired corporate outcome; the ambiguity was reserved for the national-security justification.

Enforcement weakened as Trump intervened

The administration’s conduct elsewhere makes the reassurance to Nvidia more consequential. The Atlantic reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick reassigned agents responsible for combating the smuggling of artificial-intelligence chips to his personal security detail. Officials said the move stripped the department of essential expertise. Nvidia chips barred from sale to China have nevertheless appeared there.

That does not establish Huang’s responsibility for smuggling or prove the allegations surrounding his personal relationship. It does show an administration weakening specialized enforcement capacity while the president pushes to restore Nvidia’s chief executive and waves away concerns he later acknowledges are still being examined.

The imbalance is revealing. Career enforcement work can be displaced to serve a Cabinet secretary’s personal needs, while a politically connected corporate leader receives direct presidential intervention. Institutional capacity becomes expendable; proximity to executive power becomes decisive.

The market is “free” until the ruler wants a favor

Richardson’s central argument is that Republican devotion to free markets, cultivated as party doctrine since Ronald Reagan, served as a “smoke screen” for concentrating wealth. The Nvidia episode gives that critique a concrete form. The administration is not withdrawing government from the economy. It is personalizing government’s role in it.

Richardson compares the emerging arrangement to Russia’s oligarchic system and argues that Trump is also moving toward a state-directed model associated with China, with the administration demanding a share of private economic activity. The evidence reported here supports the narrower and still damning conclusion: Nvidia’s board reportedly sought protection from federal punishment, and Trump offered it in connection with a leadership decision he favored.

This is not deregulation. It is discretionary rule by political indulgence. A company does not rely on a general law applied equally; it seeks an assurance from the official who controls the enforcement machinery. The supposed liberation of business from government ends with business dependent on the president’s goodwill.

As The Atlantic’s Adam Serwer has observed, Republicans tend to discover an objection to government intervention in private enterprise when that intervention benefits people who are not rich. Here, intervention favored the leader of one of the world’s most powerful technology companies. AlterNet reports that Republican lawmakers largely avoided the controversy rather than defend the market principles their party claims to hold.

Investors were left pricing presidential favor

Markets initially rewarded Huang’s restoration. Nvidia shares surged 31 percent on Monday, and Trump reportedly may have gained as much as $15 million from his Nvidia holdings during that rally. The next day, the stock fell 6 percent and helped pull the Nasdaq down 1.5 percent.

Those movements do not by themselves establish why investors bought or sold. But they show the volatility created when corporate governance, federal enforcement and presidential intervention become entangled. Investors are no longer evaluating only a company’s products, leadership and legal exposure. They must also assess whether the president’s blessing will hold, whether his account of an investigation will change, and whether agencies responsible for enforcing export restrictions retain the personnel to do their jobs.

Richardson notes that even oligarchs operating under autocrats shelter wealth in countries where law constrains rulers. Nvidia’s reported experience illustrates why. A presidential promise not to punish can sound reassuring only after the possibility of arbitrary punishment has become credible. Once that is the operating premise, the con is complete: government has not left the boardroom. The president has entered it.

item.title: DC insider lays out GOP nightmare —and 'final repudiation of MAGA'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Steve Schmidt’s promised “final repudiation of MAGA” is not an election result. It is a sweeping forecast: the former Republican strategist told journalist Tara Palmeri on Tuesday that Donald Trump has damaged the Republican Party so deeply that Democrats could dominate Washington after 2028 and Republicans might not regain the presidency before 2040. The prediction is extraordinary, but the institutional failure behind it is already plain. Republican leaders repeatedly chose Trump, empowered him and made his conduct the party’s inheritance.

A forecast, not a settled realignment

Schmidt predicted that the next electoral backlash against Republicans would exceed the one he described as having hit the party in the midterms. He envisioned a Democratic president in 2028, a Senate majority exceeding 60 seats and a House advantage of 100 seats. From there, he said, the United States could function as a predominantly one-party country for longer than eight years, with political competition occurring mainly among Democratic factions.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Those numbers are Schmidt’s projections, not reported outcomes. His argument is that Trump’s political residue will outlast Trump himself: even after the present order has been dismantled, he said, future Republican candidates will still face voters asking, “but what about Trump?”

That is the “GOP nightmare” in concrete terms. Schmidt believes Republicans have attached their identity so completely to one president that changing candidates will not erase the association. A party cannot spend years making Trump its leader, message and test of loyalty, then expect voters to regard the next nominee as an unrelated product.

Schmidt illustrated the complacency he hears among Republican associates with a scene from The World According to Garp. After an airplane crashes into a house under consideration, Robin Williams’ character concludes that the property is now safe because another crash is astronomically unlikely. The analogy is pointed: Republicans are treating one electoral wreck as protection against another when it may instead be evidence of the same unresolved danger.

Democratic weakness is not Republican absolution

Schmidt did not describe Democrats as popular. He said the party’s congressional brand remains “as unpopular as MAGA” and predicted that prospective presidential candidates would try to separate themselves from leaders such as Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer and House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries.

That distinction matters because AlterNet’s account is not evidence of a Democratic revival driven by public confidence in Democratic leadership. Schmidt’s case is that Republicans have made their own liability so large that Democratic unpopularity may not save them.

This is less a compliment to Democrats than an indictment of the political system’s narrow choices. Voters can dislike the Democratic establishment and still reject a Republican Party bound to Trump. Treating every Democratic gain as an endorsement of Schumer, Jeffries or the party’s congressional operation would conceal the mechanism Schmidt is describing: a governing party can manufacture victories for an unpopular opposition by making itself even less acceptable.

It would also misdirect responsibility. Democratic leaders may fail to inspire voters, but they did not force Republican officials to subordinate their party to Trump. Republicans held the agency to nominate him, defend him and make loyalty to him a prerequisite for influence. Schmidt’s forecast assigns the resulting exposure to the institution that created it.

The bill belongs to the enablers

“Everything must be knocked down, and the rule of law restored,” Schmidt said. He argued that Republicans will spend years answering for enabling what he called Trump’s corruption and that rebuilding the party afterward will be slow.

That claim identifies the real power structure more accurately than narratives centered on Trump’s personality alone. A president does not transform a major party without lawmakers, operatives and candidates deciding that compliance is safer or more profitable than resistance. Schmidt’s prediction may prove wrong in its timing, scale or certainty, but the accountability he describes cannot honestly stop with Trump.

Nor does Schmidt see an obvious Republican successor capable of escaping the trap. He said a viable candidate would need to think quickly and articulate a coherent vision, purpose and message—and added that several names currently discussed near the top of the field do not meet that standard.

The Republican problem, then, is not simply finding a more polished nominee. It is asking voters to detach the party from conduct its own leaders enabled while offering candidates produced by the same political machinery. Schmidt has supplied a dramatic timetable for collapse. The more immediate fact is harsher: Republicans made Trump’s record their collective record, and no rebranding exercise can decide when voters will stop remembering it.

item.title: When Enough Became a Dirty Word: How Capitalism Lost Its Way
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
From Henry Ford’s courtroom defeat to the modern obsession with perpetual growth, American capitalism has increasingly confused building prosperity with extracting wealth.

I recently came across a brilliant comedy skit on YouTube.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A group of corporate executives were running around like headless chickens, screaming in panic. Some were desperately reassuring themselves that everything would be okay, despite clearly not believing a word of it.

Standing amid the chaos were two remarkably calm individuals: James Sinegal, co-founder of Costco, and Don Vultaggio, co-founder of AriZona Beverages.

In the skit, Sinegal asks Vultaggio why everyone is panicking. Apparently, their customers are angry because they keep raising prices.

Sinegal is baffled. He recalls threatening an executive who suggested raising the price of Costco’s famous hot dog combo. Vultaggio is equally perplexed. His company is profitable, debt-free, and owns its infrastructure. Why would he need more?

The two eventually decide to go on Reddit and read about how much their customers love them.

It is satire, of course. But the business philosophies it depicts are very real.

And beneath the humor lies a devastating indictment of modern American capitalism.

Two businessmen behaving like businessmen have somehow become the punchline of a comedy sketch because their behavior is now considered extraordinary.

When Capitalism Actually Made Sense

At its most basic level, capitalism promises a relatively straightforward arrangement.

Someone produces a good or service. Someone else finds value in that good or service and willingly exchanges money for it. The producer makes a profit, employees earn a living, customers receive something they want, and the enterprise continues operating.

It is a mutually beneficial transaction.

There is nothing inherently objectionable about making a profit. Profit compensates entrepreneurs for their investments, risks, efforts, and innovations. It provides resources for expansion, research, and resilience against economic downturns.

But there is a fundamental difference between making a profit and treating every dollar that could conceivably be extracted from another human being as money that rightfully belongs to you.

Somewhere along the way, American corporate culture began erasing that distinction.

And one of the most famous legal milestones in that transformation occurred more than a century ago.

The Original Sin: Dodge v. Ford

In 1916, Henry Ford found himself in an unusual position: his company was making an extraordinary amount of money, and he wanted to use that money to expand production, employ more workers, and make automobiles more affordable.

Ford understood something that should be painfully obvious to anyone with even a rudimentary understanding of economics: making your product accessible to more people can be an excellent business strategy.

The Dodge brothers, John and Horace, who collectively owned 10% of Ford Motor Company, had other ideas. They wanted additional dividends.

They sued.

In 1919, the Michigan Supreme Court delivered its ruling in Dodge v. Ford Motor Company, including a sentence that would haunt American corporate philosophy for generations:

“A business corporation is organized and carried on primarily for the profit of the stockholders.”

The court upheld an order requiring Ford to distribute approximately $19.3 million in special dividends, although it allowed his industrial expansion to proceed.

To be legally precise, the ruling did not impose a universal obligation on American corporations to maximize every conceivable dollar of profit. It also recognized considerable managerial discretion over business decisions.

Nor should Henry Ford be romanticized as some benevolent industrial saint. His motivations were complex, his labor practices were often controlling, and the Dodge brothers were also emerging competitors.

Nevertheless, the principle articulated in that ruling became a cornerstone of the shareholder-primacy philosophy.

The corporation’s purpose was increasingly understood not as producing something useful, sustaining employment, or building a lasting institution, but as generating financial returns for its owners.

It would take decades for that philosophy to reach its modern extremes.

Milton Friedman and the Intellectual Justification for Greed

In 1970, economist Milton Friedman published his famous essay, The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits.

Friedman argued that corporate executives were agents of shareholders and that spending corporate resources on independent social objectives could amount to spending other people’s money without their consent.

His argument included qualifications concerning the law, ethical customs, and the rules of fair competition. Those qualifications, however, rarely receive the same attention as the essay’s headline.

What entered the popular corporate consciousness was a considerably simpler proposition:

Make money. Everything else is secondary.

Employees, customers, communities, and the environment increasingly found themselves competing for consideration against the financial interests of shareholders.

But the cultural transformation was far from complete.

Enter the Yuppies.

The Generation That Made Greed Fashionable

The 1980s gave us the Yuppie: the young urban professional whose identity was increasingly defined by income, possessions, status, and professional advancement.

The Porsche. The Rolex. The designer suit. The Manhattan apartment.

The aspiration was no longer merely financial independence. It was financial superiority.

Consider the quintessential ambition associated with that culture: making a million dollars by age 30.

Not necessarily accumulating a million dollars through years of disciplined saving, investing, and productive work. The more extravagant version of the fantasy was earning a million dollars in a single year before reaching 30.

An exceptional financial outcome was being marketed as a reasonable benchmark for personal success.

Oliver Stone’s 1987 film Wall Street was intended, in part, as a critique of this mentality. Gordon Gekko’s infamous “Greed is good” speech was supposed to expose the moral bankruptcy of a culture that had elevated wealth accumulation above almost everything else.

Instead, some viewers decided that Gordon Gekko was a role model.

The warning became a recruitment advertisement.

The Yuppies did not invent greed. What their cultural moment helped accomplish was something arguably more consequential: it transformed greed from a character flaw into a professional qualification.

And their spiritual descendants are everywhere today.

They sell hustle culture, glorify billionaires, promise overnight fortunes, and treat ordinary salaried employment as evidence of insufficient ambition.

Apparently, making a comfortable living is now a form of failure.

Wall Street’s Three-Month Attention Span

Combine that cultural obsession with wealth with the institutional pressures of modern financial markets, and the result is corporate short-termism.

A CEO who invests heavily in infrastructure, employee training, product quality, and customer satisfaction may depress earnings for several quarters.

Another CEO who dismisses thousands of employees, reduces product quality, increases prices, and postpones necessary maintenance may produce an immediate improvement in financial results.

Under poorly designed compensation and governance systems, the second CEO can be rewarded more handsomely than the first.

The long-term consequences are somebody else’s problem.

By the time customers abandon the company, experienced employees have disappeared, infrastructure begins failing, and the brand’s reputation has deteriorated, the executives responsible may have already collected their bonuses and moved on.

Imagine evaluating the health of a forest by how much timber you managed to sell during the last three months.

That is what happens when financial performance becomes detached from the long-term health of the enterprise generating it.

We All Need to Be Amazon

Another particularly destructive development is the assumption that every successful business must eventually become an empire.

A regional supermarket chain that provides excellent service, employs thousands of people, generates healthy profits, and enjoys tremendous customer loyalty should be considered a success.

Instead, it is expected to expand.

Then expand again.

Then acquire competitors.

Then enter unrelated markets.

Then expand some more.

A software company with 50 employees, a reliable product, satisfied customers, and sustainable recurring revenue should likewise be considered a successful enterprise.

Instead, modern entrepreneurial culture increasingly tells its founders that they need venture capital, exponential growth, international expansion, and a billion-dollar valuation.

Not every bookstore needs to become Amazon. Not every restaurant needs to become McDonald’s. Not every software company needs to become Microsoft.

There is nothing inherently wrong with expansion. But expansion should serve the interests of the enterprise, not become its reason for existing.

A business that remains profitable for 50 years without becoming a multinational conglomerate has not failed.

It has achieved something that countless supposedly revolutionary startups never will: sustainability.

I Got Mine. Fuck Everyone Else.

Perhaps the most socially corrosive component of this transformation is the increasingly celebrated philosophy of individual accumulation without collective responsibility.

Employees become expenses.

Customers become revenue streams.

Communities become markets.

Competitors become acquisition targets.

And the company itself becomes a financial instrument from which wealth can be extracted.

The fundamental economic contradiction is almost comical.

Every corporation wants customers with substantial disposable income. Yet many of those same corporations devote enormous resources to suppressing labor costs.

Every corporation wants consumers to spend freely. Yet many continually increase prices, introduce additional fees, and convert previously purchased products into recurring subscriptions.

Every corporation wants customer loyalty. Yet too many behave as though loyalty were a renewable resource that could be harvested indefinitely without replenishment.

Individually, some of these decisions may appear financially rational. Collectively, they can undermine the consumer economy upon which those corporations depend.

Capitalism requires customers.

And customers are not an independently occurring natural resource. They are, overwhelmingly, the employees of other businesses.

The Imaginary Loss of Money You Never Earned

One of the most revealing characteristics of modern corporate thinking is the treatment of foregone potential profit as an actual financial loss.

Suppose a company sells a product for one dollar. After accounting for all its expenses, it earns twenty cents in profit.

It has made money.

Its obligations are covered. Its employees are paid. Its customers are satisfied. Its business is sustainable.

But a consultant determines that customers would probably tolerate paying a dollar and fifty cents.

Suddenly, management begins behaving as though the company is losing fifty cents on every sale.

It is not.

That money never belonged to the company. It was never earned. It was merely a hypothetical opportunity to extract additional revenue from its customers.

There is a legitimate place in business analysis for opportunity costs. But treating every opportunity to increase margins as an obligation creates a system in which no amount of profitability can ever be considered sufficient.

And once that mentality becomes institutionalized, the concept of enough disappears entirely.

Two Men Standing Amid the Chaos

Which brings us back to James Sinegal and Don Vultaggio.

Costco’s famous $1.50 hot dog and soda combination has remained at that price since 1985. Sinegal’s legendary resistance to increasing its price has become part of American business folklore.

AriZona’s signature 99-cent cans have similarly become a symbol of resistance to relentless price increases, even though not every retailer sells them at that price.

Neither company is a charity.

Neither company has abandoned capitalism.

Costco is a publicly traded corporation. AriZona is privately held. Their ownership structures differ, but both demonstrate that profitability and consumer goodwill are not mutually exclusive.

They recognize that maintaining affordable prices can generate customer loyalty, strengthen brand recognition, encourage repeat business, and provide a competitive advantage.

While other corporations spend millions attempting to manufacture an emotional connection with consumers, these companies receive extraordinary amounts of voluntary publicity from people celebrating their business practices.

No advertising agency can manufacture the kind of goodwill that comes from decades of demonstrating that you will not squeeze your customers simply because you can.

That goodwill is not corporate altruism.

It is sound business.

Capitalism Does Not Require Infinite Greed

None of this should be mistaken for nostalgia for some imaginary golden age of capitalism.

American capitalism has always contained exploitation, monopolization, abusive labor practices, and enormous concentrations of wealth. The past was hardly a paradise of mutually beneficial commerce.

But acknowledging those historical failures does not require accepting the proposition that perpetual extraction is the only possible way to organize a market economy.

A business can be profitable without maximizing every possible margin.

An entrepreneur can be wealthy without needing to become wealthier every year.

A corporation can serve its shareholders without treating its employees and customers as adversaries.

A successful company can remain a successful company without aspiring to become an empire.

There is no economic law requiring a businessman who owns his factories, has paid his debts, provides employment, satisfies his customers, and earns a comfortable fortune to demand even more.

That is not an unavoidable feature of capitalism.

It is a choice, reinforced by a particular set of cultural values, financial incentives, and institutional arrangements.

And choices can be changed.

The Radical Concept of Enough

Perhaps the most disturbing thing about that YouTube skit is how little exaggeration it requires.

Two businessmen stand calmly amid a collection of panicking corporate executives because they understand something that should be elementary.

Customers are not enemies.

Employees are not merely liabilities.

Profit is not synonymous with greed.

Growth is not synonymous with success.

And a prosperous business does not become a failure simply because its owners have decided that they already have enough.

More than a century after Dodge v. Ford, half a century after Friedman’s essay, and four decades after Gordon Gekko became an unlikely cultural icon, we have reached a point where ordinary commercial prudence looks like an act of rebellion.

The greatest indictment of modern American capitalism is not that James Sinegal and Don Vultaggio are exceptional businessmen.

It is that their philosophy has become exceptional at all.

Capitalism did not need to become a system of perpetual extraction. We made it one by turning the pursuit of prosperity into an inability to recognize when we had achieved it.

item.content:encoded:
Stephen Miller is the “son” in question—not literally, but as the political heir Jonathan V. Last argues Donald Trump would prefer over Vice President JD Vance or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. After Trump floated Miller as a possible 2028 presidential candidate at a recent press conference, Last wrote in The Bulwark that the chief of staff offers what Trump’s would-be successors do not: no independent constituency, no separate political machine and no plausible center of power outside Trump himself.

The remark does not establish that Miller will run or that Trump has selected him. It does, however, expose the governing logic behind Trump’s apparent lack of interest in anointing the Republican figures already maneuvering for 2028. The succession Trump could most comfortably tolerate is one that does not actually require him to surrender control.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A successor without independence

AlterNet reports that Trump suggested, in a half-joking manner, that Miller would be a stronger 2028 candidate than Vance or Rubio. Last interpreted Miller’s appearance at the same press conference as an effective audition for Trump’s endorsement.

That assessment rests on three conditions Last believes Trump would impose on any successor: Trump must remain the campaign’s central figure, retain control of the Republican Party and trust the nominee completely. Miller, whose political identity has been built around Trump and Trumpism, could satisfy all three.

Unlike Vance and Rubio, Miller has not constructed an obvious presidential brand distinct from the president he serves. Last argued that a Miller campaign would consequently be staffed by Trump’s people and organized much like another Trump campaign. Miller would not inherit the movement so much as provide a legally eligible vehicle for its founder to continue directing it.

That is the political significance of Trump’s suggestion. A normal succession transfers authority. This model preserves the existing hierarchy by elevating a subordinate whose principal qualification is that he has nowhere else to stand.

The family model of party control

Last’s “son Trump always wanted” formulation is deliberately caustic, but it identifies the dynastic structure beneath the speculation. In his telling, Trump’s ideal arrangement would be to hand the nomination to one of his children, ensuring that the family’s interests, the party apparatus and the presidential campaign remained fused.

Last dismissed that prospect with personal assessments of Ivanka, Donald Jr. and Eric Trump, while noting that Barron Trump is too young. Barron, now 20 according to the report, could not meet the Constitution’s presidential age requirement until the 2044 election. AlterNet adds that Tiffany Trump, whom Last did not discuss, would turn 35 by Inauguration Day and therefore could be eligible in 2028.

But constitutional eligibility is not the same as political viability, and Last’s argument does not identify any Trump child preparing a credible campaign. Miller matters in this analysis because he could perform the function of a dynastic heir without belonging to the family: absolute alignment without an independent claim to the inheritance.

Loyalty as the qualification

Last described Vance and Rubio as ambitious “shapeshifters” whose loyalty ultimately belongs to themselves. That is his characterization, not an established fact. Both men have their own careers, constituencies and reasons to seek power, however faithfully they currently serve Trump. In the political order Last describes, that ordinary presidential ambition becomes a liability because it creates the possibility of autonomy.

Miller’s advantage is the opposite. Last called him Trumpism’s “truest true-believer” and portrayed Trump’s confidence in him as total. He concluded that Miller is “worshipful, aligned, smart, and ruthless”—the qualities behind the metaphorical son favored over both biological heirs and conventional successors.

The framing risks turning a consequential concentration of power into palace gossip. The relevant issue is not whether Trump feels paternal affection toward Miller or privately dislikes one of his children. It is that the reported 2028 calculation prizes personal submission over an independent mandate. Vance and Rubio would seek to become president in their own right. Miller’s supposed appeal is that his candidacy could keep Trump functionally at the center.

Trump’s comment may have been only a provocation, and Last’s column remains analysis rather than confirmation of a campaign plan. Yet the choice of Miller as the joke’s answer is revealing. Even in jest, Trump bypassed the vice president and secretary of state to elevate the aide whose lack of political independence could make him the safest custodian of Trump’s control.

item.content:encoded:
Joy Reid questioned an “official story” that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s girlfriend was suspected of spying for China, then advanced a different and even more explosive theory: that unnamed forces were trying to seize control of Nvidia and install Israelis at the top. But in the remarks reported by AlterNet, Reid offered no factual basis for either the alleged espionage narrative or the purported takeover. What she did identify clearly was the political vulnerability underneath the speculation: American growth, retirement savings and financial markets have become dangerously dependent on an artificial-intelligence boom concentrated among a handful of technology companies.

That concentration is the consequential story. Reid’s cover-up theory is not established by the reporting, and her vague reference to “some Israelis” obscures rather than identifies who supposedly holds power, what mechanism they could use or what evidence connects them to Nvidia.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A market shock becomes a conspiracy narrative

Speaking on her YouTube program with her husband and co-host, Jason Reid, Reid linked several developments: an AI-driven market selloff, reported scrutiny of Nvidia’s accounting and claims about Huang’s personal relationship.

“I'm still not 100% sure I believe the official story about Jensen Huang's girlfriend being a spy,” she said. “I don't know if that is true, but I do know that there is an attempt to take over his company and put some Israelis in charge of it, which is weird.”

The distinction inside that statement matters. Reid explicitly acknowledged uncertainty about the suspected-spy claim. She expressed no such caution about the alleged effort to take over Nvidia, yet the AlterNet account does not identify the supposed organizers, describe a proposed transaction or explain what Reid meant by putting Israelis “in charge.” Her assertion therefore does not substantiate a cover-up. It replaces one unverified story with another.

That is political misdirection of its own. Nationality is not an institutional actor. If investors, directors, regulators, creditors or rival companies are attempting to change Nvidia’s leadership or ownership, those are the relevant parties to name. Reducing an alleged power struggle to “some Israelis” supplies an ethnic and national label where evidence about decision-making authority should be.

The concrete risk is concentrated economic power

AlterNet reported that the AI selloff began on Nov. 5, when the Nasdaq recorded its worst day in 19 months. Chipmakers led the decline as investors reconsidered how quickly the United States could continue constructing AI data centers, with losses spreading elsewhere in the market.

Reid argued that the resulting panic exposed how heavily the economy depends on AI investment. She said the Nasdaq was down for the year, described AI as a bubble and asserted that much of American economic growth now consists of data-center construction.

Those claims point toward a legitimate question of political economy: who allowed national growth, market confidence and household retirement wealth to become so exposed to the fortunes of a narrow technology sector? Corporate executives direct investment. Fund managers channel workers’ savings into the market. Federal policymakers shape the tax, trade, energy and regulatory conditions supporting the AI buildout. Those institutions possess actual authority. A suspected spy story does not explain their decisions.

Jason Reid put the household consequence more bluntly, noting that ordinary people’s 401(k)s and investments were tied to the decline. He said the selloff had erased two years of gains in a day and accused political leaders of neglecting domestic economic instability while debating further support for Israel. He did not spare either party: “Whoever's in charge, get rid of them because they do not care.”

The frustration is intelligible, but the scale of the claimed loss should remain attributed to him. A sharp market decline can damage retirement balances without establishing that every gain nationwide was erased, just as a selloff cannot by itself prove that AI is a bubble.

Scrutiny requires names, mechanisms and evidence

Nvidia’s importance gives rumors surrounding Huang unusual power. When one company sits near the center of a capital-intensive boom, allegations about its management can move beyond corporate gossip and unsettle markets holding the savings of millions of people. That makes disciplined reporting and commentary more necessary, not less.

Reid is right to scrutinize an “official story” rather than accept it automatically. Skepticism, however, is a method of testing claims; it is not permission to announce a more politically charged claim without showing how it works. The reported remarks do not establish that the spy allegation was manufactured to conceal economic volatility, that Nvidia faced a coordinated takeover or that Israeli actors were behind one.

What the episode does establish is less exotic and more damning. American households can be forced to absorb the consequences when political and financial institutions yoke broad prosperity to speculative enthusiasm around a few powerful companies. Turning that structural exposure into a story about an unnamed mistress and vaguely identified foreigners leaves the responsible institutions conveniently out of focus.

item.content:encoded:
New reporting places the central responsibility for Nvidia’s disputed chip sales not with the company but with the Trump administration, which reportedly authorized the transactions through the Commerce Department. If that account holds, the scandal is serious for President Donald Trump because the conduct at issue would reflect White House policy—and possibly presidential intervention—not a company evading federal controls.

Fox Business senior correspondent Charles Gasparino said Tuesday that the emerging evidence indicates Nvidia broke no law when it sold chips destined for mainland China because the company had received approval from the Trump administration. That distinction matters legally for Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Politically, it redirects scrutiny toward the officials who possessed the authority to approve the sales.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Commerce approval moves responsibility upward

Nvidia has faced accusations that it sold banned chips to companies in Singapore that subsequently shipped them to China. Gasparino’s reporting presents a materially different account: Nvidia acted with the Commerce Department’s permission.

“A fair reading of the evidence” suggests no laws were broken by Nvidia, Gasparino wrote, because the company received the department’s authorization. He also said he did not believe Huang knowingly violated export restrictions.

That does not settle what happened. Atlantic staff writer Shane Harris cautioned that “the jury is still out on what the evidence shows.” But it does establish the question the administration must answer: If federal officials approved the business, who authorized it, under what policy, and for whose benefit?

AlterNet reports that scrutiny is concentrating on Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, amid allegations that he intentionally permitted the sales to enrich himself and political allies and may have acted with the knowledge of others in the White House. Those claims remain allegations in the supplied reporting. They nevertheless concern the exercise of government power, not merely corporate compliance.

The administration cannot coherently treat a transaction as a national-security betrayal when describing Nvidia’s conduct and as permissible commerce when accounting for its own authorization. If Commerce approved the sales, responsibility follows the approval chain.

Trump intervened before the facts were settled

The controversy is also sharpening around Trump’s personal involvement. According to Harris, the president assured Nvidia’s board that Huang was not implicated in criminal conduct even though the evidence remained unresolved.

A president publicly clearing a corporate executive is not equivalent to a legal finding. It is an intervention by the country’s most powerful official in a matter that could face congressional and potentially criminal scrutiny. The immediate concern is not that Trump’s assurance proves an improper bargain; the reporting does not establish that. It is that he placed presidential authority behind Huang’s exoneration before the factual record had been settled.

Gasparino framed the core policy problem plainly: Why has the White House imposed a less onerous China trade policy in a national-security sector than it has applied to Canada? He also asked what role Huang played in shaping that policy and what motivated him. Those are questions, not findings. They are also the questions that become unavoidable once the administration’s approval replaces corporate evasion as the working account of the transaction.

Paul Krugman and others have called the chip exports “treason.” That language is political characterization, not a reported legal conclusion. The more precise charge raised by the story is that officials may have weakened export controls governing strategically important technology, then allowed public suspicion to settle first on the company operating under their authorization.

Republican anger narrows the White House’s escape route

The administration’s problem is no longer confined to Democratic criticism. AlterNet reports that Republican senators Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, Kevin Cramer of North Dakota and Tom Cotton of Arkansas are calling for inquiries. Cotton said, “Congress has much to investigate.” Some conservatives have gone further, calling for Trump’s impeachment and removal.

Harris described Republican lawmakers as frustrated by the administration’s incoherent chip policy and disturbed by Trump’s personal intervention. He argued that the episode combines national-security, policy and political crises, while giving an incoming Democratic congressional majority grounds to investigate allegations ranging from cronyism and self-dealing to the government’s handling of artificial intelligence.

That breadth is not incidental. Advanced-chip export controls sit at the intersection of industrial policy, military competition and enormous private fortunes. The officials setting the rules therefore wield power over both national-security policy and access to lucrative markets. Any evidence that those rules were relaxed for favored actors—or that officials stood to benefit—would demand scrutiny of the decision-makers, not a ritual prosecution of the company that obtained their permission.

The most consequential fact reported so far is also the simplest: Nvidia may not have bypassed the government at all. It may have gone through it. If Commerce authorized the sales and Trump then intervened to absolve Huang, the White House cannot displace accountability onto Nvidia while withholding an account of its own decisions. Congress now has a concrete chain of authority to examine, beginning with the officials who could say yes.

item.title: Top psychologist: Trump’s 'needy' ego could be used to trick him
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump might be coaxed into supporting universal health coverage if the policy were packaged as a monument to Donald Trump. That is the proposition psychologist John D. Gartner endorsed in an AlterNet interview after Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed offered to call Medicare for All “TrumpCare” if presidential vanity could help get it enacted. Gartner called the tactic logical but made no prediction that it would succeed. The idea is less a clever political hack than an indictment of p
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump might be coaxed into supporting universal health coverage if the policy were packaged as a monument to Donald Trump. That is the proposition psychologist John D. Gartner endorsed in an AlterNet interview after Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed offered to call Medicare for All “TrumpCare” if presidential vanity could help get it enacted. Gartner called the tactic logical but made no prediction that it would succeed.

The idea is less a clever political hack than an indictment of presidential government organized around one man’s appetite for praise. If access to health care can rise or fall on whether Trump receives sufficient credit, then policy is no longer being judged primarily by cost, coverage or public need. The price of admission is personal tribute to the official who already holds the most powerful office in the country.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“TrumpCare” as a bargaining chip

AlterNet interviewer Matthew Rozsa pointed to El-Sayed’s proposal as evidence that Democrats might set aside their own desire for recognition and let Trump claim a signature progressive achievement. Trump shared El-Sayed’s post, which Rozsa treated as an indication that the president might at least be receptive.

A repost is not a commitment, however, and Gartner did not pretend otherwise. “Whether it would work, I don’t know,” he said. His narrower assessment was that praise and affection can influence Trump, a method Gartner said foreign leaders have already recognized and employed.

That distinction matters. The evidence presented establishes an opening for flattery, not Trump’s support for Medicare for All, a legislative agreement or even sustained interest. The headline-friendly notion that Trump can be “tricked” into doing good gets ahead of the reported facts. What Gartner actually described was an uncertain attempt to align a public benefit with Trump’s demand for admiration.

Even so, the proposal identifies a real power imbalance. El-Sayed can offer a name. Trump, as president, can lend an administration’s political machinery to a policy or bury it. Calling that exchange ego management should not obscure who possesses the institutional leverage.

A vulnerability, not a governing strategy

There is an obvious temptation to celebrate any tactic that could deliver health care to millions. If ceremonial credit were the only concession required, declining it on grounds of political pride would be difficult to defend. Rozsa invoked Richard Nixon’s consideration of a broad health-care plan in the early 1970s to argue that partisan competition over credit can obstruct policies politicians otherwise claim to support.

But governing by flattery carries consequences beyond branding. A president who can be steered toward a beneficial policy through adulation can also be steered elsewhere by people offering praise for less benign purposes. Foreign leaders, wealthy donors, corporate executives and ideological courtiers generally have more access and more resources for that contest than patients seeking medical care.

The scheme therefore exposes a structural danger even if it works once: public policy becomes a competition to satisfy the president’s emotional needs. Constituencies unable or unwilling to flatter him enter negotiations at a disadvantage, while those already close to power gain another tool for converting access into outcomes.

Diagnosis cannot substitute for evidence

Gartner framed Trump’s conduct through “malignant narcissism,” a concept he said combines pathological narcissism with paranoia, psychopathy and sadism. He acknowledged that it is not a diagnosis contained in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders. He nevertheless applied it to Trump in sweeping terms, arguing that the president does not care about Americans’ welfare and enjoys the suffering produced under his leadership.

Those are Gartner’s judgments, not facts established merely by his professional credentials. His discussion moved from Trump’s documented public conduct—including grandiose social-media images, repeated claims of superior expertise and his felony conviction—to assertions about Trump’s inner life and capacity for cruelty. The conduct can be examined directly. Claims about hidden motives and private gratification remain interpretations, however emphatically Gartner states them.

The distinction is especially important because Gartner escalated from a discussion of political vanity to a comparison with Adolf Hitler’s final destructive orders. He invoked Hitler’s Nero Decree to suggest that a leader who identifies himself with the world might seek to destroy it when his own power collapses. The interview supplied no reported Trump action equivalent to that order. The analogy expresses Gartner’s warning about a possible psychological trajectory; it does not establish that Trump has adopted such an intention.

Gartner also offered conspicuously charitable readings of other presidents. He argued that Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden, whatever their egos or failures, believed they were acting for the country. That formulation turns contested presidential records into presumed good intentions while denying Trump any such presumption. Bush’s invasion of Iraq, which Rozsa raised as an obvious complication, demonstrates why inferred benevolence is a poor standard for judging state power. Consequences do not become less destructive because a president may have believed in his own righteousness.

The presidency should not require emotional tribute

The strongest case against rule by ego does not depend on diagnosing Trump from afar or comparing him to history’s most notorious dictator. It rests on the political arrangement described in the interview itself: an enormously powerful officeholder may be unusually responsive to praise, and people seeking policy outcomes are considering how to exploit that response.

If flattering Trump could secure universal coverage, lawmakers would have a duty to weigh the opportunity seriously. They would also have a duty to write durable legislation, defend its substance and prevent presidential branding from becoming personal ownership of a public program. Health care would still be financed, administered and delivered through institutions—not bestowed by a benefactor whose name had been placed on the package.

El-Sayed’s gambit may be shrewd. It is not reassuring. A government that must tell its president he is magnificent before it can meet ordinary human needs has not discovered a shortcut around dysfunction. It has disclosed where the dysfunction sits.
