item.title: Lawyer Trump wants jailed warns US is in 'constitutional crisis'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Marc Elias, the Democratic election lawyer Donald Trump has said should be jailed, argues that the United States is already in a constitutional crisis—not approaching one. On The Atlantic’s Autocracy in America podcast, released Tuesday, Elias said the defining problem is an executive branch acting outside constitutional limits while the political system offers no clear remedy capable of stopping it. item.content:encoded:
Marc Elias, the Democratic election lawyer Donald Trump has said should be jailed, argues that the United States is already in a constitutional crisis—not approaching one. On The Atlantic’s Autocracy in America podcast, released Tuesday, Elias said the defining problem is an executive branch acting outside constitutional limits while the political system offers no clear remedy capable of stopping it.

His argument does not rest on Trump’s insults alone. Elias pointed to reported attempts by the administration surrounding the 2026 midterms to enlist federal power against election officials, mail voters, political opponents and members of Congress. The election ultimately remained free and fair, he said, because those efforts failed—not because the administration respected the boundaries of its authority.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An election can survive an attack without disproving it

Elias cited a Justice Department threat of criminal enforcement against election officials to pressure them into counting ballots according to the administration’s preference. He also described an effort to involve the U.S. Postal Service in pursuing mail voters. After Election Day, he said, Trump continued using the Justice Department against political opponents and threatening Democratic senators, while federal officials warned that members of Congress conducting oversight could face criminal investigation.

Those claims describe a power structure, not a partisan shouting match. Election workers count ballots, voters cast them and lawmakers conduct oversight, but the executive branch controls the federal agencies Elias says were used or threatened against them. Treating the resulting conflict as generalized political dysfunction would misidentify who possesses the coercive machinery.

The distinction also matters when judging the midterm result. Elias said administration efforts to restrict mail voting, halt the full California count and block Alaska’s certification did not succeed. He does not expect Trump’s subsequent questioning of the results to prevent certification or the formation of the new Congress.

That outcome may tempt institutions to declare the system healthy because it reached the correct procedural endpoint. Elias’s warning is more exacting: a completed count does not erase attempts to interfere with it. Institutional resistance prevented the alleged abuses from determining the result; it did not make those alleged abuses harmless.

Trump’s demand for punishment is part of the record

Elias founded Democracy Docket and leads the Elias Law Group after years of election litigation against Trump. Trump has responded by calling him names and saying he should be imprisoned.

Elias offered a useful test stripped of Washington’s habitual euphemisms: if a foreign leader demanded the jailing of an opposition party’s lawyer immediately before an election, American observers would recognize it as evidence of authoritarianism. Anne Applebaum, the historian who hosts the podcast, noted that governments in Russia, Belarus and Venezuela have imprisoned opposition lawyers.

The comparison does not establish that the United States has duplicated those regimes. It identifies the political function of the rhetoric. A president calling for an opposing lawyer’s incarceration is not ordinary legal criticism. It places state punishment into partisan combat and signals that representing the opposition can itself be treated as suspect.

Applebaum pressed Elias on whether a Democratic lawyer could make the constitutional-crisis case without appearing merely partisan. Elias replied that opposition parties are often the institutions forced to sound such alarms. He also noted that he has sued Democratic-controlled New York and California over voting rules.

Partisanship may shape who raises the warning, but it does not answer the evidence behind it. The relevant question is whether federal officials used or threatened government power as Elias described—not whether the person documenting that conduct represents Democrats.

Election denial is being promoted, not retired

Elias expects the immediate certification process to hold, but he anticipates a widening movement to add the 2026 midterms to the elections Trump’s allies portray as stolen. By 2027, he predicted, the “big lie” will have expanded to incorporate claims about both 2016 and the 2026 contests, following the pattern established after the 2020 election.

That narrative does not need to overturn the current result to serve a purpose. Repeated fraud claims can make every unfavorable outcome presumptively illegitimate and every effort to control counting rules appear justified in advance. Election denial becomes an operating doctrine: victory proves the voters spoke, while defeat proves the system cheated.

House Republicans’ elevation of Jim Jordan—whom Elias described as an election denier—to their next leadership role shows why the denial campaign cannot be dismissed as a fringe grievance. Congressional leadership confers authority, attention and institutional protection. Promoting a figure associated with rejecting election legitimacy embeds that politics inside the body charged with certifying results and checking executive power.

Elias does not expect the crisis he describes to ease before 2028. For now, he defines his own task narrowly: preventing a failed election one cycle at a time while others try to build a broader consensus against the abuse of federal power. It is a grim division of labor. The immediate objective is no longer simply administering elections well; it is keeping officials with the machinery of the state from converting partisan demands into enforceable commands.

item.title: Blanche refuses to say Huang was probed immediately after Trump says he was
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to say whether the Justice Department investigated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after President Donald Trump told CNBC that officials had conducted a “pretty good investigation” and concluded Huang was “exonerated.” Blanche instead denied understanding repeated questions about the president’s claim, leaving the administration unable—or unwilling—to provide a coherent account of what scrutiny occurred, what conduct was examined, or what “exonerated” was supposed t
item.content:encoded:
Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to say whether the Justice Department investigated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang after President Donald Trump told CNBC that officials had conducted a “pretty good investigation” and concluded Huang was “exonerated.” Blanche instead denied understanding repeated questions about the president’s claim, leaving the administration unable—or unwilling—to provide a coherent account of what scrutiny occurred, what conduct was examined, or what “exonerated” was supposed to mean.

The contradiction matters because Trump invoked the authority of a federal investigation to defend a decision he said he made concerning Huang. When reporters tried to establish whether that investigation existed, the official supposedly positioned to know would not confirm it.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump claimed an investigation cleared Huang

During a Monday morning CNBC call-in, Trump was asked what the attorney general had told him about Huang’s potential criminal liability. Trump answered that “they did a study,” conducted a “pretty good investigation,” and determined that Huang “himself” was exonerated.

Trump did not identify who performed the study or investigation, according to AlterNet’s account. But his wording placed the Justice Department’s investigative machinery behind the conclusion. “Exonerated” was not presented merely as Trump’s personal assessment; it was offered as the result of an official process.

At a later press conference announcing a cyber-scam “crackdown,” a reporter asked Blanche whether the Justice Department had, in fact, investigated Huang. Blanche did not answer directly. He instead said Trump had consulted “a lot of people” before making a decision to “reinstate” Huang, though the supplied reporting does not explain what reinstatement meant.

Blanche then vouched broadly for the president’s account while withholding the facts needed to evaluate it.

“What he was saying was true. What he was saying was exactly right,” Blanche said. He added that if the Justice Department had information that Huang was committing crimes, “that is certainly something I would’ve told the president.”

That formulation answered a different question. Whether Blanche possessed evidence of criminal conduct is not the same as whether the department investigated Huang, interviewed him, reviewed evidence concerning him, or reached any formal conclusion about his liability.

The attorney general retreated into ambiguity

When another reporter again asked whether Huang had been investigated, Blanche claimed not to understand.

“What does that mean, for what? I don’t understand the question,” he said. Blanche added that reports based on “leaks or sources or whatever” did not suggest Huang was under investigation, at least from what he had seen.

The evasion produced an obvious conflict. Trump had described a study and investigation that cleared Huang. Blanche, while insisting Trump was exactly right, said he had not even seen reporting that Huang had been under investigation. Both claims cannot be made intelligible without information Blanche declined to provide.

He then framed further questions as unfair to Huang and to the process. But reporters were not responsible for publicly attaching the language of investigation and exoneration to Huang. Trump did that. Asking the Justice Department whether the president accurately described its work is scrutiny of executive power, not speculation manufactured by the press.

The administration thus used official secrecy asymmetrically: Trump could cite an investigation to legitimize his decision, while Blanche could invoke fairness and confidentiality to avoid confirming whether that investigation happened. The authority of law enforcement remained available for the president’s defense; its underlying facts remained unavailable for examination.

Export-control questions went unanswered

A reporter subsequently asked how officials could rule out Huang’s potential criminal liability while an Export Control Act investigation was reportedly still underway. The reporter also asked whether the FBI had interviewed Huang about Alice Huang, whose identity and role are not explained in AlterNet’s account.

Blanche again rejected the premise rather than clarifying the record.

“When you say it is ongoing, I don’t know what you are talking about,” he said, noting that the Justice Department has “hundreds, if not more,” export investigations underway at any given time. He said he did not know which import-export investigation the reporter meant and could not predict whether a future inquiry might produce a different result.

Blanche then described the department’s ordinary procedure: investigators work with the FBI or other law-enforcement partners, and an indictment follows if they uncover evidence of a crime. That general description still did not establish what happened in Huang’s case—or whether there was a Huang case at all.

No criminal wrongdoing by Huang is established in the supplied reporting, and Blanche’s refusal to answer is not evidence that Huang committed any offense. It is evidence of something narrower and politically consequential: the administration made a public claim of investigative vindication, then withheld confirmation of the investigation on which that claim supposedly rested.

The unanswered question is not whether reporters chose the correct synonym for “exonerated.” It is whether Trump cited a real Justice Department process, misstated what officials told him, or converted informal assurances into the language of legal clearance. Blanche had several opportunities to resolve that discrepancy. He chose instead to certify the president’s story without supplying the fact at its center.

item.title: Political insider reveals why Republicans will back Trump’s impeachment
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republicans will back President Donald Trump’s impeachment only if keeping him becomes more dangerous to their own careers than removing him. That is the argument political analyst Jonathan Rauch made Tuesday on conservative commentator Charlie Sykes’s podcast—not a disclosure of an existing Republican plan, as the headline implies, but a prediction that electoral pressure, congressional findings and escalating concern about Trump’s conduct involving Nvidia could eventually break the party’s loy
item.content:encoded:
Republicans will back President Donald Trump’s impeachment only if keeping him becomes more dangerous to their own careers than removing him. That is the argument political analyst Jonathan Rauch made Tuesday on conservative commentator Charlie Sykes’s podcast—not a disclosure of an existing Republican plan, as the headline implies, but a prediction that electoral pressure, congressional findings and escalating concern about Trump’s conduct involving Nvidia could eventually break the party’s loyalty.

The forecast is not yet a revolt

Rauch argued that Trump could be impeached and removed within the next several years or resign under threat of impeachment, following Richard Nixon’s model. His political case rests on the 2028 election: Republican candidates would have to run with a deeply unpopular president from their own party still defining the ticket.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

“Donald Trump—apart from the people in his base who are hanging on to him, which is about, what, 25 percent of the country at most—is hated,” Rauch said. “People have had enough. They want him out.”

Those remarks describe Rauch’s assessment, not polling presented in AlterNet’s report. More importantly, they identify the incentive that might move Republican lawmakers. Rauch is not predicting an institutional awakening. He is arguing that self-preservation could eventually accomplish what constitutional duty has not.

That distinction matters. Republicans possess congressional power now. If they later turn against Trump because his approval becomes an “untenable headwind,” their reversal would not demonstrate that the relevant conduct suddenly became unacceptable. It would show that tolerating it had finally become electorally expensive.

Nvidia scrutiny creates the possible break point

The immediate pressure concerns Trump’s reported actions involving Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang. AlterNet characterizes the matter as raising conflict-of-interest and national-security concerns, though the supplied report does not detail the underlying conduct. It says Republican lawmakers, including an increasing number of MAGA-aligned senators, have announced plans to investigate the company and the administration.

That is the concrete institutional development. An investigation can establish facts, widen political permission for dissent and give lawmakers a procedural route away from a president they previously protected. It can also become theater: a display of oversight that contains outrage without imposing consequences. Which function it serves will depend on what Congress finds and what Republican members do with those findings.

Rauch’s substantive argument is that Trump’s dereliction of duty could become so apparent that preventing further damage draws overwhelming bipartisan support. His legal point is narrower and important: impeachment does not require prosecutors to identify a statutory crime. If Congress concludes that Trump endangered the country without technically committing one, lawmakers may still decide that the conduct warrants removal.

That principle closes off a familiar escape route. Members of Congress cannot honestly treat the absence of a criminal charge as the absence of constitutional responsibility. Impeachment is a political remedy for abuses of public power, and Congress—not a criminal court—decides whether the threshold has been met.

Conservatives are beginning to name the remedy

Rauch is not alone in placing removal back into the discussion. Pete Laffin, a senior editor at the conservative Washington Examiner, wrote that “impeachment + removal is a real possibility.”

Greg Nunziata, a constitutional lawyer who previously served as counsel to the Senate Judiciary Committee and Senate Republican Policy Committee and advised Marco Rubio when Rubio was a senator, made the institutional stakes explicit. “The only solution the Founders give us for something like this is impeachment and removal,” he wrote. “When we take impeachment off the table, as we effectively have, we leave open a wide field for ruinous executive misconduct.”

Fox Business senior correspondent Charles Gasparino went further, describing the scandal as having “all the earmarks of a modern-day Watergate” and saying Trump’s conduct had made impeachment efforts “a lot easier.”

These statements establish growing conservative discussion, not a congressional coalition ready to remove Trump. No Republican votes, commitments or formal impeachment effort are identified in the supplied report. The claim that lawmakers “will be forced” to act therefore runs ahead of the evidence. Political pressure can create an incentive; it cannot cast the votes.

The emerging argument is nevertheless revealing. Republican officials may eventually decide that Trump is expendable, but the projected timing exposes the governing logic: investigation first, electoral danger next, constitutional courage only if the numbers demand it. If impeachment becomes viable, the decisive question will not be whether Republicans discovered Congress’s power. It will be how much damage they accepted before using it.

item.title: Troubling trend as Trump keeps dismissing major spy threats
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump repeatedly discounted intelligence that challenged his preferred narrative, according to an analysis highlighted by AlterNet, culminating in his administration’s reported failure to disrupt an alleged scheme that diverted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China. The pattern matters because the president—not intelligence analysts—holds the power to act on classified warnings, enforce export controls and decide whether inconvenient assessments shape policy or disappear beneath p
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump repeatedly discounted intelligence that challenged his preferred narrative, according to an analysis highlighted by AlterNet, culminating in his administration’s reported failure to disrupt an alleged scheme that diverted Nvidia artificial-intelligence chips to China. The pattern matters because the president—not intelligence analysts—holds the power to act on classified warnings, enforce export controls and decide whether inconvenient assessments shape policy or disappear beneath personal loyalty.

The immediate controversy centers on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, with whom he was reportedly having an affair. Alice Huang is alleged to be a Chinese spy, and her Singapore company, Megaspeed, reportedly purchased $4.8 billion in Nvidia AI chips that were later diverted to China in violation of U.S. export controls. Those remain allegations under investigation, not established findings of guilt.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

What is less ambiguous in the reporting is Trump’s intervention on Jensen Huang’s behalf. After Huang stepped down, he returned to his position nine days later while the investigation continued. Trump publicly advocated for his reinstatement.

Warnings reached the White House, action did not follow

The administration was reportedly briefed months before the controversy became public. Julia Curlee, a former CIA officer who worked on China and the Middle East and served on Trump’s National Security Council during his first term, said the White House had sufficient warning and repeated opportunities to respond as a chip-diversion network developed through Megaspeed and other offshore data operations in Southeast Asia.

“It’s clear that the White House was warned, had adequate opportunities to take action,” Curlee said, but “it just failed to act.”

That account places responsibility where it belongs. Intelligence agencies can collect information and present assessments; they cannot compel a president to heed them. If the reported briefings occurred as described, this was not principally an intelligence failure. It was a failure by officials with executive authority to use information already delivered to them.

Trump’s support for Huang’s return also exposes the hierarchy of concern. An executive entangled in an active national-security investigation received presidential advocacy. The alleged diversion of tightly controlled technology received, according to Curlee, no timely White House response. The administration’s conduct did not resolve the allegations against Huang, but it did signal whose professional standing commanded Trump’s attention.

Intelligence becomes disposable when it contradicts Trump

The Guardian analysis cited by AlterNet presents the Nvidia episode as part of a broader practice: Trump rejects intelligence when it conflicts with his own beliefs or political claims.

Author Robert Trait pointed to Trump’s handling of several previous assessments. Trump reportedly disregarded warnings about Iran’s capacity to withstand a war and close the Strait of Hormuz. At the 2018 Helsinki summit, he sided with Russian President Vladimir Putin’s denial over the conclusions of U.S. intelligence agencies. He also fired Defense Intelligence Agency chief Lt. Gen. Jeffrey Kruse after Kruse contradicted Trump’s claims about attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities.

Those episodes differ in subject and consequence, but the institutional mechanism is consistent. The president receives analysis meant to constrain fantasy with evidence. When that analysis threatens his preferred account, he dismisses the assessment, attacks the institution or removes the official responsible for contradicting him.

Curlee said other administrations have ignored or politicized intelligence, but argued that Trump’s stands apart for its disregard of analysis prepared to inform presidential decisions. She identified the approach to war with Iran as especially revealing, saying the administration shut out years of warnings about how Iran would respond.

This is not ordinary disagreement between policymakers and analysts. Intelligence assessments do not dictate policy, and presidents are entitled to question them. But scrutiny means testing evidence. The conduct described here is something else: treating information as credible only when it ratifies the president’s position. That turns intelligence from a decision-making resource into a loyalty test.

Discretion has given way to presidential favoritism

Former CIA analyst Fulton Armstrong described another institutional deterioration. In earlier practice, he said, officials handling a sensitive counterintelligence concern might privately warn the American involved and even discuss using the foreign contact to transmit disinformation. The objective was practical: protect intelligence, limit damage and potentially turn an adversary’s operation against itself before a public scandal erupted.

Armstrong argued that Trump’s first term, what he called “do-nothingism with Biden,” and nearly two years of a second Trump administration had changed the intelligence community so deeply that such practical responses were no longer permitted.

That assessment spreads responsibility across administrations, but the Nvidia reporting identifies a more immediate chain of power. Trump’s White House was allegedly warned. His administration reportedly did not act. When Huang left his job, Trump pushed for his return. However the continuing investigation ultimately resolves the underlying allegations, those presidential choices already show how national-security machinery can be subordinated to personal judgment.

The misdirection would be to treat this primarily as a lurid affair or an intelligence-community lapse. The consequential question is not whether analysts noticed a possible breach. According to the reporting, they did. It is what the officials empowered to respond chose to do with the warning—and why the president used his influence to defend an executive’s position while the investigation remained open.

item.title: Evangelicals rattled as Trump picks hate over heaven
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump said he would not forgive political enemies including James Comey and Nancy Pelosi because he hates some of them and “always will”—even when the question explicitly linked forgiveness to entering heaven. The remark, made in a 60 Minutes interview earlier this month, has forced several prominent Christian supporters to confront what years of political accommodation allowed them to avoid: Trump is not merely clumsy with their faith’s language. On one of Christianity’s central commands
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump said he would not forgive political enemies including James Comey and Nancy Pelosi because he hates some of them and “always will”—even when the question explicitly linked forgiveness to entering heaven. The remark, made in a 60 Minutes interview earlier this month, has forced several prominent Christian supporters to confront what years of political accommodation allowed them to avoid: Trump is not merely clumsy with their faith’s language. On one of Christianity’s central commands, he openly rejected it.

The response has rattled parts of Trump’s religious coalition, but there is little evidence yet of a rupture. White evangelical support has survived every previous collision between Trump’s conduct and the beliefs his allies claim to defend. The immediate political question is whether this declaration of permanent hatred will be treated differently—or absorbed as one more acceptable cost of access to presidential power.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump made the contradiction unmistakable

Ross Douthat asked Trump whether he could forgive adversaries such as Comey and Pelosi and thereby get into heaven. Trump answered plainly: “I probably cannot do that now because I do hate some of my enemies, and I always will.”

That answer leaves little room for the familiar rescue operation in which supporters reinterpret Trump’s words as humor, imprecision or media distortion. He was asked about forgiveness and salvation. He chose enduring hatred.

For Christians, forgiveness is not an ornamental virtue reserved for sermons. The Lord’s Prayer ties the believer’s request for forgiveness to the forgiveness extended to others. The Gospel of Luke records Jesus asking forgiveness for the people executing him. Trump’s answer did not reveal confusion about an obscure doctrine. It rejected a basic teaching in direct terms.

Jack Graham, pastor of Prestonwood Baptist Church in Plano, Texas, responded by posting John 14:6, in which Jesus identifies himself as the way to the Father. “Everyone including the President needs to nail this down,” Graham wrote.

Graham is not a distant critic. He has long supported Trump and serves on the advisory board of the president’s Religious Liberty Commission. His warning therefore carries an unavoidable second meaning: a religious leader close enough to advise Trump is now publicly telling him that presidential status supplies no exemption from the faith’s requirements.

Rod Dreher, the Eastern Orthodox writer and author of The Benedict Option, was blunter. “My God. My God. The pettiness and hatred in that man’s heart,” he wrote. Dreher has said he voted for Trump in 2024, largely because of JD Vance.

Franklin Graham, who once credited divine intervention with helping elect Trump the first time, also issued a pointed reminder. “Heaven has borders. Heaven has unique and very strict entrance requirements,” he said, adding that entry requires repentance and faith in Christ.

Religious loyalty has outlasted religious offense

Trump has supplied Christian supporters with years of evidence about his relationship to their professed beliefs. He called Second Corinthians “two Corinthians,” could not identify a favorite Bible verse, said he had never asked God for forgiveness and posted an AI-generated image apparently depicting himself as Jesus.

Those episodes did not seriously dislodge his standing. In an October PBS News/NPR/Marist poll, 66 percent of white evangelicals approved of him. The durability of that support suggests the coalition has not primarily depended on Trump demonstrating Christian knowledge, humility or repentance. It has depended on what his presidency can deliver—and on whether allied religious leaders are willing to separate political utility from personal conduct.

The latest remark is harder to file under mere religious illiteracy. Misnaming a biblical book can be dismissed as ignorance. Declaring permanent hatred after being asked about forgiveness is a statement of disposition. Trump identified enemies, affirmed his hatred and rejected the possibility of relinquishing it.

That matters beyond theology because Trump was speaking about named political opponents. A president’s enemies are not simply people he dislikes in private. They are figures exposed to the attention and authority of the executive branch. The institutional power belongs to Trump, not to pastors posting corrective verses after the fact. When a president publicly defines political adversaries through lasting hatred, the relevant issue is not just whether clergy consider the sentiment sinful. It is what that sentiment may mean when attached to presidential power.

Democrats see an opening, not yet a realignment

Democrats are already looking for electoral movement among Christian voters. In a NORC survey conducted after the midterms, the party gained several percentage points among born-again Christians, Catholics and Protestants. Several pastors and ministers were also elected.

Christopher Hale, a former Democratic operative who now writes a newsletter about Catholicism, argued that Trump “has opened himself up ... by defiling basic Christian teachings.” Even a gain of two or three percentage points among churchgoing Christians, Hale said, would be politically significant.

That is an opportunity, not proof of a lasting shift. One survey showing movement after the midterms does not establish that Trump’s statement caused it, and the reported evangelical approval figure shows how much loyalty remains intact.

The sharper test is for the Christian leaders now objecting. Their criticism acknowledges the theological breach, but criticism alone does not alter the power arrangement. Trump still occupies the presidency. Graham still holds a place on his religious-liberty advisory body. Franklin Graham’s institutions still possess the influence that made his warning newsworthy. Dreher’s revulsion follows his vote.

Trump’s answer was not disguised. He said hatred would endure, even at the cost posed in the interviewer’s question. The remaining ambiguity lies with the supporters who heard him: whether their objections mark a limit on political allegiance, or merely the latest pastoral reprimand issued after allegiance has already been secured.

item.title: MAGA Americans who fled to Texas from California are on the run again
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republicans who moved from California to Texas in search of permanent conservative rule are reconsidering their destination after Democrats reportedly captured the Texas governorship, a U.S. Senate seat, other statewide offices and the state House. They are not literally “on the run.” Some are considering another move, while the relocation industry that sold Texas as a political refuge is rapidly rewriting its pitch. The episode, reported by The Wall Street Journal and recounted by AlterNet, is
item.content:encoded:
Republicans who moved from California to Texas in search of permanent conservative rule are reconsidering their destination after Democrats reportedly captured the Texas governorship, a U.S. Senate seat, other statewide offices and the state House. They are not literally “on the run.” Some are considering another move, while the relocation industry that sold Texas as a political refuge is rapidly rewriting its pitch.

The episode, reported by The Wall Street Journal and recounted by AlterNet, is less a migration crisis than a crisis of expectations. These voters treated Republican control not as a contingent result of elections but as an amenity they had purchased with their new homes. When Texas voters disrupted that arrangement, the customers began shopping again.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Political defeat becomes a real-estate problem

Cara Jensen, a 63-year-old auto-damage appraiser, left California for North Texas because she considered the region “patriotic, pro-family” and compatible with her conservative Christian beliefs. She described California’s governor as a “piece of crap” and told the Journal she was “terrified that Texas is going to turn into California.”

Karen Gebhart reacted to the election results with the same sense of displacement. “My heart sank to my feet, and I said, ‘Where am I going to go next?’” she told the newspaper. Gebhart is now considering Arkansas, where she admires Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders. “I’ll live in a tent on her front yard, I don’t care,” she said.

That language reveals the political premise behind these moves. California was not merely a place with policies Jensen and Gebhart opposed; it was territory to escape. Texas was attractive because Republican power appeared secure. Once Democrats won, the state’s other qualities abruptly became less decisive.

But losing an election does not make conservatives refugees, and living under officials chosen by other voters is not persecution. The framing elevates ordinary democratic defeat into personal exile while erasing the agency of the Texans who produced the result.

The industry changes its sales pitch

Businesses have turned partisan sorting into a relocation product. The Journal reported that firms have long helped conservative families leave California, New York and Illinois for reliably Republican states. Democratic gains in Texas, Arizona, North Carolina and Georgia have unsettled that business model, while real-estate agents and elected officials in Louisiana, Idaho, Tennessee and other Republican strongholds are already courting potential movers.

One Oklahoma advertisement made the transaction explicit: “Ready to get the heck out of Texas? Oklahoma’s up I-35.”

Conservative Move, a Dallas-area referral service that promises to help clients find “the right red state,” felt the change immediately. Co-founder Paul Chabot said the company’s Texas leads “largely evaporated” after the election. Its website then recast Texas from a safe destination into “a battleground,” arguing that conservatives who relocate there can help keep it competitive.

The product had not changed; the marketing had. When Texas looked politically secure, the company sold sanctuary. After Democrats won, it sold enlistment.

During a webinar featuring agents from five states, Chabot called the election “a little crazy,” characterized the outcome as a fluke and described incoming conservatives as reinforcements: “We’re the cavalry coming.” Yet he also acknowledged that post-election interest had shifted overwhelmingly toward Florida. The rhetoric urged customers to hold Texas while the leads went elsewhere.

Gerrymandering offers another kind of security

A live poll during the webinar showed Tennessee drawing 43 percent of attendee interest. South Dakota, Nevada and “another state” each received 10 percent. Texas received none.

AlterNet attributed Tennessee’s continued Republican strength in part to gerrymandering. That distinction matters. A state can remain “red” because its electorate consistently supports Republicans, because political migration reinforces that advantage, or because officials have designed districts to dilute opposing votes. To a relocation industry selling predictable partisan control, the mechanism may matter less than the durability of the result.

That is the sharper political meaning of the search for the next “safe” state. These movers are not simply seeking neighbors who share their beliefs. They are seeking jurisdictions where electoral uncertainty has been minimized—whether by demographics, migration or maps drawn by incumbent power.

Some former Californians are reportedly considering returning west, reasoning that if Democratic government is unavoidable, California’s weather becomes attractive again. Others are looking to Florida as “the new Texas.” The promised refuge keeps moving because no state is exempt from politics, demographic change or voters who decline to guarantee one faction permanent control.

item.title: Trump’s 'turmoil'-rocked FBI loses another top official: insiders
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The FBI is poised to lose the career official running its daily operations, extending a leadership crisis created under President Donald Trump by installing loyalists, sidelining experienced personnel and leaving critical posts unfilled. Deputy Director Christopher Raia plans to retire in December after less than a year in the job, three people familiar with the unannounced personnel decision told The Washington Post , according to AlterNet. Raia’s expected departure matters because he was not m
item.content:encoded:
The FBI is poised to lose the career official running its daily operations, extending a leadership crisis created under President Donald Trump by installing loyalists, sidelining experienced personnel and leaving critical posts unfilled. Deputy Director Christopher Raia plans to retire in December after less than a year in the job, three people familiar with the unannounced personnel decision told The Washington Post, according to AlterNet.

Raia’s expected departure matters because he was not merely another executive passing through. Colleagues reportedly regarded him as a stabilizing presence in an agency whose leadership has been reorganized around Trump’s political orbit. FBI Director Kash Patel has not publicly addressed the planned retirement or identified a successor.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The professional in a leadership team of loyalists

Raia is a career FBI official who previously led the bureau’s New York field office and oversaw counterterrorism cases. He became deputy director in January, replacing Dan Bongino, a right-wing podcaster and former Secret Service agent who had never worked for the FBI before joining its leadership.

Although Raia sometimes echoed Patel’s rhetoric, people familiar with his tenure told the Post that he brought a calmer and more professional presence to the bureau’s upper ranks. That description is revealing less as personal praise than as an indictment of the structure around him: basic institutional experience had become the exception at an agency whose leaders possess immense investigative and surveillance authority.

The Trump administration also departed from the FBI’s usual leadership model by appointing former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey as a co-deputy director alongside Bongino. Bailey had no FBI experience and had endorsed Trump’s debunked claim that the 2020 election was stolen. He resigned in September and has not been replaced.

Bongino and Bailey were anomalies in a position traditionally held by career FBI veterans respected inside the bureau. Their elevation nevertheless reflected a clear choice by the administration: political alignment could substitute for knowledge of the institution being managed.

Turnover as a governing method

The bureau’s instability did not arise spontaneously. Under Patel, Bongino and Bailey, scores of experienced officials were pushed out, the Post previously reported. Those departures included personnel who had worked on investigations connected to Trump or who opposed some of Patel’s initiatives. Some removals continued while Raia served as deputy director.

That record gives the word “turmoil” a cause. It is not weather afflicting the FBI from outside. Trump selected the leadership, Patel presided over the bureau, and officials with politically inconvenient histories or professional disagreements lost their positions. Whatever the individual rationale for each personnel action, the cumulative result has been a thinner layer of institutional experience and a workforce repeatedly shown that proximity to investigations involving the president can carry professional consequences.

Raia’s retirement would now remove the senior official responsible for day-to-day operations while Bailey’s former post remains empty. The immediate consequence is another vacancy at the top of an agency already subjected to sustained turnover. The political consequence is equally plain: as career officials disappear, Patel gains more room to shape the bureau without the internal restraint supplied by experienced leaders who understand both its powers and its obligations.

The vacancy Patel has not explained

The reporting does not establish why Raia plans to retire, and his departure should not be presented as proof of a specific dispute with Patel or Trump. What it does establish is the institutional setting in which he is leaving: a career official expected to depart after under a year, two inexperienced political appointees already gone, scores of seasoned personnel pushed out and no publicly named replacement.

Patel’s silence leaves FBI employees without an answer about who will run the bureau’s daily work after December. That uncertainty is not chiefly the responsibility of departing officials. It belongs to the administration that destabilized the leadership ranks and to the director who has yet to explain how he intends to fill them.

item.title: Trump’s dirty secret exposed by Nobel economist
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Paul Krugman says the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is not principally about alleged affairs. It is about whether Nvidia profited from restricted chip technology reaching China through intermediaries while senior Trump administration officials knew of the risk and declined to intervene. That is the “dirty secret” teased by AlterNet’s headline: Krugman alleges not mere negligence, but tacit government approval—and, more explosively, corruption. The reporting presented here establish
item.content:encoded:
Paul Krugman says the scandal surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is not principally about alleged affairs. It is about whether Nvidia profited from restricted chip technology reaching China through intermediaries while senior Trump administration officials knew of the risk and declined to intervene. That is the “dirty secret” teased by AlterNet’s headline: Krugman alleges not mere negligence, but tacit government approval—and, more explosively, corruption. The reporting presented here establishes that officials were warned and that Nvidia disputes the underlying allegations; it does not independently establish Krugman’s claims that President Donald Trump had a financial stake or that his administration received a “cut.”

The board restores Huang as the security questions remain

Nvidia’s board voted Monday to reinstate Huang, less than two weeks after he resigned amid reports of extramarital affairs. One alleged relationship involved Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom U.S. officials reportedly suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The personal scandal offers an easy, lurid frame. It also narrows the field of responsibility to one executive’s private conduct. Krugman argues that this framing obscures the institutionally consequential question: whether Nvidia made restricted chips available to China indirectly, whether the company understood where the technology was going, and why federal officials allegedly failed to stop it.

“The real story about Nvidia is that treason was an important part of its business model,” Krugman said. That is Krugman’s accusation, not an established legal finding. His underlying contention is that sales routed through third parties helped Nvidia’s bottom line while delivering proscribed technology to a U.S. adversary. “This is not something where they innocently thought that Singapore was really buying all of these chips,” he said.

Nvidia says allegations concerning Megaspeed were investigated and debunked. The New York Times also reported that U.S. officials initially did not believe Jensen Huang knew about Alice Huang’s alleged intelligence work. Those distinctions matter: a suspected intelligence connection is not proof of espionage, and a disputed export scheme is not itself a treason conviction. But neither point resolves the separate question of what administration officials knew and what they chose to do.

Washington reportedly received a classified warning

According to the Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the production of a classified memorandum alerting senior U.S. officials to Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang. Axios reported that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick received the memo. Krugman further said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent tried to halt sales to Megaspeed, but Lutnick declined to act.

If that account is accurate, the administration was not simply blindsided by conduct discovered after the fact. Officials had received a warning, and at least one cabinet secretary reportedly sought action. The relevant decision was then Lutnick’s alleged refusal to intervene. That is where the story moves beyond Huang’s relationships and into the exercise of state power: export restrictions mean little when the officials empowered to enforce them can disregard an identified risk.

Trump has defended Huang as a “fine person.” That endorsement answers none of the policy questions. Huang’s character is not the operative standard for controlling sensitive technology, and presidential approval is not a substitute for enforcement.

Krugman’s corruption charge outruns the evidence presented

Krugman alleges the administration tolerated the sales because its officials were “basically in on it” and benefiting “one way or another.” He also accused Lutnick of indirectly profiting from Nvidia’s conduct, described a donation to Trump’s library as a bribe intended to prevent consequences, and said Trump “clearly had some kind of stake.”

Those are grave claims. The supplied reporting does not provide the facts necessary to establish a payoff, a quid pro quo, or Trump’s alleged stake. A donation can create an obvious conflict concern without proving bribery. An official’s inaction after receiving a warning can warrant investigation without, by itself, proving that the official was paid to remain passive.

Krugman’s strongest evidence-grounded argument is therefore narrower than his most incendiary language: senior officials reportedly knew of the concern, one sought to restrict sales, and another declined to act. That alleged sequence is serious on its own. Inflating it into a proven bribery scheme without the supporting evidence risks giving the administration an escape hatch—allowing officials to rebut the least substantiated accusation while avoiding scrutiny of the documented warning and the reported refusal to intervene.

Democrats inherit a test of oversight, not messaging

Krugman believes Nvidia’s board expects future Democratic congressional majorities to behave as “paper tigers.” He rejects advice that Democrats focus exclusively on “kitchen table issues,” arguing that they must investigate unethical, illegal and what he calls treasonous conduct.

That choice is often falsely presented as governing versus investigating. Congress has oversight authority precisely because private wealth and executive power can converge beyond public view. Examining who received the classified memo, what restrictions applied, why Bessent reportedly sought to stop the sales, and why Lutnick allegedly declined would not be a distraction from material politics. It would address who gets to profit, who absorbs national-security risks, and whether politically connected corporations face rules that exist only on paper.

The sex scandal centers Huang and invites spectacle. The consequential record centers officials who possessed enforcement power. Nvidia’s board has already restored its chief executive. The unresolved question is whether Congress will examine the government decisions that made reinstatement appear like a manageable corporate gamble.

item.title: Trump sinking into scandal more destructive than Epstein: political guru
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump publicly claimed credit for pressuring Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang despite concerns involving an alleged affair with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence and the diversion of restricted AI chips to China. David Rothkopf, a former Clinton administration official and Daily Beast analyst, argues that the episode could become more damaging to Trump than the Jeffrey Epstein scandal—not because that prediction is established fact, but because the a
item.content:encoded:
AlterNet reports that President Donald Trump publicly claimed credit for pressuring Nvidia to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang despite concerns involving an alleged affair with a woman tied to Chinese intelligence and the diversion of restricted AI chips to China. David Rothkopf, a former Clinton administration official and Daily Beast analyst, argues that the episode could become more damaging to Trump than the Jeffrey Epstein scandal—not because that prediction is established fact, but because the allegations combine presidential intervention, private financial interests and national-security policy in one combustible story.

The scandal Rothkopf describes is not simply that Trump defended a powerful executive. It is that the president reportedly intervened after being briefed months earlier about the underlying concerns, while members of his administration faced their own allegations of helping Nvidia circumvent export controls. If that account holds, the central issue is the use of state power to protect politically connected economic interests despite warnings from within the government.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A president claiming personal control

Trump did not distance himself from Huang’s return. According to AlterNet, he “loudly and proudly” promoted his role in pushing Nvidia to restore Huang as chief executive after the alleged relationship and chip-transfer concerns had surfaced.

That boast matters. It places Trump’s agency at the center of the decision rather than allowing the administration to present the outcome as a routine corporate matter. Nvidia may be a private company, but export controls on advanced chips are an instrument of federal national-security policy. A president who pressures the company’s leadership while dismissing intelligence concerns is not merely expressing an opinion about corporate governance. He is putting presidential authority behind one side of a dispute with direct consequences for US policy toward China.

Rothkopf called the decision “insane” during Tuesday’s episode of The Daily Beast Podcast. His broader prediction—that the affair will eclipse Epstein as the defining scandal of Trump’s administration—is necessarily speculative. But his stated reason is concrete: he sees an administration subordinating national security to the economic interests of people close to power.

“They have gone too far in taking their own private economic interests and selling American national security down the river in order just to make an extra buck or to cover up the fact that they have been reckless in the past,” Rothkopf told host Joanna Coles.

The conflict surrounding Howard Lutnick

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick is a crucial figure in the account because his department sits near the machinery of export enforcement. AlterNet reports that Lutnick has been accused—including by some people inside the administration—of helping Nvidia evade controls intended to restrict chip sales to China.

The financial entanglement makes those accusations more consequential. Cantor Fitzgerald, Lutnick’s former firm and now run by his sons, reportedly holds a major stake in Nvidia. That does not by itself prove that Lutnick altered policy for financial gain. It does establish the kind of conflict that demands scrutiny: a Cabinet official implicated in decisions affecting a company in which his family’s firm has a substantial interest.

The administration’s power is institutional, not rhetorical. Trump can direct executive policy and exert political pressure; Lutnick occupies an office responsible for commerce policy; Nvidia stands to profit from access to the Chinese market. The weaker actors in this story are not the president, the Cabinet secretary or the semiconductor giant. They are the government personnel whose warnings, according to Rothkopf, were ignored and whose ability to enforce restrictions depends on political superiors willing to let them do it.

Warnings from inside the government

Rothkopf suggested that disclosures about the woman’s alleged contacts with Chinese intelligence originated with US officials who considered the situation a security problem. He cited reporting by The New York Times that, he said, showed she had been in regular contact with Chinese intelligence for months.

“Where do you think all the stories about Jensen Wang’s girlfriend’s ties to Chinese intelligence came from?” Rothkopf asked, using a different surname while discussing Huang. “They came from people in the United States government who felt that it was a problem.”

He then alleged that Trump and Lutnick knew about those contacts. AlterNet separately reports that Trump had been briefed months earlier but chose not to act. Those remain attributed claims in the supplied reporting, not adjudicated findings. Their political significance lies in the sequence Rothkopf describes: officials raised concerns, senior figures knew of them, and Trump later celebrated his intervention on Huang’s behalf.

That sequence undercuts any attempt to cast the controversy as bureaucratic confusion. Rothkopf’s account describes a warning system functioning well enough to alert the people in charge—and political leaders then making a decision that ran against those warnings.

Impunity as policy

Rothkopf called the episode an example of “‘broligarchic’ impunity,” a useful description of the power arrangement at issue. The allegation is not merely that wealthy technology executives enjoy access. It is that access can become protection: corporate interests receive presidential advocacy, officials responsible for regulation face financial-conflict allegations, and national-security objections become obstacles to be overridden.

His forecast that further disclosures will emerge may or may not prove correct. But Trump’s reported conduct has already sharpened the stakes. By claiming personal credit, the president attached himself to the decision and made it harder to blame anonymous aides, corporate lawyers or an unwieldy export bureaucracy.

The unresolved question is therefore not whether Rothkopf has correctly ranked this scandal against Epstein. Scandals are not measured by a pundit’s prediction. The consequential question is whether Trump and Lutnick used federal power to favor Nvidia after receiving warnings about Chinese intelligence contacts and restricted technology transfers. AlterNet’s account places that question squarely inside the administration—and Trump’s own boast leaves him little room to pretend the decision belonged to somebody else.

item.title: Congress has a weapon against Trump he may have forgotten about
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Congress can enforce its own subpoenas through inherent contempt, an authority that allows either chamber to detain and punish a defiant witness without relying on the Justice Department to prosecute. According to AlterNet, some House Democrats were considering reviving that long-dormant power as they prepared to investigate the Trump administration—an administration already signaling that it would treat congressional oversight as criminal aggression and use executive power to shield itself. The
item.content:encoded:
Congress can enforce its own subpoenas through inherent contempt, an authority that allows either chamber to detain and punish a defiant witness without relying on the Justice Department to prosecute. According to AlterNet, some House Democrats were considering reviving that long-dormant power as they prepared to investigate the Trump administration—an administration already signaling that it would treat congressional oversight as criminal aggression and use executive power to shield itself.

The immediate conflict was unusually explicit. After Democrats announced plans for investigations, President Donald Trump called them “EXTORTIONISTS” who should be imprisoned and directed Attorney General Todd Blanche, the Justice Department and the FBI to investigate Democrats, AlterNet reported. Two days later, White House counsel Will Scharf warned incoming House Oversight chair Robert Garcia that aggressive subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Those statements were not legal arguments delivered at a safe institutional distance. They were threats from the executive branch against legislators preparing to scrutinize it. Garcia said he would not be intimidated and planned to subpoena Blanche on his first day as chair. The confrontation therefore concerned more than what any investigation might uncover: It concerned whether a president can neutralize Congress’s investigative power by controlling the officials responsible for enforcing it.

The enforcement trap is the point

Congress ordinarily responds to a rejected subpoena by referring the witness to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution. That procedure works only if prosecutors are willing to act against the administration that employs them.

The contrast in recent cases is stark. Under President Joe Biden, the Justice Department prosecuted former Trump advisers Peter Navarro and Steve Bannon for contempt of Congress; both were convicted and imprisoned. But when House Democrats subpoenaed White House counsel Don McGahn in April 2019, Trump ordered him not to comply and Attorney General Bill Barr’s department declined to intervene. Democrats went to court, and McGahn did not testify until June 2021, after Trump had left office. Even then, AlterNet reported, questioning was limited to material already public.

Delay was not incidental to that strategy. An investigation that produces testimony after the relevant administration is gone has been deprived of much of its power to expose conduct, shape legislation or stop ongoing abuse.

Blanche has reportedly said his department will defend Trump officials whom Democrats seek to question. Whatever legal claims those officials might raise in individual cases, the institutional arrangement is plain: Congress would be asking a Trump-controlled Justice Department to punish Trump officials for obstructing scrutiny of Trump. That is not independent enforcement. It is a veto placed in the hands of the target.

Congress once guarded its own authority

Inherent contempt offers a route around that veto. The power is not a speculative loophole or a recent partisan invention. Congress has used it repeatedly, and the Supreme Court has upheld it.

In 1795, the House detained two men accused of trying to bribe members in connection with a land scheme. In 1821, the Supreme Court recognized Congress’s authority to arrest and hold people who obstructed its proceedings, reasoning that a legislature unable to defend its work would be vulnerable to disruption and conspiracy.

The power has also served ugly causes. In 1860, a Senate committee led by Virginia slaveholder James Mason jailed abolitionist Thaddeus Hyatt for three months after he refused to testify about John Brown. That episode does not negate the authority; it demonstrates that congressional power, like prosecutorial power, acquires its legitimacy from its use and purpose, not merely its pedigree.

Congress later deployed inherent contempt while investigating executive-branch scandal. During the Teapot Dome inquiry, the Senate sent its deputy sergeant at arms to Cincinnati to arrest banker Mally Daugherty, the attorney general’s brother, after he ignored a subpoena. The Supreme Court upheld Congress’s authority again in 1927.

The last reported use came in 1934. William MacCracken, a lawyer for the airlines and a former federal aviation regulator, destroyed records sought by a Senate investigation into the secret allocation of airmail contracts. Senate staff recovered and reconstructed documents from the trash. The Senate arrested MacCracken, tried him and imposed a 10-day jail sentence, which a unanimous Supreme Court upheld.

These precedents do not dictate how a modern detention would operate, nor do they erase potential disputes over executive privilege. They do establish that Congress need not always beg executive officials to enforce legislative authority against the executive itself.

Republicans already endorsed the weapon

Republicans would have difficulty presenting inherent contempt as unthinkably radical. In July 2024, 204 House Republicans voted for a measure that would have held Attorney General Merrick Garland in inherent contempt and fined him $10,000 a day for withholding a recording involving Biden. The measure failed by six votes. Trump endorsed the effort, writing that Garland “should be held in INHERENT CONTEMPT.”

That record matters because the dispute is not really over whether the power exists. It is over whether members of Congress consider it legitimate only when aimed at a rival administration.

Garland also issued a Justice Department opinion arguing that inherent contempt could not be used against executive officials protected by a presidential privilege claim. Trump officials could invoke that position. But executive privilege is not a blanket immunity for every official, donor, business partner or private intermediary connected to a president. Nor can the Justice Department’s opinion settle the scope of Congress’s constitutional authority merely because executive officials would prefer that result.

That distinction explains AlterNet’s argument that investigators could begin with private citizens involved in administration dealings. Such witnesses would have a weaker basis for claiming executive privilege, and compelling their testimony would test whether Congress is prepared to enforce subpoenas before plunging into the hardest constitutional confrontation.

A power unused becomes permission

Representatives Ted Lieu and Jamie Raskin had already explored a formal process for inherent contempt. Lieu said he had discussed the issue with Democratic leadership, and the two lawmakers worked on a 2020 proposal to incorporate an enforcement system into House rules, though it was never adopted.

Congress also possesses less dramatic leverage through appropriations and confirmation votes. But those tools operate through bargaining and can produce wider damage, including funding standoffs. Inherent contempt addresses the obstruction itself: a named witness receives a lawful demand and faces a consequence for refusing it.

The harder question is not whether Congress has weapons. It is whether lawmakers will accept the political responsibility that comes with using them. Arresting or fining a witness would provoke a fierce institutional fight and require clear procedures, disciplined targeting and defensible claims. Yet declining to enforce subpoenas carries its own consequence. It tells an administration that threats from the White House, protection from the attorney general and delay in the courts are enough to make congressional oversight optional.

Trump and his allies have already framed investigation as criminal persecution while reserving prosecution and contempt powers for their own opponents. If Congress answers that intimidation with subpoenas it has no intention of enforcing, the administration will not have defeated legislative oversight through a novel constitutional theory. Congress will have surrendered it.

item.title: The right-wing hypocrisy over Trump’s Nvidia CEO bailout
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump personally pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate CEO Huang 11 days after directors fired him, then publicly claimed credit: “I convinced them and got it done.” According to former Labor Secretary Robert Reich’s account in AlterNet, the intervention came despite unresolved national-security concerns involving Huang and Nvidia—and amid financial ties connecting Trump to both the executive and the company. That is not a free market. It is presidential power deployed on behalf of a favo
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump personally pressured Nvidia’s board to reinstate CEO Huang 11 days after directors fired him, then publicly claimed credit: “I convinced them and got it done.” According to former Labor Secretary Robert Reich’s account in AlterNet, the intervention came despite unresolved national-security concerns involving Huang and Nvidia—and amid financial ties connecting Trump to both the executive and the company.

That is not a free market. It is presidential power deployed on behalf of a favored corporation and its chief executive, with public authority, private wealth and national-security policy tangled together. The remarkable part is not merely that Trump interfered. It is that conservative institutions that denounced government intervention in Elon Musk’s satellite businesses have largely declined to apply their stated principles when Trump is doing the intervening.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A firing reversed from the White House

Trump did not disguise his role as indirect persuasion or routine economic policy. He told CNBC that he personally contacted Nvidia’s board and secured Huang’s return.

A president pushing corporate directors to reverse a personnel decision is an unusually direct exercise of political pressure over a private company. Reich writes that Nvidia’s board was also assured it would be protected from legal liability, making the episode more than presidential commentary on a corporate dispute. The administration reportedly offered institutional protection while Trump pressed for the outcome he wanted.

The board had fired Huang only 11 days earlier. Reich’s account says American intelligence believes Huang had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy who was funneling Nvidia’s advanced artificial-intelligence chips to China’s military. Robert Lighthizer, Trump’s first-term trade representative, compared the alleged technology transfer to Soviet acquisition of American atomic secrets during the Cold War.

Those are allegations and intelligence assessments, not convictions. But they describe precisely the kind of concern that would ordinarily provoke demands for investigation from politicians who treat technological competition with China as a defining national-security struggle. Reich reports that some congressional Republicans have challenged Trump’s unsupported assurances that the concerns surrounding Huang and Nvidia were resolved. Their limited resistance, however, has not matched the conservative outrage directed at proposals to constrain politically disfavored billionaires.

The free-market principle has a partisan exemption

Reich previously proposed nationalizing Musk’s Starlink and StarShield operations because their dominance had allowed one billionaire’s decisions to affect Ukraine and, by extension, American foreign policy. Fox News accused him of threatening the free market. The Washington Examiner called the proposal “categorically un-American,” while Reason argued that technological innovation fails when government interferes. Musk said Reich should be jailed.

Whatever one thinks of nationalization, that proposal at least presented a recognizable public-policy argument: strategic infrastructure with military consequences should not depend upon the discretion of a single private owner. Trump’s intervention at Nvidia was not a general rule for safeguarding critical technology. It was pressure applied to one company to restore one executive.

The conservative response exposes what the rhetoric was protecting. Government interference is condemned when it threatens private control or billionaire profits. It becomes tolerable when Trump uses the presidency to favor executives, waive costs or elevate share prices. “Free markets” function here less as a governing principle than as a veto against public accountability—one that can be suspended whenever presidential favoritism benefits the correct faction of capital.

Financial ties sharpen the conflict

Reich reports that Huang donated $1 million to Trump’s inauguration and $25 million toward his White House ballroom. He also writes that Trump owns at least $12 million in Nvidia stock.

Those facts do not, by themselves, establish why Trump intervened. They do create glaring conflicts around a presidential decision that could benefit Nvidia and its returning CEO. A president with a substantial reported investment in a company used his office to influence its board after receiving major financial support from the executive he wanted restored. Treating that arrangement as ordinary economic stewardship requires ignoring the incentives in plain view.

The Nvidia episode also fits a broader method of personalized economic management. According to Reich, the Trump administration has taken direct stakes in Intel, critical-minerals producers and L3Harris’s missile business. It granted Apple a China-tariff exemption worth billions of dollars. In the previous year, it also made the federal government a revenue-sharing partner in certain Nvidia chip sales to China.

These interventions are not evidence of an administration opposed to state power in commerce. They show an administration willing to use that power selectively—through ownership, exemptions, revenue agreements, liability protection and pressure on corporate boards. The operative question is who receives the favor and on what terms.

National security becomes negotiable

Trump’s reported conduct does not resemble socialism or communism, despite the labels routinely thrown at policies that subordinate private profit to public objectives. Reich identifies it as crony capitalism: state power arranged around politically connected companies and executives, without a consistent public rule governing who receives protection or punishment.

That distinction matters because the administration’s defenders cannot plausibly claim that markets must remain untouched by government. Trump is touching them constantly. Nor can they credibly argue that national security automatically takes precedence over commerce when his administration reportedly shares revenue from certain Nvidia sales to China and he personally intervenes for an executive facing national-security scrutiny.

The unresolved issue is not whether government should ever influence strategically important industries. It already does. The issue is whether that influence serves a defined public purpose or the financial and political interests clustered around the president.

In Nvidia’s case, Trump supplied the clearest available account of who exercised the decisive power. The company’s board fired Huang. The president called. The board reversed course. Trump then announced that he had “got it done.” The conservative institutions that once presented government noninterference as an American principle have been left with a revealing choice: scrutinize the exercise of presidential power, or admit that their objection was never to government intrusion itself.

item.title: Andrew Weissmann to Trump subpoena dodgers: You can still go to jail
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Trump administration officials who defy congressional subpoenas could still be jailed even if the Justice Department protects them and President Donald Trump promises pardons. Former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann says Congress can ask federal judges to enforce its subpoenas through civil contempt—a coercive process beyond the president’s pardon power. That distinction matters because the conventional enforcement system depends on an executive branch that may have every incentive to shield
item.content:encoded:
Trump administration officials who defy congressional subpoenas could still be jailed even if the Justice Department protects them and President Donald Trump promises pardons. Former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann says Congress can ask federal judges to enforce its subpoenas through civil contempt—a coercive process beyond the president’s pardon power.

That distinction matters because the conventional enforcement system depends on an executive branch that may have every incentive to shield its own officials. Congress can issue demands, but criminal contempt referrals ordinarily pass through the Justice Department. If department leaders refuse to prosecute administration allies, the referral becomes political theater backed by no immediate consequence.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The protection racket built into criminal contempt

Weissmann’s warning came during an appearance with Bulwark publisher Sarah Longwell, following journalist Catherine Rampell’s interview with Rep. Jamie Raskin about prospective House oversight. Rampell asked how Congress could enforce subpoenas against an administration that repeatedly obstructed investigators during Trump’s first term.

The familiar route is criminal contempt. Congress refers a defiant witness to the Justice Department, which can prosecute—as it did with former Trump adviser Steve Bannon. But Weissmann identified two weaknesses that become decisive when the executive branch is protecting the people Congress seeks to investigate.

First, a loyalist Justice Department can decline to prosecute. Second, even a later prosecution under a different administration could be neutralized by a presidential pardon. In that arrangement, the institution under scrutiny controls the machinery used to punish obstruction by its own allies.

“The criminal side is not going to be a particularly useful sort of cudgel to get people to comply,” Weissmann told Longwell. That is less a defect in Congress’s investigative authority than a consequence of relying on executive officials to enforce it.

A court order Trump cannot pardon away

Civil enforcement offers a different route. Congress can sue to enforce a subpoena, obtain a judicial ruling on the witness’s privilege claims and seek a court order requiring testimony or documents. Continued defiance can then expose the witness to civil contempt and confinement.

Civil contempt is not punishment for a completed federal crime. It is pressure intended to secure compliance with a court order. That means a president cannot erase it with a pardon.

A witness jailed on that basis, Weissmann explained, “holds the keys to their jail cell”: comply and the confinement ends. Under the rules he described, a recalcitrant witness may be confined for as long as 18 months or until the relevant proceeding concludes. If a judge determines that confinement is no longer coercive because the witness will not yield, the witness must be released from civil confinement, although separate criminal exposure may remain.

This is not an automatic congressional power to imprison political opponents. Judges would first decide whether the subpoena is enforceable and whether asserted privileges excuse noncompliance. The crucial point is institutional: once a federal court orders compliance, neither a protective attorney general nor a presidential pardon can dissolve the civil order.

The organized-crime precedent

Weissmann drew on his experience prosecuting organized crime in the Eastern District of New York. He cited Domenico Cefalu, a Gambino crime family member who later became the organization’s boss.

After prosecutors granted Cefalu immunity and secured an order compelling his testimony, he still refused to speak. A judge held him in civil contempt, and Cefalu spent the maximum 18 months confined without testifying. Prosecutors subsequently brought criminal contempt charges as well.

The comparison does not make administration officials mobsters. It demonstrates that civil contempt is a functioning judicial instrument, not a speculative loophole invented for a confrontation with Trump. Federal courts have used confinement to compel testimony from witnesses who believed silence was worth the cost.

Oversight requires choosing an enforceable weapon

Weissmann’s proposed strategy would not make congressional oversight quick. Civil litigation can consume time, and judges—not lawmakers—would control whether and how contempt sanctions are imposed. But it would remove two veto points from Trump’s hands: a Justice Department’s refusal to prosecute and the president’s ability to pardon federal crimes.

That is the political meaning of the warning. An administration can turn criminal contempt into an empty threat by capturing the prosecutor and protecting the offender. It cannot, by those means alone, nullify a federal judge’s civil contempt order.

Officials considering blanket defiance would therefore be betting on more than Trump’s protection. They would be betting that Congress declines to seek judicial enforcement, that a court rejects the subpoena, or that they can endure confinement rather than comply. A pardon would not open that cell.
