item.title: Trump snubbed as North Korean dictator rolls out red carpet for 10 nations
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Kim Jong Un did not meet Donald Trump during the U.S. president’s latest trip through Asia. Days later, the North Korean leader personally welcomed ambassadors from 10 countries in Pyongyang, using a revived diplomatic ceremony to make the distinction unmistakable: North Korea is pursuing relationships it considers useful, and Washington is not currently among them. The event was more than an elaborate snub. As reported by The Wall Street Journal from North Korean state media, it presented Kim a
item.content:encoded:
Kim Jong Un did not meet Donald Trump during the U.S. president’s latest trip through Asia. Days later, the North Korean leader personally welcomed ambassadors from 10 countries in Pyongyang, using a revived diplomatic ceremony to make the distinction unmistakable: North Korea is pursuing relationships it considers useful, and Washington is not currently among them.

The event was more than an elaborate snub. As reported by The Wall Street Journal from North Korean state media, it presented Kim as a leader choosing his diplomatic partners from a position strengthened by closer ties with China and Russia—not as an isolated ruler waiting for another summit with an American president.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A selective display of openness

Ambassadors from Russia, Sweden, Vietnam and seven other countries sat in bright red armchairs inside a red-carpeted hall as Kim accepted their credentials. He declared North Korea ready to expand “friendship and cooperation” with countries that respect its sovereignty and behave favorably toward it.

That language made diplomatic access explicitly conditional on Pyongyang’s security interests. Kim did not mention the United States, but the exclusion required little decoding. During a visit to Russia the previous week, senior North Korean official Jo Yong Won accused Washington of an “inveterate hostile policy” and said it was pushing the country’s security environment toward “unpredictable danger.”

Kim also attacked attempts to restrict the rights of sovereign states, a familiar North Korean description of U.S. pressure. The ceremony therefore paired an invitation with a warning: governments willing to engage on Pyongyang’s terms may receive an audience, while Washington’s demand for nuclear concessions no longer guarantees even a meeting.

Sweden’s inclusion gave the spectacle additional weight. The country has historically served as a channel between North Korea and the West and became the first Western nation to return diplomats in September 2024 after Pyongyang’s pandemic border closure drove out most Western embassies and international organizations. Even so, few permanent United Nations personnel have returned. This was not a general reopening so much as a controlled one, with Kim deciding who enters and under what conditions.

Trump’s personal diplomacy lost its leverage

Trump met Kim three times during his first term, turning negotiations over North Korea’s nuclear program into leader-to-leader theater. Those talks collapsed in 2019 without an agreement. Since then, according to the reporting, North Korea has expanded its military and nuclear arsenal and has said it will not resume negotiations unless it is recognized as a nuclear power.

That record undercuts the premise that Trump’s presence in Asia would itself draw Kim back to the table. A summit is valuable to Pyongyang only if it advances Pyongyang’s objectives. Kim has already received the prestige of meetings with a U.S. president; another photo opportunity offers less when Washington is not prepared to grant the status North Korea demands.

The balance around Kim has also changed. He appeared alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at a military parade in Beijing last year. Former South Korean nuclear envoy Lee Do-hoon told the Journal that Chinese and Russian backing leaves Kim with little reason to hurry into another meeting with Trump.

Calling the episode merely a personal “snub” risks reproducing Trump’s preferred understanding of foreign affairs: powerful men exchanging attention, praise and access. The consequential development is not that Kim withheld a meeting from Trump. It is that the United States presently lacks sufficient leverage—or an acceptable offer—to make such a meeting worthwhile to him.

Kim turns protocol into a claim of authority

Sunday’s credential ceremony restored a practice no North Korean ruler had personally performed in decades. Kim Il Sung, North Korea’s founder and Kim Jong Un’s grandfather, routinely received ambassadors. After his death in 1994, that responsibility passed to the head of the legislature. A constitutional change in March returned the power to Kim Jong Un.

The revival consolidates symbolism as well as protocol. Kim was not simply hosting diplomats; he was publicly occupying a function associated with the regime’s founding patriarch and placing himself at the center of North Korea’s selective return to international contact.

State media supplied the imagery and the quotations, so the ceremony should be understood as a managed political presentation. Its intended message was nevertheless clear: North Korea can receive foreign representatives, deepen relationships and stage the rituals of state legitimacy without conceding anything to Washington.

Trump traveled through Asia hoping for another encounter. Kim instead assembled diplomats from 10 other countries and demonstrated that access to him is no longer a prize the American president can presume is available.

item.title: Trump reduced to 'a trapped animal' that everyone can 'manipulate': insider
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Rick Wilson’s “trapped animal” is Donald Trump: a president the former Republican strategist describes as increasingly desperate, poorly guarded and susceptible to anyone who understands his appetites. On the Fast Politics podcast, Wilson argued that Susie Wiles’s ouster as White House chief of staff removed a crucial restraint, leaving Trump more likely to mistake flattery for friendship and branding tricks for policy victories. The claim is not that Trump has lost power. He still commands the
item.content:encoded:
Rick Wilson’s “trapped animal” is Donald Trump: a president the former Republican strategist describes as increasingly desperate, poorly guarded and susceptible to anyone who understands his appetites. On the Fast Politics podcast, Wilson argued that Susie Wiles’s ouster as White House chief of staff removed a crucial restraint, leaving Trump more likely to mistake flattery for friendship and branding tricks for policy victories.

The claim is not that Trump has lost power. He still commands the presidency. It is that the people around him may have become less capable of managing how he uses it—and that domestic politicians and foreign leaders can exploit the resulting weakness.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A president baited by his own name

Wilson and podcast host Molly Jong-Fast pointed to Trump’s unexpectedly warm behavior toward New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed. Jong-Fast suggested Trump has “a strange affinity for charismatic, progressive men,” but the more concrete vulnerability was considerably simpler: Trump likes winners, and he likes seeing his name attached to things.

El-Sayed reportedly demonstrated the point by suggesting that a universal health care proposal could be branded “Trumpcare.” Trump then shared an image of the proposal on Truth Social, provoking anger among MAGA supporters.

“He does like a winner, and he has an even bigger vulnerability for anything with his name on it,” Wilson said. In his telling, Trump “takes the effing bait” because Wiles is no longer present to warn him: “Sir, no, this is a trap, sir.”

That description turns a consequential policy dispute into a story about personal vanity, but it also exposes something more serious. A president’s susceptibility to praise is not merely an embarrassing character defect when a flattering pitch can reach the machinery of the federal government. El-Sayed’s maneuver, as described by Wilson, was clever political salesmanship. Trump’s response suggests that access to presidential attention may depend less on ideology or policy detail than on knowing which ego button to press.

Wiles was a restraint, not the source of authority

Wilson’s account assigns Wiles an important role: she apparently helped Trump recognize or avoid obvious political traps. Her departure, he argued, left no comparable figure capable of interrupting him before impulse became public action.

But that framing can also misdirect responsibility. A chief of staff may control access, impose discipline and warn a president against reckless choices. She does not possess the president’s constitutional authority. If Trump shares a proposal because it bears his name, embraces an adversary’s suggestion because it flatters him or treats powerful foreign leaders as personal friends, those remain Trump’s decisions.

The institutional failure lies partly in a White House built around managing one man’s impulses. A functional presidency should not depend on a single aide repeatedly telling its occupant that praise may be manipulation. Wiles’s reported value was therefore also an indictment of the structure she helped operate: presidential discipline had been outsourced to a gatekeeper, and her removal exposed how little discipline existed beneath it.

Wilson suggested Trump may be reaching for attention-grabbing ideas to escape what he called a punishing cycle of “bad news, doom, depression, failure, foreign espionage” and other crises. That is an interpretation, not an established account of Trump’s motives. But it fits the political behavior Wilson described: a president seeking relief from damaging headlines becomes especially receptive to anyone offering admiration, novelty or a nominal victory.

Foreign flattery carries higher stakes

Wilson saw the same vulnerability during Trump’s recent overseas trip, which ended with a controversial meeting involving Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Trump called the two authoritarian leaders his “friends.”

Friendship language has long allowed Trump to present proximity to powerful rulers as evidence of diplomatic mastery. It can also blur the obvious fact that Xi and Putin lead states with interests that frequently conflict with those of the United States. Their incentives are not personal loyalty to Trump. They are strategic advantage.

“It really struck me how small and desperate he feels now,” Wilson said. He described Trump as diminished from the political figure his opponents had confronted for a decade: “This is now a sort of trapped animal, and he’s getting less impressive by the minute.”

Wilson then supplied the consequential part of the argument. Foreign observers, he said, may now see Trump as “easy to manipulate,” weak and playable. AlterNet’s account provides Wilson’s assessment, not evidence of what Xi, Putin or other foreign officials privately concluded. Still, Trump’s public celebration of them as friends matters because it advertises the personal terms on which he prefers to understand power.

The danger in this reported pattern is not that Democrats have discovered a clever way to sell Trump universal health care. It is that the same president who can be nudged by a flattering label holds authority over diplomacy, national security and the federal government. “Trumpcare” may expose the mechanism almost comically. Xi and Putin have far more consequential reasons to study it.

item.title: Trump humiliated as thousands snub his memecoin gala at his golf club
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump’s latest $TRUMP memecoin gala drew only a couple dozen investors to his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, on Sunday, according to AlterNet—despite invitations reportedly going to thousands. The collapse in attendance tracked the collapse in the product: a token that peaked near $73 after its January 2025 launch was worth roughly 85 cents at the time of the report, leaving investors with enormous losses after Trump had already earned more than $600 million from the venture. A presiden
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump’s latest $TRUMP memecoin gala drew only a couple dozen investors to his golf club in Sterling, Virginia, on Sunday, according to AlterNet—despite invitations reportedly going to thousands. The collapse in attendance tracked the collapse in the product: a token that peaked near $73 after its January 2025 launch was worth roughly 85 cents at the time of the report, leaving investors with enormous losses after Trump had already earned more than $600 million from the venture.

A presidential sales event with few buyers left

The gala was billed as a VIP event for people holding $TRUMP tokens. But the threshold for entry had fallen to as little as $518 invested, AlterNet reported. At the first memecoin dinner in May 2025, attendees needed holdings worth at least $55,000 to qualify.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

That decline measures more than waning enthusiasm. It shows how thoroughly the venture’s hierarchy had inverted. The presidency supplied the brand, Trump’s golf club supplied the venue, and investors supplied the money and market demand. Once the token had lost more than 98 percent of its peak value, the remaining holders were offered another opportunity to gather around the man who had already profited.

Many declined. AlterNet reported that most of the largest stakeholders did not attend, while those who did were initially left outside in the rain because of delays. The Daily Beast reported that guests eventually received bags containing Trump “Victory” perfume, a “Coin Club” bookmark and a $TRUMP-branded hat. The four largest token holders in attendance were awarded 18-karat gold watches; each reportedly had at least $1 million invested.

The gifts preserved the language of exclusivity after the market had stripped away much of its substance. An event once restricted to people with tens of thousands of dollars in tokens was now trying to fill seats with holders of a few hundred dollars’ worth.

The office is part of the product

Kevin O’Leary, former NBA player Tristan Thompson and boxer Floyd Mayweather appeared before Trump entered, according to AlterNet. Trump delivered prepared remarks and then opened the floor to questions.

That scene matters because this was not merely a celebrity promoter tending to a failed endorsement. It was the sitting president appearing at his own property to encourage interest in a financial asset bearing his name—an asset from which he had reportedly made hundreds of millions of dollars while buyers absorbed the crash.

The report does not establish what each attendee paid, when each bought or whether each sold. It does establish the venture’s basic allocation of power and consequence: Trump controlled the political brand and benefited from the token, while holders bore the exposure to its falling price. Calling them “investors” can obscure that asymmetry. They could buy access to the coin and, for some, a room with the president. They could not control the conduct or prestige that gave the token its speculative appeal.

The gala therefore functioned as another sales instrument. Access to presidential attention was not incidental to the commodity; it was among the commodity’s principal attractions.

Musk replaces the missing reckoning

When one attendee asked about Elon Musk—who had reportedly declared himself “not MAGA” after Republican midterm losses—Trump answered with a familiar mixture of praise and insult.

“He’s 80 percent super-genius and 20 percent I refuse to say what that is,” Trump said. “He’s a very unusual guy.”

The exchange gave the room a piece of political theater while diverting attention from the transaction surrounding it. The consequential question at a gathering of battered token holders was not Trump’s latest appraisal of another billionaire. It was why the president was using his office, name and property to sustain interest in an asset that had enriched him as its value disintegrated for buyers.

The sparse crowd supplied its own answer. Whatever loyalty, access or promotional spectacle once drove demand, thousands of invitees reportedly decided the offer was no longer worth accepting. Trump still had the presidency, the golf club and the proceeds. Many of his customers had an 85-cent token—and not even enough interest left to collect the hat.

item.title: 'Big Short' legend names the one thing that could trigger the next meltdown
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Steve Eisman says the next financial rupture could begin with the failure of OpenAI or Anthropic. His argument is not merely that investors have overvalued artificial intelligence, but that a small group of technology companies has built a chain of spending commitments so concentrated that one broken link could halt chip orders, data-center construction and related investment—then push the United States into recession. That is a warning about institutional choices, not technological fate. Execut
item.content:encoded:
Steve Eisman says the next financial rupture could begin with the failure of OpenAI or Anthropic. His argument is not merely that investors have overvalued artificial intelligence, but that a small group of technology companies has built a chain of spending commitments so concentrated that one broken link could halt chip orders, data-center construction and related investment—then push the United States into recession.

That is a warning about institutional choices, not technological fate. Executives, financiers and dominant cloud providers have tied an extraordinary share of corporate spending and market value to two AI developers whose long-term economics Eisman doubts. The risk, in his telling, comes from concentrated power and mutually dependent balance sheets masquerading as broad-based growth.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The boom rewards spending before sustainability

Speaking with Steven Bartlett on The Diary of a CEO, Eisman compared the AI boom with the dot-com bubble. The internet did create vast fortunes and durable infrastructure, he noted, but investors first poured money into young companies with little revenue. Many collapsed. Later companies such as Google inherited infrastructure financed during the wreckage and built successful businesses atop it.

AI may be following that pattern: a consequential technology surrounded by an investment mania. That distinction matters. A bubble does not require the underlying invention to be useless. It requires capital to outrun viable demand.

Eisman described an early phase of “token maxing,” when corporate leaders pushed engineers to use AI services without regard to cost. “I don’t care what the costs are. Just use it,” he said, characterizing the instructions some chief executives gave their employees. According to Eisman, Uber exhausted its AI budget in three months, while some companies spent as much as $500 million before appreciating the scale of their usage.

Those expenses could initially be recorded as evidence of surging demand. But compelled experimentation is not the same thing as stable consumption. When executives order indiscriminate use, providers receive revenue while customers are still discovering whether the product justifies its cost. Eisman said that token maxing stopped during the summer and that cheaper Chinese models began taking market share.

This is the boom’s central misdirection: spending generated by executive mandates is presented as market validation, while the durability of that spending remains unsettled.

Two companies support a much larger chain

At the top sits Nvidia, which Eisman described as the world’s largest company by market capitalization. He said its revenue grew by more than 100 percent in its most recent quarter—a measure of the scale of AI infrastructure spending, but not proof that the pace can continue.

The customer base is heavily concentrated. According to Eisman, five customers provide 70 percent of Nvidia’s revenue. They include Google, Amazon and Microsoft, along with Meta and Oracle. Those corporations have diversified businesses and can absorb substantial investments. But Eisman argued that their AI revenue is itself unusually dependent on OpenAI and Anthropic: roughly 70 percent of the AI revenue generated by Microsoft, Amazon and Google comes from those two developers, he said.

That creates a circular structure. OpenAI and Anthropic pay cloud companies; cloud companies order chips and equipment to fulfill commitments associated with those AI developers; chip sales and data-center construction then bolster the market’s AI growth story. Each layer can appear strong while much of the underlying demand traces back to the same narrow source.

“If either one of these two were to die, the entire chain would stop,” Eisman said. He predicted an immediate recession in that scenario as companies ceased ordering chips and related equipment.

That remains Eisman’s forecast, not an established outcome. But the concentration he describes exposes the weakness beneath claims that AI growth is distributed across the economy. Multiple corporate names do not necessarily mean multiple independent sources of demand.

Wall Street has made concentration look like diversification

The exposure extends far beyond companies branded explicitly as AI businesses. Eisman said technology accounts for 40 percent of the S&P 500. Including communications companies such as Google, Meta and Amazon raises the figure to 50 percent. Adding utilities, investment banks financing the buildout and industrial companies supplying power brings the AI-linked share to 65 percent, by his calculation.

Healthcare and consumer staples are the major sectors he identified as remaining outside the trade.

That composition turns a wager on a developing technology into a marketwide dependency. Investors buying a broad index may believe they are spreading risk across the economy while acquiring extensive exposure to the same capital-spending cycle through chipmakers, cloud providers, utilities, banks and industrial suppliers. Diversification on paper can conceal concentration in practice.

Eisman knows the architecture of such concealment. Recalling the subprime mortgage collapse, which he famously bet against, he said Wall Street had built an industry rewarded for loan volume rather than loan quality. Firms continued originating mortgages because their incentives paid them to keep the machinery running. He said his bet against that system earned about $1 billion.

The AI structure is not identical. Eisman said the dot-com crash primarily harmed investors and technology companies while consumers remained comparatively insulated. His present concern is that AI investment has become too large and too entangled with the broader economy for another collapse to stay contained.

The midterm explanation is missing

Eisman said he had considered betting that the AI bubble would burst, but that the 2026 midterm elections changed his thinking. AlterNet’s account does not explain why the elections altered the wager. The headline’s promised trigger is therefore clearer than the reported political reason for declining—or reconsidering—the bet.

What the interview does establish is Eisman’s preferred failure scenario: one of the two dominant AI developers falters, infrastructure orders freeze, the economy contracts and growth eventually resumes on a sounder footing. He called that the more likely course.

The political calendar may influence when investors expect officials, regulators or corporate leaders to tolerate a correction, but the supplied reporting does not provide Eisman’s reasoning. Inventing one would only replace the market’s speculative story with a political one.

The concrete warning is severe enough without embellishment. Corporate executives and financial institutions have concentrated enormous commitments around OpenAI and Anthropic, while the resulting spending supports much of the valuation attributed to the wider AI economy. If Eisman is right, the next meltdown will not be caused by ordinary users losing interest in a novelty. It will follow from powerful institutions building too much of the economy around two companies—and calling that concentration growth.

item.title: 'Liberal psyops' aren't enough to beat the right-wing media machine
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Democratic National Committee’s FactPostNews operation may make the party quicker at circulating damaging clips of Donald Trump and other Republicans, but it cannot by itself overcome the structural advantage enjoyed by the right. The problem is not merely that Republicans produce more effective propaganda. It is that wealthy owners and concentrated technology platforms exercise disproportionate control over the systems that decide which messages travel, which scandals acquire urgency and wh
item.content:encoded:
The Democratic National Committee’s FactPostNews operation may make the party quicker at circulating damaging clips of Donald Trump and other Republicans, but it cannot by itself overcome the structural advantage enjoyed by the right. The problem is not merely that Republicans produce more effective propaganda. It is that wealthy owners and concentrated technology platforms exercise disproportionate control over the systems that decide which messages travel, which scandals acquire urgency and which conduct becomes background noise.

That distinction matters because a better Democratic content shop is still renting space inside an information economy built and governed by someone else. AlterNet argues that Democrats can compete there only temporarily; changing the balance of power requires antitrust enforcement and regulation aimed at the corporations controlling distribution, surveillance and artificial intelligence.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Trump’s conduct becomes ordinary by repetition

At an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Trump reportedly closed his eyes during a speech by Chinese President Xi Jinping as the moment appeared on a large screen in the media center. Reporters laughed and took photographs. Yet the episode did not generate the kind of sustained American controversy that similar evidence of frailty produced for Joe Biden.

The Bulwark’s Sarah Longwell describes a recurring Trump tactic: take an alleged Democratic vulnerability—Hillary Clinton’s email server, Hunter Biden’s laptop or “sleepy Joe”—then engage in comparable conduct on a scale so large that conventional political discussion cannot process it. In her account, excess itself becomes protection.

That explanation gives too much agency to an abstraction called “the discourse.” News judgment is made by executives, editors, producers, platform owners and ranking systems. They decide what receives repetition and what disappears. Fox News and the right-wing media industry plainly participate in that process, but AlterNet also places Twitter, Meta, TikTok and increasingly CBS News and CNN within a broader apparatus that normalizes Republican framing.

The result is an asymmetry, not collective bewilderment. Biden’s age became a crisis for his presidency and party; Trump’s visible lapses are more readily treated as routine. Americans can consequently encounter Republican descriptions of Democratic positions more often than the positions themselves. AlterNet argues that this distortion materially shaped the 2024 election.

FactPostNews treats attention as political terrain

The DNC’s response has been to turn a campaign project into FactPostNews, a collection of social-media accounts that finds embarrassing or politically damaging Republican footage, presents it in factual packaging and distributes it through allied creators. Writing in Liberal Currents, Denny Carter summarized the purpose without euphemism: “Everything was designed to make Democrats look good and Republicans look bad — you know, the very point of effective propaganda.”

That is a departure for an organization AlterNet characterizes as historically anxious about message discipline and reluctant to give independent creators room to operate. Democratic money continued flowing heavily toward television advertising even as its persuasive reach diminished. FactPostNews at least recognizes that political communication now depends on constant circulation through fragmented networks, not merely a polished commercial purchased every two years.

Calling the project “liberal psyops,” however, risks making a conventional party messaging operation sound more subversive—and more powerful—than the reporting establishes. It is organized persuasion conducted in public through social-media accounts. Its significance lies not in covert sophistication but in the DNC finally accepting that facts do not distribute themselves and that democratic values require advocates capable of telling a coherent story.

Carter proposes one: “Democracy vs. autocracy, dignity vs. oppression, constitutional rule of law vs. totalitarian lawlessness, good vs. evil.” The formulation is blunt because the contest is not a seminar. But even an effective story remains dependent on privately controlled channels that can amplify it, bury it, monetize it or surround it with hostile reinterpretation.

The platform owners had policy interests of their own

AlterNet connects the information imbalance to a more concrete conflict over corporate power. Before the 2024 election, the Biden administration sued Apple over alleged smartphone-market abuses, following cases targeting Amazon and Google for alleged anticompetitive conduct. Biden also issued executive orders addressing concentrated power across the economy. His formulation was straightforward: “Capitalism without competition isn’t capitalism. It’s exploitation.”

His administration similarly pursued restrictions on artificial intelligence, citing risks to privacy, national security, elections and public trust while acknowledging the technology’s potential benefits. Those policies threatened the ambitions and profits of the companies positioned to dominate AI. Kamala Harris represented the prospect that enforcement would continue.

AlterNet argues that technology executives responded by removing platform restraints under the banner of free speech as Harris faced an online environment saturated with abuse. The New York Times, writing in July 2024, described political attacks intensified by prominent politicians, artificial intelligence and a fragmented collection of lightly moderated platforms.

The relationship between those corporate policy interests and Harris’s treatment online is politically important, but the evidence supplied does not establish a coordinated scheme to defeat her. It does establish aligned incentives: executives resisting regulation controlled systems central to the circulation of political information, while one party promised relief from the policies they opposed.

Trump subsequently revoked Biden’s AI rules and allowed the antitrust drive to stall, according to AlterNet. His administration aligned with Silicon Valley during a huge expansion of AI infrastructure. The benefits were concentrated among firms building the technology; the political and environmental costs became increasingly visible as data centers spread.

The tech backlash changed the incentives

AlterNet describes the 2026 midterms as a rejection of both Trump and technology monopolists, with one advocacy organization calling them “the first AI and tech accountability election.” The article points to a rapid change in corporate rhetoric: Elon Musk, after spending half a billion dollars supporting Republican candidates, said he had never been MAGA; Palantir chief Alex Karp emphasized a progressive identity; Sam Altman adopted “human-first” language amid opposition to data centers; and Jeff Bezos was expected to promote green energy as scrutiny of those facilities intensified.

Those reversals do not prove repentance. They show executives responding to a changed political market. When association with Trump offered deregulation and access, they cultivated it. When public anger threatened their businesses, they reached for the language of progress, privacy and environmental responsibility.

Some of AlterNet’s gravest claims remain allegations and predictions. It says Apple and Google executives appeared to have improperly secured tariff exemptions from Trump, and it alleges that Nvidia’s former chief executive collaborated with the Chinese Communist Party in ways that harmed U.S. security. The article also cites a Washington Post report that the Trump administration approved sales of Nvidia AI-chip technology to China in return for a share of the revenue. Those claims require their stated attribution; they should not be converted into settled findings by the force of an editorial argument.

What is clear within the account is that corporate leaders perceived a renewed threat of enforcement. Representative Jamie Raskin introduced the Antitrust Accountability and Transparency Act in October, saying antitrust policy must serve the public rather than conglomerates and well-connected lobbyists. With Raskin set to chair the House Judiciary Committee in January, and Senator Chris Van Hollen promising to prioritize a bipartisan antitrust measure shelved in 2022, the prospect of legislation was no longer abstract. Other congressional Democrats were also preparing bills addressing AI, consumer protection, prices and public trust.

Distribution power is the real prize

The strongest case for antitrust here does not depend on pretending that breaking up technology companies will produce neutral media. No information system is free of institutional choices, economic incentives or political pressure. Antitrust can, however, reduce the ability of a few executives to impose those choices across nearly every channel at once.

That is why FactPostNews is at most an interim tool. Democrats need the capacity to contest lies and circulate evidence in the environment that exists. But if they treat improved propaganda as the final objective, they accept the concentrated structure that makes propaganda so potent—and leave its owners in charge of the terms.

Product-liability rules, AI regulation and antitrust enforcement operate upstream of the next viral clip. They target who owns the channels, who bears the costs of harmful products and whether dominant firms can convert economic control into political leverage. The corporate rush to recover progressive branding suggests that executives understand the danger to their power. Democrats will reveal whether they understand it too when those executives arrive with conciliatory slogans, campaign money and lobbyists asking Congress to leave the machinery intact.

item.title: Trump acting 'like a toddler' with embarrassing new posting 'blitz'
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Donald Trump marked a reported trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin by publishing 26 images that cast the three presidents as a new “Big Three” entitled to shape the world’s future. The “toddler” comparison came from veteran Washington reporter Simon Marks, who described Trump’s Saturday posting spree as the performance of a child returning from a party eager to display his new friends. The mockery is memorable; the underlying politics are more consequential. An American preside
item.content:encoded:
Donald Trump marked a reported trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin by publishing 26 images that cast the three presidents as a new “Big Three” entitled to shape the world’s future. The “toddler” comparison came from veteran Washington reporter Simon Marks, who described Trump’s Saturday posting spree as the performance of a child returning from a party eager to display his new friends. The mockery is memorable; the underlying politics are more consequential. An American president was presenting personal acceptance by two authoritarian leaders as both a diplomatic achievement and a source of his own legitimacy.

A summit inflated into a world order

According to Marks’s analysis for The i Paper, which AlterNet highlighted, Trump filled his Truth Social account with photographs and AI-generated scenes from meetings held on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. The captions repeatedly placed Trump, Xi and Putin together as coequal global figures.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

One post compared their meeting with the 1945 Yalta summit, pairing images of Trump, Xi and Putin with Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin and Franklin D. Roosevelt beneath the caption “The Great Powers 1945, 2026.” Another AI-generated image showed the three contemporary presidents striding together past their national flags, though the synthetic display reportedly included errors in those flags.

The analogy did more than flatter Trump. Yalta involved sweeping decisions by Allied leaders as the Second World War approached its end. Marks reported that the four-point Shenzhen declaration was far narrower. Trump nevertheless promoted the meeting as the beginning of a “G3,” enlarging a limited diplomatic document into the supposed birth certificate of a new great-power directorate.

That substitution—imagery for substance, personal stature for policy—is the central maneuver. The posts offered no need to demonstrate comparable results if Trump could manufacture comparable iconography.

Recognition as presidential currency

Several posts stressed that Xi regarded Trump as an equal, while others attacked Barack Obama’s conduct around foreign leaders as supposedly submissive. The contrast revealed the metric Trump wanted his audience to use: diplomacy judged not by what the United States secured or surrendered, but by whether another powerful man appeared to grant Trump sufficient status.

The Putin material made that politics of recognition even more explicit. Trump published an image labeling the Russian president “My Friend,” which AlterNet reported drew widespread online ridicule as needy and embarrassing.

Marks argued that no other modern American president had treated relations with a foreign leader as a purely personal bond rather than one conducted for the country the president represents. Whatever the historical sweep of that claim, it identifies the institutional distortion visible in the posts themselves. Trump did not advertise a public benefit from friendship with Putin. He advertised the friendship.

That is not merely undignified presentation. When the president depicts diplomacy as a private relationship among dominant personalities, national interests become secondary to his standing within their circle. Xi and Putin lead states with their own strategic objectives. Trump’s feed recast them as characters in a story about Trump being accepted.

Putin withheld the validation

Even the proposed “Group of Three” remained more aspiration than established arrangement in the reporting. When BBC correspondent Steve Rosenberg asked Putin on Friday whether the G3 represented a new mechanism for addressing global problems, Putin replied: “Not yet.”

The answer stopped short of endorsing Trump’s framing while leaving it tantalizingly unresolved. Marks suggested that those two words would encourage Trump to believe the possibility remained open.

That exchange exposes the imbalance beneath the pageantry. Trump devoted a 26-post promotional barrage to declaring the arrival of an exclusive global club; Putin retained the power to decide whether the club existed at all. The American president supplied the ad campaign, the AI mythology and the professions of friendship. His purported friend supplied only “not yet.”

item.title: GOP rebels reject Trump’s hardball ultimatum in bitter RNC power struggle
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republican National Committee members are challenging President Donald Trump’s chosen chairman despite a private warning that Trump could deprive the party organization of his fundraising appearances and the use of his name and likeness. The revolt followed Republicans’ November 3, 2026, midterm losses, when Democrats captured both chambers of Congress, and it has turned January’s RNC leadership vote in Arizona into a test of whether the committee exists to win elections or to protect Trump’s co
item.content:encoded:
Republican National Committee members are challenging President Donald Trump’s chosen chairman despite a private warning that Trump could deprive the party organization of his fundraising appearances and the use of his name and likeness. The revolt followed Republicans’ November 3, 2026, midterm losses, when Democrats captured both chambers of Congress, and it has turned January’s RNC leadership vote in Arizona into a test of whether the committee exists to win elections or to protect Trump’s control of the party machinery.

The challenger is not an anti-Trump outsider. RNC Co-Chair KC Crosbie of Kentucky supports Trump’s agenda and serves within the committee’s leadership. Her offense, in the White House’s view, is contesting the authority of Joe Gruters, the chairman Trump selected in 2025.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

An electoral defeat becomes a loyalty test

Crosbie entered the race two days after the midterms. In a letter to the RNC’s 168 members, she described the results as “a serious setback” and called for “an honest account” of the party’s failures.

That is an ordinary demand after an electoral defeat. Trump and Gruters’ allies have treated it as insubordination.

The Associated Press reported that Trump told members privately he could withhold valuable fundraising appearances and withdraw permission for the RNC to use his name and likeness if they removed Gruters. He reinforced the message publicly on Truth Social, calling Gruters a “MAGA Warrior” and issuing his “Complete and Total Endorsement.”

The distinction between endorsement and ultimatum matters. Trump is entitled to support a candidate. But threatening to withhold assets on which the national party has made itself dependent turns that support into institutional leverage. The arrangement also exposes the weakness Trump’s dominance has created: an organization tasked with electing Republicans can be pressured through access to one politician’s brand.

The dissent is coming from inside Trump’s party

The White House cannot easily dismiss Crosbie’s campaign as a hostile takeover by ideological opponents. The dispute is among Trump supporters, some of whom argue that the committee’s first obligation is winning elections rather than operating as the president’s personal political apparatus.

“There’s a fiction flying around that you’re not allowed to run against anyone endorsed by President Trump. That’s complete nonsense,” Virginia RNC member Patti Lyman told The Washington Post.

There is precedent for defiance. Crosbie defeated Gruters, then backed by Trump, in the 2023 contest for RNC treasurer. That history helps explain why the current challenge is being taken seriously: Trump’s endorsement is powerful inside the committee, but it has not always been decisive.

Crosbie is organizing accordingly. Ahead of the secret-ballot vote at the RNC’s January 2027 winter meeting in Arizona, she circulated an anonymous member survey to inform a proposed reform plan. Rather than building an outside pressure campaign, she is relying on relationships among committee members—the people who will actually cast the ballots.

That strategy keeps the conflict where the power resides. Public loyalty performances may shape the atmosphere, but the chair will be chosen by the committee, in secret, after its members have seen what unquestioned obedience produced at the ballot box.

Party money under scrutiny

The leadership fight also concerns how the RNC uses its resources. Dissident members are seeking a forensic audit of committee spending, moving the argument beyond the midterm result and toward the stewardship of the institution itself.

Federal filings highlighted by The Independent showed that the RNC spent about $59,000 over eight months on “media preparation,” principally hair and makeup services for Trump and administration officials. Members have also questioned the committee’s hiring of the daughter of former White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles.

Gruters defended the media-preparation payments by saying the party covered them so taxpayers would not. That response addresses who did not pay, but it does not settle the committee members’ underlying question: why a political organization funded to elect Republicans assumed those costs, and whether its spending reflects institutional priorities or proximity to the White House.

The audit demand therefore cuts to the structure of Trump’s control. A national committee can remain formally separate from a president while directing money, staffing and organizational attention toward his circle. If members cannot scrutinize those decisions without being accused of disloyalty, accountability has been replaced by personal allegiance.

The machinery of 2028 is at stake

The next chair will oversee consequential parts of the 2028 Republican presidential contest, including party rules, the debate schedule and the nominating calendar. Control of that office is consequently more than a reward for loyal service after a bad election cycle. It can shape the field in which Trump’s successor is chosen.

That makes the White House intervention especially revealing. Trump is not merely defending Gruters’ record. According to the reported private warning, he is using his fundraising value and political identity as bargaining power against the committee members responsible for judging that record.

January’s ballot will not determine whether the Republican Party remains Trump-aligned; both candidates are supporters of his agenda. It will determine something narrower and more concrete: whether RNC members retain enough independent authority to replace a Trump-selected chairman after losing Congress, demanding an audit and being warned that dissent could cost the committee access to the president himself.

item.title: A deadly disease from the past returns — and Trump could make it worse
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: The Trump administration is proposing to keep a stricter silica exposure limit for miners while weakening the monitoring and enforcement needed to make that limit real. The Mine Safety and Health Administration’s plan would give mine operators more control over when workers’ air is tested, tolerate readings above the nominal threshold before imposing fines, and make certain medical examinations voluntary. The result, health and labor advocates warn, could be another generation of miners developi
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration is proposing to keep a stricter silica exposure limit for miners while weakening the monitoring and enforcement needed to make that limit real. The Mine Safety and Health Administration’s plan would give mine operators more control over when workers’ air is tested, tolerate readings above the nominal threshold before imposing fines, and make certain medical examinations voluntary. The result, health and labor advocates warn, could be another generation of miners developing an incurable disease before anyone detects it.

This is not an outbreak from an unknowable source. Black lung is a documented occupational disease caused by inhaling coal dust and fine silica particles. Its resurgence follows failures to control exposure in workplaces governed by mining companies and federal regulators—not bad choices by miners who accepted dangerous work in exchange for a middle-class income.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A protection delayed for half a century

Black lung, formally known as coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, scars and stiffens lung tissue. The disease is progressive, incurable and potentially fatal. Silica particles can penetrate deep into the lungs, causing severe inflammation and, in some cases, progressive massive fibrosis.

During the 1960s and 1970s, as many as one-third of miners with more than 25 years underground tested positive for black lung, according to the National Institutes of Health. Pressure from the United Mine Workers of America helped produce the Federal Coal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969, which mandated regular inspections. Disease rates eventually fell to a historic low in the 2000s.

Then they reversed. Black lung rates have returned to a 50-year high and continue to rise. Research led by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health found increases across every age group, including miners in their 20s and 30s. In federal screenings conducted over the past three years, more than one-third of Central Appalachian miners again tested positive.

The Biden administration responded in 2024 by setting the permissible exposure limit for respirable crystalline silica at 50 micrograms per cubic meter of air, the same threshold used by the Occupational Safety and Health Administration in other industries. Coal companies were supposed to begin complying in April 2025. The rule also covered metal and nonmetal mines extracting products ranging from copper and critical minerals to sand, stone and gravel.

Mining companies challenged the regulation, and a federal appeals court put it on hold while reviewing their claims. Miners therefore remain governed by a framework dating largely to the early 1970s, which effectively permits exposure around 100 micrograms per cubic meter—roughly twice the stricter limit.

The number stays; its enforcement shrinks

MSHA’s proposed revision preserves the 50-microgram figure. That allows the administration to advertise continuity while changing the machinery that determines whether the limit protects anyone.

Brendan Muckian-Bates, a policy analyst with the Appalachian Citizens’ Law Center, told Grist that the revisions could effectively nullify the new standard. The proposal includes a 21 percent testing margin of error, meaning a company would be fined only when a sample exceeds the stated limit by at least that amount. Muckian-Bates said this would functionally allow another 10 micrograms of exposure.

The proposal also removes the requirement that every underground mine conduct air sampling once every six months. Operators would instead evaluate when changing conditions might raise exposure and test “as frequently as necessary.” A company remaining below the enforcement threshold could decide that further sampling was unnecessary and go more than six months without testing.

That arrangement transfers practical authority from a mandatory schedule to the businesses being regulated. The companies that bear the cost and legal risk of unfavorable measurements would gain greater discretion over when those measurements occur.

For new workers at metal and nonmetal mines, the administration would also make medical examinations voluntary rather than mandatory. Advocates and health professionals say those initial exams establish a baseline that can help determine whether lung disease later resulted from workplace exposure. Because silica-related damage may take decades to appear, eliminating a required baseline does not eliminate disease. It makes its occupational origin harder to establish.

“What we have in the pipeline right now is not going to show up until like 20 years later,” Muckian-Bates said. The danger is a cohort of workers becoming ill without knowing it “until it’s too late.”

Deregulation has a price tag—and a beneficiary

MSHA placed the proposal in the Federal Register on November 12 and opened a 60-day public-comment period through January 11, with a virtual meeting scheduled for December 15. The agency did not answer Grist’s questions. A Labor Department spokesperson instead directed interested people to the comment process and said MSHA would review submissions before issuing a final rule.

The administration has been less evasive about the proposal’s governing purpose. In the Federal Register, MSHA said the rule “is expected to be a deregulatory action” and cited President Donald Trump’s executive order, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.”

MSHA estimates that the changes would save the mining industry $28.7 million annually, primarily by reducing monitoring costs. Coal companies would account for $2.43 million of those savings.

That calculation identifies the policy’s immediate winners with unusual clarity. Companies save money when they test less. Workers absorb the uncertainty, and potentially the disease. The savings arrive on corporate balance sheets each year; the lung damage may not become visible for decades.

A flawed rule is still better than the status quo

The choice is complicated by the court-ordered delay. Virginia Tech mining expert Emily Sarver told Grist that the 2024 regulation had enforcement problems, including a sampling system involving numerous laboratories rather than MSHA labs. She described that arrangement as chaotic and said the newer proposal may be preferable to years of continued delay under the inadequate legacy standard.

“I don’t think our current legacy rule is sufficiently protective,” Sarver said. Although the 2024 version appeared stronger on paper, she added, it contained practical problems.

That is a case for fixing implementation, not for handing mine operators broader discretion over exposure monitoring. Yet the litigation and regulatory revision have created a familiar trap: an overdue protection is suspended, then its weaknesses are invoked to justify a more industry-friendly replacement while workers remain exposed under rules rooted in the Nixon era.

John Robinson knows what that delay means in a human body. Diagnosed with black lung at 47 after working in Virginia mines, he is now 60 and serves as vice president of the National Black Lung Association. His wife, Vonda Robinson, is the organization’s president.

John Robinson described an industry that recruits workers with good wages, then discards them when illness leaves them unable to work. He and Vonda intend to continue pressing for stronger protections even if the changes come too late to help older miners.

“If us older coal miners don’t get nothing out of this,” he said, they may still help those coming behind them—the workers who could become “extremely sick.”

Black lung’s return is not history mysteriously repeating itself. Regulators already know the contaminant, the exposure pathway, the required limit and the consequences of waiting. The unresolved decision is whether a federal safety rule will constrain the companies producing the hazard, or merely preserve a protective number while letting those companies decide how often anyone checks.

item.title: Trump staffer accidentally leaks Smithsonian overhaul plan — on the DC Metro
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: A White House policy aide exposed a draft plan to seize tighter political control of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History by displaying it on his laptop aboard Washington’s Metro. The aide was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser on President Donald Trump’s Domestic Policy Council. According to reporting published by AlterNet, a fellow passenger photographed the document and sent the images to ProPublica, revealing proposals to purge museum leaders, dictate exhibits
item.content:encoded:
A White House policy aide exposed a draft plan to seize tighter political control of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History by displaying it on his laptop aboard Washington’s Metro. The aide was Sam Bock, a 27-year-old associate policy adviser on President Donald Trump’s Domestic Policy Council. According to reporting published by AlterNet, a fellow passenger photographed the document and sent the images to ProPublica, revealing proposals to purge museum leaders, dictate exhibits and rewrite educational material around the administration’s preferred version of patriotism.

The accidental disclosure is embarrassing. The substance is more serious: an administration campaign against alleged “ideological capture” appears to contemplate replacing the museum’s professional judgment with White House ideological supervision.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

A political purge disguised as renewal

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” contained 25 proposed actions. Among them were the removal of museum director Anthea Hartig and roughly a dozen other senior administrators and curators. The draft also envisioned permanent exhibitions called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance” and “Great Families of American History,” along with a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum entrance.

Those are not modest corrections to a curatorial program. Combined with the proposed firings, they describe an effort to determine who may interpret American history and what conclusions visitors should be encouraged to draw from it.

Some language remained conspicuously unfinished. Handwritten notes included “announce exciting cool exhibit on D-Day” and “no X rated exhibitions policy.” Another curriculum proposal offered two possible titles—“Architects of Liberty” or “Profiles in Liberty”—for lessons centered on Washington and other “Heroic Men of Courage.” The phrasing suggests a political branding exercise still under construction, but the institutional target was already clear.

The White House did not answer questions about the draft. Bock, a former staffer for Ohio Republican Rep. Jim Jordan, also did not respond, and the Smithsonian declined to comment. The available reporting therefore does not establish which proposals received final approval. It does establish that an adviser in the White House office responsible for the administration’s Smithsonian campaign possessed a detailed overhaul plan.

From denunciation to control

The draft follows months of organized pressure. On July 4, the White House released a 162-page attack accusing the history museum of promoting “radical activist ideology.” Congress then held two hearings, and Trump issued an executive order requiring signs outside the museum warning visitors about its supposed “ideological capture.”

Those signs had not yet appeared when the draft was photographed in late October. But the campaign had already helped drive Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie Bunch from his post, according to the reporting. The proposed next phase would go beyond public denunciation by changing personnel, exhibits, grants, traveling programs and classroom materials.

The plan called for abandoning a diversity style guide, reconsidering grants to organizations labeled “woke third parties” and halting the traveling exhibition “The Bias Inside Us.” It also proposed eliminating the online immigration module “Becoming US” and replacing it with a founders-centered curriculum explicitly described as aligned with “patriotism, not ideology.”

That opposition is itself ideological. “Patriotism” does not become politically neutral because the White House uses it as a label. Here it functions as an instruction about emphasis: elevate heroic founders and inherited Western greatness while removing material the administration associates with diversity, immigration and structural inequality.

The administration’s earlier report claimed that museums should include slavery and Jim Crow rather than whitewash them. It argued that the Smithsonian had failed to explain how the United States developed into its present form. But the leaked draft shows how quickly a demand for the “whole story” can become a mechanism for disciplining those who tell it. Firing curators and prescribing heroic themes does not broaden historical inquiry. It establishes political boundaries around it.

Federal funding supplies the leverage

The Smithsonian is designed to retain institutional independence, but that independence has an obvious vulnerability: the federal government supplies most of its funding, exceeding $1 billion annually. Its leadership is also unusually exposed. Bunch has departed, the institution must choose his successor, and vacancies have accumulated on its 17-member governing board as private members’ terms expire without replacements.

The board includes the chief justice, the vice president, six members of Congress divided between the parties and nine private citizens selected by other board members. That structure was meant to insulate the institution from direct presidential command. Money, vacancies and leadership turnover nevertheless give the executive branch substantial leverage even without formal authority to dictate every curatorial decision.

Before Trump tried to remove National Portrait Gallery director Kim Sajet last year, no president had attempted to fire a Smithsonian executive. The institution resisted that intervention, although Sajet ultimately left. The draft plan’s proposed removal of Hartig and numerous senior employees would turn an exceptional incursion into a governing method.

The museum is not beyond criticism. Since opening in 1964, it has repeatedly struggled over how to tell a coherent national story without flattening a vast and divided country. A commission in 2001 urged a more unified narrative and fewer concessions to political correctness. After George Floyd’s murder in 2020, Bunch led a Smithsonian-wide reassessment that gave the returning Trump administration material it could attack.

The White House highlighted, among other examples, staff training material that linked museums to white supremacy, colonialism, labor abuse and the theft of cultural objects. It criticized a Ben Franklin exhibition for speculating that enslaved members of his household may have been subjected to electrical experiments. Congressional outrage also centered on a gay-history display containing a chrome-and-rubber sadomasochistic harness, apparently the inspiration for Bock’s handwritten “no X rated exhibitions” proposal.

Each subject can be debated on its merits. But the administration’s response is not merely to criticize disputed choices or commission different scholarship. The draft proposes removing officials, stopping exhibitions and imposing interpretive rules from the White House. It uses selected provocations as justification for authority over an institution holding millions of artifacts and serving nearly 2 million visitors a year.

The leak’s Metro setting makes for an absurd Washington anecdote: a sensitive political blueprint exposed by a careless staffer in a gray tartan suit. Yet concentrating on Bock’s operational incompetence would miss the consequential disclosure. The document he left visible describes a presidency trying to convert control over funding and appointments into control over national memory—and calling that conversion “renewal.”

item.title: Bob Woodward tears into Trump with devastating comparison
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos

item.content:encoded:
Bob Woodward’s comparison is blunt: Donald Trump is “worse, much worse than Nixon.” His case rests not on temperament or aesthetics, but on two exercises of presidential power—Trump’s reported personal enrichment while in office and his decision to wage war against Iran. Woodward argues that the corruption is embedded, the aggression was avoidable, and Trump’s advisers have encouraged rather than restrained him.

Corruption measured in billions

Speaking with Axios co-founder Mike Allen on The Axios Show, Woodward said Trump had made billions of dollars while serving as president. He contrasted that scale of enrichment with an earlier political culture in which even accepting a free flight on someone else’s jet could provoke scandal.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

Woodward called Trump’s corruption “deep and embedded.” That distinction matters. His indictment is not that Trump occasionally crossed an ethical line; it is that the presidency and the president’s financial interests have become entangled on a scale Woodward considers historically exceptional.

The Nixon comparison carries particular authority because Woodward, alongside Washington Post reporter Carl Bernstein, exposed the Watergate scandal that helped drive Nixon from office in 1974. But biography is not proof, and Woodward does not ask readers to rely on biography alone. He identifies the conduct behind his verdict: immense reported gains by a sitting president and a war launched against a country that had not attacked the United States.

A war sold as presidential strength

Woodward said the defining event of Trump’s presidency may be the Iran war. He described the attack as unprovoked aggression and “a mistake,” while acknowledging that Iran is “an unsavory country.”

That qualification dismantles a familiar pretext for war: treating another government’s brutality as sufficient authorization for an American attack. As Woodward observed, applying that standard consistently would leave the United States at war almost perpetually. The relevant question is not whether Iran’s government deserves approval. It is whether its character justified Washington bringing US military force against it.

Trump has offered a radically different account. In a June appearance on The Axios Show, he presented the conflict as evidence of his power, saying there were “no limits” to it. He also claimed that his dealmaking had prevented a “worldwide depression.”

The contrast is revealing. Woodward evaluates the war through the decision to attack and the consequences that followed. Trump describes it as a demonstration of personal strength. In that framing, military violence becomes presidential branding, and the destruction borne by people beyond Washington’s reach is pushed outside the picture.

Advisers who “feed the beast”

Woodward also distinguished the machinery surrounding the two presidents. Nixon, he said, had Cabinet officials who attempted to stop wars. Trump’s administration, by comparison, is “feeding the beast” by encouraging aggression.

That does not absolve Trump, who holds the authority and owns the decision. It identifies the broader power structure that makes escalation easier: senior officials who could impose friction instead reinforcing the president’s impulses. An administration without meaningful internal restraint does not merely reflect its leader. It expands his capacity to inflict damage.

Woodward reached the same broad judgment in his 2024 book War, concluding there as well that Trump was worse than Nixon. The present comparison sharpens the basis for it. Nixon’s criminal abuse of office remains the benchmark, but Woodward argues that Trump has surpassed him through the combination of financial self-interest, military aggression and an official circle unwilling to check either.

The costs outside Washington

The war’s effects are still unfolding in Iran. President Masoud Pezeshkian said US and Israeli attacks on the country’s gas infrastructure eliminated 240 million cubic meters of daily production capacity. According to Pezeshkian, only about 100 million cubic meters had been restored as Iran prepared for a worsening winter shortage.

Those figures describe more than damaged facilities. They point to an energy deficit confronting civilians during winter, long after the attacks that produced it. Trump’s language of limitless power omits that consequence, as boasts about force usually do.

Woodward’s comparison is therefore devastating for a specific reason. Nixon’s downfall established that presidential power could be abused for political survival. Woodward argues that Trump has joined personal enrichment to war-making while surrounded by officials who encourage escalation. The immediate result is not an abstract debate over historical ranking. It is an Iranian gas system still operating far below the capacity destroyed by American and Israeli attacks—and a president presenting that wreckage as proof of his strength.

item.title: Sony CEO explains why a $250M ad blitz couldn’t save GOP’s box office bomb
item.dc:creator: Paulo Santos
item.description: Republicans could buy saturation, but they could not buy an audience. After Elon Musk reportedly spent roughly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates—and after the party outspent Democrats on Senate advertising by more than $250 million by late October—Republicans still suffered major defeats, including Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s resounding loss. item.content:encoded:
Republicans could buy saturation, but they could not buy an audience. After Elon Musk reportedly spent roughly half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates—and after the party outspent Democrats on Senate advertising by more than $250 million by late October—Republicans still suffered major defeats, including Texas Senate nominee Ken Paxton’s resounding loss. Sony chief executive Rothman’s explanation is blunt: money cannot rescue a political product voters do not want, especially when the campaign has no persuasive message and delivers its attacks through obsolete channels.

A financial advantage mistaken for political power

Writing in The New York Times, Rothman compared the Republican campaign to a failed movie launch. “Spending money, even tens or hundreds of millions of dollars, without a message that spurs people to action is like lighting the cash on fire,” he wrote.

Help fuel the work. Independent analysis doesn’t fund itself:
☕ Buy us a coffee

The distinction matters. Wealth can purchase airtime, consultants and repetition. It cannot guarantee that voters will accept what they are being sold. Republicans treated their overwhelming financial advantage as if exposure itself were persuasion. According to Rothman, Democrats instead prevailed through stronger messages and campaigns rooted in recognizable communities.

He pointed to Democratic victories by Annie Andrews in South Carolina, Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and Gina Hinojosa in Texas, along with Mary Peltola’s win in Alaska. Peltola’s “Fish, Family, Freedom” slogan compressed local identity and political appeal into three memorable words. Julia Letlow, meanwhile, narrowly became the first Republican woman elected to represent Louisiana in the Senate, evidence that the lesson is not simply that one party possesses an automatic communications advantage. Candidates still have to give particular voters a reason to choose them.

That is what the spending numbers obscure. The institutional power belonged to the billionaires, party committees and campaign professionals deciding where the money went and what it said. Voters were not confused by failing to obey the advertising imbalance. The people controlling Republican resources made an expensive strategic choice, and the candidates bore the consequence.

Republicans flooded a shrinking channel

Rothman also identified a basic failure of distribution. Republicans concentrated heavily on conventional television advertising in Texas and Ohio, even as audiences have fragmented across digital and social platforms. At Sony, he wrote, five employees now work in digital and social marketing worldwide for every one assigned to legacy media.

Viewers of the Ohio State and University of Texas football games on the Saturday before the election were bombarded with negative advertisements targeting Sherrod Brown and James Talarico. Both men nevertheless became senators-elect by comfortable margins.

The failure was not a shortage of attacks. It was the assumption that repeatedly placing those attacks in front of a large television audience would produce the intended political response. Republican strategists used the mechanics of mass broadcasting long after mass attention had splintered—and relied on negativity without establishing a compelling affirmative case.

That makes the “box office bomb” comparison more than a Hollywood flourish. A studio can saturate television with trailers, but it cannot compel people to buy tickets. A political donor can dominate the airwaves, but not dictate how citizens interpret the pitch. Musk’s reported spending bought extraordinary access to voters’ screens. It did not buy their allegiance.

The post-defeat scramble for an explanation

Donald Trump reportedly responded to the midterm setbacks by moving between denial and anger. That reaction shifts attention away from the decisions that produced the losses: candidates selected, messages approved, media purchased and a governing brand that money alone could not make attractive.

An emerging argument that the United States is returning to “four-party politics” offers another way to interpret the result. Catholic University professor emeritus John Kenneth White described Democrats as divided between moderates—whom he credited as the 2026 majority-makers—and socialists seeking a larger government. Republicans, in his account, are splitting between Trump loyalists and Reagan-era conservatives.

That framework may describe genuine ideological tensions, but it does not erase the immediate verdict delivered by the campaigns themselves. Republicans possessed the larger advertising arsenal and deployed it according to a dated theory of voter behavior. Democrats, Rothman argued, more effectively matched message, candidate and audience.

The revealing fact is not that money suddenly stopped mattering. It plainly determined who could blanket major broadcasts and who could afford a quarter-billion-dollar Senate advertising advantage. The limit appeared elsewhere: concentrated wealth could amplify the Republican message, but it could not make that message persuasive. Republicans did not lose because voters somehow failed to notice them. They spent lavishly to ensure voters did—and many voters rejected what they saw.
